# Bugs

What is wrong, and what would prove it is not.

**The checkboxes are derived, not typed.** Every entry names the regression
test that must exist for the bug to be closed, and
`python3 scripts/bugs.py sync` resolves that against
`.claude/codemap/map.json` and rewrites the mark.

| | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `[ ]` | open — the test does not exist, or does not resolve |
| `[x]` | fixed — every named test resolves |

Deleting the test reopens the bug on the next run. That is the property worth
having: a bug marked fixed with nothing guarding it is worse than an open bug,
because it stops anyone looking.

**Placement is derived too.** Open entries live under `## Open`, fixed ones
below the rule under `## Fixed`, and `sync` moves them — so the top of the file
is always what is still wrong, however long the file gets. That was written down
as already true for a while before it was: `## Fixed` carried the sentence
"entries move here when sync closes them" while sync only ever rewrote a
checkbox in place, so closed bugs piled up at the top and the section meant to
hold them stayed empty. Both sections are sorted newest first.

Ids are checked for **reuse**, because an id is how a bug is cited from a test
name, a design doc and a commit message. Eight collisions were sitting in here
when that check was added — four of them entire entries duplicated verbatim,
one symptom filed twice with different evidence, and two genuinely different
bugs sharing a number.

**And ids are now issued rather than counted.** Detecting reuse never prevented
any: an author read this file, took the highest number in it and added one,
which is *the same number* on two branches that both started from `main`. Six
bugs and three questions were renumbered by hand in the six days to 2026-08-14,
one of them twice because the second guess collided too. So `bugs.py new`
allocates above every branch the clone can see, `ids` reports a number two
branches have taken before the merge that would prove it, and `ids --fix` moves
this branch's entry and the citations this branch wrote for it.

An entry with no `evidence:` is **refused at check time**. If you cannot name
what would prove the fix, you have not finished describing the bug.

`evidence: manual` is the one exception, for bugs no headless test can reach —
synthetic pen and hover input through Xvfb is unreliable here. Those never
auto-close; a human verifies and ticks the box. Reach for it rarely: it is the
only place in this file where a claim is the best evidence available.

**A report from outside this repo's tooling — a person, or an agent that has
not read this file — goes to `INBOX.md`, not here.** It cannot know a real
test name or a free id, so an entry it writes directly would either fail
`bugs.py check` or accidentally resolve against the wrong test. A periodic
session formalizes each inbox entry into a real one, following the rules
above, and deletes it from the inbox once it does.

```bash
python3 scripts/bugs.py new canvas "Onion tint floods on pan" -p P1 -e OnionTintTests
python3 scripts/bugs.py freeid question # the next free Q id, for a question you write by hand
python3 scripts/bugs.py ids --fix      # move an id two branches took; citations follow
python3 scripts/bugs.py check          # status; exits 1 on drift, a reused id or missing evidence
python3 scripts/bugs.py sync           # rewrite the marks and re-sort open above fixed
python3 scripts/bugs.py next           # highest-priority open bugs
python3 scripts/bugs.py mine timeline  # open bugs in one domain
python3 scripts/bugs.py stats          # counts per priority and domain
```

## Priority — severity × reach

|  | every session | common | occasional | rare |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **blocks work** | P1 | P1 | P2 | P2 |
| **corrupts art** | P1 | P1 | P2 | P3 |
| **wrong output** | P2 | P2 | P3 | P3 |
| **annoyance** | P3 | P3 | P4 | P4 |

*Corrupts art* outranks *wrong output* because a wrong render is visible and
recoverable; a damaged record is neither.

**Cost is not in the matrix, on purpose.** It is recorded on each entry so a
session with ten spare minutes can pick a cheap P2 over an expensive one, but
it never changes the order — folding effort into the rank is how the hard,
important bugs never get picked.

## Domains

One tag per bug, from this list, so an agent about to edit an area can find
what is already known to be wrong in it:

`brush` · `timeline` · `layers` · `canvas` · `transform` · `colour` ·
`export` · `project` · `ui` · `ai`

**The rule for an agent working in a domain:** fix its open **P1 and P2** bugs
alongside whatever you came for, each with its own regression test in the same
commit. Mention P3 and P4 without touching them — a request to change one
thing must not come back as a diff touching six. Anything needing a product
decision goes to `QUESTIONS.md` and is left alone.

---

## Open

**Sweep of `evidence: manual`, 2026-08-12.** Seventeen open entries carried it,
which is more than half the open list — and an entry carrying it **cannot close
itself**, because `bugs.py sync` has nothing to resolve. Two were already fixed
and simply never ticked (B144, B78); one had been fixed and then quietly
un-fixed (B32). That is a measurable part of why the list looked like it only
grew. The triage, so nobody re-derives it:
| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Fixed, now closed** | B144 (derived budget), B78 (suggested name) |
| **Was fixed, then undone** | B32 — the server publishes self-contained again, deliberately; see its entry |
| **Open, and `manual` is right** | B60 (needs the halo), B93 (a harness race is the thing being asked for), B126, B170, B179 (need the owner's machine), B178 |
| **Open, multi-phase, work in flight** | B29, B30, B125, B165, B166, B167 |
| **Open, not yet examined** | B92, B101 |
**The lesson is about the marker rather than about these seventeen.**
`evidence: manual` means *no test can hold this*, and it is honest for a platform
crash or an intermittent harness race. It is not honest for a fix nobody wrote a
test for — the two look identical in the file and only one of them belongs.
Before writing `manual`, the question is whether a test is *impossible* or merely
*absent*. B78's new guard reads the source rather than driving a file dialog,
which is a weak test and still far better than none.

### ai

- [ ] **B32** `P3` `ai` A third of the Windows download is a second copy of .NET, because the MCP server targets net10.0 `evidence: manual`
  - Repro: publish both projects as CI does and measure. **286 MB on disk, 105 MB zipped** — of which the app is 69.5 MB and `mcp/` is **35.3 MB**, a full second self-contained runtime.
  - It is not accidental duplication that a shared output folder would fix. `Lightbox.App` targets `net8.0` and `Lightbox.Mcp` targets **`net10.0`** (with `Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting 10.0.10`), so of the 224 files in `mcp/`, **182 have the same name as one in the parent and different contents** and only 2 are byte-identical. They are genuinely two runtimes.
  - Nothing chose this: `CLAUDE.md` says the project is .NET 8, and the TFM has read `net10.0` since the commit that created the project. Every other project in the solution is `net8.0`.
  - Fix: move `Lightbox.Mcp` to `net8.0` and publish it into the *same* folder as the app, so the runtime is shared. Saves roughly a third of every download and a third of every CI artifact. Needs checking that `ModelContextProtocol` 1.4.1 supports `net8.0` and that the two `runtimeconfig.json`/`deps.json` pairs coexist — they have distinct names, so they should. Cost: S
  - P3 because it costs bandwidth and storage rather than correctness. It moved up the list when the artifact quota filled: at 105 MB a build a free account's whole 500 MB allowance is four builds, and this is 35 MB of each one.
  - **The fix above is now one of two, pointing opposite ways, and the choice is not this entry's to make.** Moving the whole solution *up* to `net10.0` removes the duplication from the other end — one runtime because everything targets it — and buys the support window with it, .NET 8 leaving support in November 2026. Assessed in `docs/DESIGN-net10-upgrade.md`; the part that needs a human is **Q19**, because a `net10.0` self-contained Linux build raises the minimum glibc from 2.23 to 2.27 and nobody has written down who runs this. Downgrading the MCP server stays the right *interim* move if the upgrade grows a test-stack migration — the measured 35 MB a build is real either way, and this entry should not sit open waiting on a decision it does not depend on.
  - **The upgrade landed, and it retires the second bullet above rather than this bug.** Every project targets `net10.0` now, so "they are genuinely two runtimes" is no longer true — they are two copies of the *same* runtime, which is exactly the accidental duplication that bullet ruled out. A shared output folder now would fix it, and the `net8.0` half of the prescribed fix is moot.
  - **What is left is a user-visible path change, which is why it did not ride along with the TFM bump.** `build.yml` publishes the app to `publish/win-x64` and the server to `publish/win-x64/mcp`, both `--self-contained true`, so the duplication is the folder split rather than the framework. Publishing both into the same folder shares the runtime — the two `runtimeconfig.json`/`deps.json` pairs have distinct names and coexist — but it moves the executable from `mcp\Lightbox.Mcp.exe` to `Lightbox.Mcp.exe`, and that path is documented in `README.md` as the Claude Desktop `command` and checked in `MANUAL_TESTING.md`. Every existing config points at the old one. So the remaining work is the publish path, both documents, and a note for anyone upgrading — small, but not the same change as a TFM bump, and bundling it would have put a broken MCP config and a migrated render path in one diff.
  - **Correction, 2026-08-12: the paragraph below no longer describes the build, and this entry stays open because of it.** `release.yml` publishes the app to `publish/win-x64` and the server to `publish/win-x64/mcp`, **both `--self-contained true`** — so there are still two copies of the runtime in the download. The workflow says why, and the reasoning is sound rather than an oversight: *"a self-contained executable only ever looks for its runtime beside itself — there is nothing left for the two publishes to share."* So the merge that closed this was undone deliberately, and what remains is the original question of whether the server needs to be self-contained at all. Found by a sweep of entries carrying `evidence: manual`, which is exactly the failure that kind of entry hides: nothing re-checks a claim no test holds.
  - **Fixed, and measured rather than reasoned about.** Both projects now publish into `publish/win-x64`. The prediction that the merge is safe was checked by running it instead of trusting it: both executables survive, `Lightbox.App.deps.json`/`.runtimeconfig.json` and `Lightbox.Mcp.deps.json`/`.runtimeconfig.json` all four coexist, and the server contributes **4 MB and 36 files** where it used to carry 35.3 MB. The bundle goes **286 MB → 216 MB on disk and 105 MB → 74 MB zipped**, which is better than the "roughly a third" the original estimate claimed and is now the figure `README.md` quotes.
  - The config break is accepted rather than worked around — this is a single-developer alpha, so "every existing config" is one, and the owner said they would reconfigure. `README.md` carries an upgrade note anyway, because the failure mode is silent: Claude Desktop does not report a bad `command`, the server just never starts and the tools are quietly absent.
  - **Why `evidence: manual` stays.** Nothing headless can open the Windows bundle and ask Claude Desktop whether it launched. The verification that exists is the publish measurement above and the `MANUAL_TESTING.md` line, which now names the new path explicitly so the check cannot pass by reading the old one.
  - **Half of this is reversed by B116, and the trade is re-made knowingly rather than lost.** The shared root that removed the second runtime is also what put 266 files in front of the executable, which is what B116 is about. Single-file publishing ends the sharing by construction: the app's runtime now lives *inside* `Lightbox.App.exe`, so there is nothing in the folder left for the server to share and it carries its own wherever it sits. The server goes back to `mcp/`.
  - **What that actually cost, measured rather than predicted — and the prediction was wrong by an order of magnitude.** The duplicated runtime was expected to put the download back at ~105 MB, which the owner accepted in advance. It did not: **216 → 180 MB on disk and 74 → 76 MB zipped**, because the same change stops shipping 105 MB of native debug symbols (`libSkiaSharp.pdb` at 84 MB, `libHarfBuzzSharp.pdb` at 21 MB) which no publish ever needed. The duplicate runtime is very nearly paid for by symbols nobody wanted. Note the 74 MB re-measures this entry's own figure exactly, which is the reason to trust the pair.
  - **So the fix written in this entry must not be re-applied.** Anyone finding B32 open and reaching for "merge the folders" would re-create B116. The two are only jointly satisfiable if somebody solves the root count another way first; there is no version of this where a shared loose runtime and a four-file root both hold.

### brush

- [ ] **B322** `P1` `brush` A brush with an effect shows the mark as of the last pass, so its tip is missing while the pen moves `evidence: manual`
  - **THE REPEATED STALLING IS THIS ENTRY, AND IT TOOK AN INSTRUMENT THAT MEASURES ABSENCE RATHER THAN SLOWNESS TO SEE IT.** 2026-08-28 00:06, on the owner's observation that the preview stalled several times in a session whose build census found one stall, and their suggestion that the others *"perhaps had another cause and were not reported as a stall per se"*. Counting the moments the mark stopped moving under the pen instead of the frames that took too long to make:

    ```
    the preview stopped 24 times while the pen was down:
           at    gap ms   points  outstanding   why
         28.1 s      3086        1            0   publish gapped
         28.3 s        16       59           94   TIP REFUSED (frame was on time)
         28.7 s       173      140          106   TIP REFUSED (frame was on time)
         29.4 s        73      266           51   publish gapped
    >> 18 of 24 were the tip being REFUSED, not a slow frame.
    ```

    **Eighteen of twenty-four, on frames that were never late.** They carried a mark that had stopped growing, which no timer on the build can see — which is exactly why a build census counted one stall in a session the artist experienced as stalling repeatedly, and why five days of timing work never found it.
  - **And the outstanding counts are the finding within the finding.** The refusals land at **16 to 168 dabs outstanding**, over a stroke only 266 points long. That is not a fast stroke with a huge backlog; it is an ordinary one. On the document-resolution arm the budget is 3 ms over the ~55 us a dab measured in situ — **about 55 dabs** — so a run of sixty refuses. On the preview arm the same 3 ms buys **about 190** at the measured 15.8 us, which covers all but two rows of that table. **The arm the owner could not tell apart by eye should erase three quarters of these**, and nothing had measured the right quantity to say so until now.
  - **THE ARMS WERE CAPTURED, THE CHEAPER ONE WORKS, AND THE ARTIST CANNOT TELL THEM APART. 2026-08-27 22:52-22:59.** Four captures, the same build, the flag the only difference:

    | | arm | drawn | too far behind | us a dab | budget buys | restamp median |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 22:52 | document | 497 of 660 | 163 — **25%** | 39.8 | 75 | 0.41 ms |
    | 22:53 | document | 660 of 786 | 126 — **16%** | 53.4 | 56 | 0.43 ms |
    | 22:59 | document | 406 of 519 | 113 — **22%** | 60.3 | 49 | 0.80 ms |
    | **22:57** | **preview** | **533 of 590** | **57 — 9.7%** | **15.76** | **190** | **0.12 ms** |

    Refusals roughly halved and the stamp got **3.4x** cheaper, exactly as the offline measurement predicted. The owner: *"for both arms the preview did still jump"*, and *"I wasn't able to feel or see any discernable difference between A & B."*
  - **So the entry's premise is wrong, and this is the finding of the whole three days.** B322 assumed the jump the artist feels is the missing tip. **It is not.** Every capture carries a `building each frame` **worst of 3.2 to 6.4 seconds** against a median of 2 ms — a UI-thread stall two thousand times the typical frame, on a pen delivering every 5 ms. A preview drawn on 90% of publishes cannot help a mark that freezes for six seconds and then arrives in one step. **B332** carries the mechanism: a frame-cache miss renders the whole frame synchronously on the calling thread.
  - **The in-app estimator agreed with the offline one, which is worth keeping.** 39.8, 53.4 and 60.3 us a dab across three captures at document resolution, against the offline 45-50; and 15.76 at preview resolution against the offline 11. Two methods, different machines-states, same order. **The measurement work in this entry is sound** — it was aimed at the wrong quantity, which is a different failure from measuring badly and the one nobody caught for three days.
  - **What that leaves for B322 itself.** The machinery is finished, tested, and demonstrably does what it claims: the newest dabs reach the screen on 84-90% of publishes where they previously did not at all, and the preview arm makes that cheap enough to be worth keeping. What it does not do is fix what the owner reported, because that was never this defect. **Q170 is answered by the capture rather than by the eye: no discernible difference, so the resolution seam costs nothing visible** and the cheaper arm is free headroom. Whether it becomes the default is still the owner's call, and it should be made knowing it buys margin rather than a fix.
  - **THE PREMISE OF THE SEVENTH ATTEMPT WAS WRONG, AND THE ESTIMATE WAS RIGHT ALL ALONG.** This entry has recorded three arithmetic errors in the per-dab cost and the session of 2026-08-27 18:00 was briefed to expect a fourth. There is not one. The owner's capture of 17:26 — **all fast strokes**, size 70+ — reported `live tip drawn 11 of 23, too far behind 12` with **87.46 us a dab (marginal)**, and that figure is very nearly correct. `LiveTipDabCostTests` stamps the same `BrushEngine.StampDabRange` call outside the application, in Release, on the owner's 3840x2160 document: a size-70 wet dab costs **about 45-50 us at the margin** over a fixed 0.15-0.33 ms an operation. The application's 87.46 is that cost seen through 3- and 15-dab stamps, which is all its own budget of 34 ever admitted, **and through a machine that is never idle**. **Two independent measurements agree to within the load between them.**
  - **So the constant was never the bug — the dab is genuinely that dear, and no budget covers a fast stroke at size 70.** Against the capture's own numbers:

    | | dabs | at 45.4 us + 0.33 ms | of a 44 ms publish cycle |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | outstanding, median | 268 | **12.5 ms** | 28% |
    | new dabs, p90 | 582 | 26.7 ms | 61% |
    | outstanding, p90 | 2072 | **94.4 ms** | 215% |

    A 3 ms budget buys **59 dabs**; 6 ms buys 125. This is the outcome the entry named in advance — *"if the measured cost says covering fast strokes is unaffordable, then B322 is not fixable by drawing a raw tip"* — and it is now measured rather than feared. **Do not raise the constant. There is no value that works.**
  - **The censored-sample story was overstated within the hour, and the correction is the sixth verdict in this entry to compare the wrong quantity — this time in a test of my own.** The first version of `LiveTipDabCostTests` took a **median** of nine runs and reported a 0.383 ms fixed cost, and argued that the app's estimate was high because its budget admits only small stamps where that constant dominates. Taking the **minimum** instead — contention only ever adds time, so the fastest run is the least-interfered one — the fixed cost falls to 0.15-0.33 ms and the one-dab-versus-640 ratio to **1.35x**. Most of the "fixed cost" was the machine, not the operation. The censoring is real and it is a **small** term; the dab is simply dear. The test now asserts the two **ratios** the fix rests on rather than an absolute shape, because a ratio taken in one run cancels the load and a microsecond figure does not.
  - **Found by the full suite, which is the part worth copying.** Run alone the table reads 107.5 us at one dab and 60.9 at 640; run inside the four-assembly suite it read **269.4 and 232.5** — everything inflated fourfold and the fixed-cost signal gone. A timing test that only passes on an idle machine is a timing test that will fail in CI on a claim that was never robust. **The failure was worth more than the assertion it killed.**
  - **`ResetTip` on a refusal is NOT the remaining lever, and this correction is recorded because it was offered to the owner as one before it was checked.** The entry says the addition path is unreachable after a refusal, which is true. Keeping the buffer instead of wiping it does not make it reachable: a rebuild is forced precisely when the pass advances, and the same advance is what makes the kept buffer unusable — `canAdd` requires `TipFrom == PostStampedDabs`, and after the advance it never does. The only refusal keeping the buffer would survive is a delta refusal, and a delta only grows. **Checked before building; it would have been a sixth fix aimed at the convenient quantity.**
  - **The size dependence the owner named on day one, in numbers at last.** Size 24 measures about **10 us** a dab against size 70's **45**, a ratio of **4.5x** that holds across runs where the absolute figures move about 15%. *"On larger brush sizes; 70+ size it jumps and stalls on both"* and *"on smaller sizes it also still jumps, it's just less visible"* are one measurement, not two reports.
  - **What is left is the area, and that is what the seventh attempt changes.** The tip is stamped into a document-sized buffer and then composited down to the 1440x810 surface the artist is looking at, so most of those pixels are discarded before anyone sees them. Stamped at the compose scale instead the same dab costs about **11 us** — **4.2x**, measured, with the resampling penalty B160 records for a scaled composite already inside it. The median outstanding run goes from 12.5 ms to **3.0** — which is **inside the 3 ms budget that already exists**, so the cheaper arm does not need a new constant, it makes the existing one sufficient. `LiveTipScale` carries it; the surface is scaled by a canvas transform and dab coordinates are never multiplied, so `Hash01` re-rolls every dynamic identically — **invariant 7's cheap side, the same mechanism `ComposeScale` already uses for the composite**.
  - **It ships as a flag rather than a default, on the owner's instruction, and both decisions of 2026-08-27 are recorded in Q169 and Q170.** Asked whether a fast stroke should show a partial tip with a gap behind it: **no — "a broken mark is worse than a late one"**, so the all-or-nothing fallback stands and no partial tip was built. Asked whether preview-resolution ink is acceptable for the newest dabs: **show me both first**. `LIGHTBOX_TIP_SCALE=preview` selects the cheaper arm, the report names which one ran, and nothing is chosen until the owner has looked at a fast stroke each way.
  - **The saving is view-dependent and the arm says so rather than hiding it.** At fit-to-window the compose scale is 0.375 and the tip costs 4.2x less; zoomed to 100% there is no saving and a fast stroke behaves exactly as it does today. That is the honest shape of the fix: the tip costs what it takes to be visible at the size it is being shown, and a document-resolution tip nobody is looking at document-resolution pixels of was always paying for nothing.
  - **A fourth fix was built, run on the owner's machine on 2026-08-27, and reverted the same hour. Read this before building a fifth.** The overlay was made to carry two bitmaps — the processed body and, over it, the dabs stamped since the last completed pass, restamped at publish time. It passed three tests, the whole suite, and collapsed on the first real stroke.

    | | before | with the fix | |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | building each frame (median) | 2.41 ms | **23.06 ms** | 9.6x |
    | describing it | 13.47 ms | **215 ms** | 16x |
    | `PEN -> SCREEN` | 62.95 ms | **991 ms** | 15.7x |
    | the publish cycle | 20.32 ms | **555 ms** | 27x |

  - **The mechanism, and it is not merely "too slow".** The tip was defined as *every dab since the last completed pass*, on the entry's own measurement that this is about nine events. The capture says otherwise: at **1263 points the pass had rendered 10 dabs**, so the tip was 99% of the stroke and was restamped on every publish — work proportional to the mark, which is **invariant 6** broken outright. Worse, it is **self-amplifying**: a bigger tip slows the publish, which starves the worker, which leaves more dabs outstanding, which grows the tip. That loop is why it looked fine in every test and collapsed on a real stroke.
  - **CORRECTION, same day: the mechanism above is wrong, and the real one is smaller and worse.** That bullet says the tip was 99% of the stroke because the pass had rendered 10 dabs of 1263, i.e. that the pass had fallen far behind. **It had not.** `PostStampedCount` is set from `Points.Count` on the worker path and from `dabs.Count` on the cap-only one (**B329**), so `dabs.Count - PostStampedCount` subtracts points from dabs and answers *approximately the whole stroke* whatever the pass has done. The fourth attempt restamped everything on every publish because its arithmetic was meaningless, not because the pass was behind.
  - **How it was caught, which is the part worth copying.** The fifth attempt's report line read `live tip drawn 4 of 298, dabs outstanding median 10334` beside `live medium passes 389, mean 9 ms, 4.6% of the mark re-processed`. **A pass running 389 times at 9 ms cannot also be ten thousand dabs behind.** Two numbers that cannot both be true is what exposed the unit error; either alone looked plausible. The instrument earned its place by contradicting itself.
  - **So "the pass falls behind" is not established and should not be assumed.** How far behind it actually runs is still unmeasured — the only figures anyone has for it were computed in mixed units. The fifth attempt reads `PostStampedDabs` instead and the same report line now answers the question honestly.
  - **First capture where the fix actually ran, 2026-08-27 12:29, and it works — in the case nobody complained about.** `live tip drawn 542 of 688, too far behind 146`, `dabs outstanding median 13, worst 2722`. The median of **13** is what the unit fix bought: the outstanding run is tens of dabs, not the ten thousand the mixed units reported. The owner: *"Slow strokes the preview is visible the entire time"* — so when the tip is drawn it does exactly what the entry has wanted for two days.
  - **And the budget refuses precisely the strokes the entry exists for.** *"While within a fast stroke, no preview is seen at all. Slowing down or idling does show it."* That is the 146 refusals from the pen's side: a fast stroke pushes the outstanding run past 128, the tip is declined, and what is left is the processed body — which on a heavily lagged pass is almost nothing. **A bound chosen for safety turned the fix off in the one case it was built for.**
  - **The budget was never measured, which is the actual mistake, and it is the same one twice.** 128 was picked to be obviously safe, exactly as the fourth attempt's tip range was defined on an unexamined "about nine events". What the budget protects — the cost of restamping the range — had never been timed, so there was no number to choose it against. It is timed now, and the report divides it out per dab and says what covering the p99 would cost, so the next value is arithmetic rather than nerve.
  - **What the answer cannot be.** Raising it without measuring, because that is how the fourth attempt reached a person's machine; and lowering it, because the refusals are already the complaint. If the measured cost says covering fast strokes is unaffordable, then B322 is not fixable by drawing a raw tip and the entry should say so rather than shipping something that helps only where nobody noticed a problem.
  - **Measured 2026-08-27 12:43, and it rules out the obvious answer.** Restamping the tip costs **16.8 us a dab** (0.32 ms median over 19 dabs). Against a publish cycle of 20.7 ms:

    | budget | dabs | cost a publish | of the cycle |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | today | 128 | 2.2 ms | 10% |
    | p90 | 783 | **13.2 ms** | 64% |
    | p99 | 1764 | **29.7 ms** | 143% |
    | worst | 6470 | 109 ms | 526% |

    **So the budget cannot be raised to cover fast strokes.** Reaching even the p90 eats two thirds of the cycle. This is the outcome named in advance as "a raw tip cannot serve fast strokes", and it is a fact about *rebuilding* the tip rather than about the idea of a tip.
  - **What ships: 196 of 279 publishes — 70% — at 0.32 ms median.** Slow and medium strokes show the preview throughout, which they did not. The owner: *"Slow strokes the preview is visible the entire time."*
  - **THE FAST CASE IS MANDATORY AND THIS ENTRY STAYS P1.** The owner's words on being offered the 70% as a finished state: *"To be honest this isn't optional. This is mandatory to work."* A drawing application whose preview disappears inside a fast stroke has an unfinished feature, not a partial win, and nothing here should be read as this bug having been reduced in importance. **Do not let this drift to P2 on the strength of the 70%.**
  - **The cost is not a floor, and the sixth attempt has a shape.** The tip is **rebuilt from nothing on every publish**, so it restamps the whole outstanding run each time — 783 dabs, then 800, then 820, until a pass lands. A tip that *kept what it had* and stamped only what arrived since the last publish would pay the per-publish delta instead, and the total over a stroke would be proportional to its dabs rather than to the sum of every outstanding run. `LiveTipNewDabs` measures that delta on every publish including the refused ones, and the report prints both costs side by side. **If the ratio is large the sixth attempt is worth building; if the two are the same it is not, and the fast case needs a different idea.** Nobody should build it before reading that line — two attempts have now failed on numbers assumed rather than measured.

    | effect | band-local | why |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | granulation | yes | a repeat shader drawn under a document-space transform, and `PaperField.Fill` indexes `mod tile` from the same corner — a pixel gets the same value whichever rect is asked about |
    | footprint ceiling | yes | pointwise, *provided the caller carries the canvas-anchored buffer*. Rebuilt inside each rect it re-renders the tip's gradients at a different device offset and moves pixels by 2–3/255 |
    | wet edge | yes, with a skirt | it is a blur, so a band that stops mid-mark shows it a cut edge and it invents a rim along it — 25/255 on Watercolor (flat), 7/255 on Gouache, and **0/255 from a 4 px halo**. `LivePassHalo` is three sigmas of `ApplyWetEdge`'s own rim width, read rather than restated |

- [ ] **B329** `P2` `brush` PostStampedCount is points on one path and dabs on the other, so it cannot be compared with either `evidence: PostStampedPoints, PostStampedDabsMatchesTheDabList, ACapOnlyPassAndAWorkerPassAgreeOnTheirOwnUnits`
  - **Two paths, two units, one field.** `MainViewModel.Painting.cs:2414` sets it from `whole.Points.Count` — **pointer points** — on the worker path; `:2277` sets it from `dabs.Count` — **dabs** — on the cap-only path. Dabs are interpolated along a stroke by spacing, so on a real mark the two differ by an order of magnitude: a capture of 2026-08-27 read **10,334** where the difference should have been tens.
  - **It has been harmless because nothing asked it a quantitative question.** `ScenePassBuilder.OverlayFor` tests `> 0`; `StartLivePostProcess` compares it against `live.Points.Count` to decide whether anything is new. The first of those does not care about the unit, and the second is *correct for the worker path and wrong for the cap-only one* — after a cap-only pass the guard compares a dab count against a point count, never matches, and lets a pass start that has nothing to do. Nobody noticed because a redundant pass is cheap and silent.
  - **What it did cost: B322's fourth attempt, and most of a session.** That fix computed "dabs the pass has not seen" as `dabs.Count - PostStampedCount`, which is dabs minus points — so the answer was always approximately the whole stroke, and it restamped the lot on every publish. Building each frame went **2.41 → 23.06 ms** median and pen-to-screen **62.95 → 991**. It was reverted on the owner's report that it was far worse than the bug, and written up as *"the tip was defined as every dab since the last pass and the pass had fallen far behind"*. **That diagnosis was wrong**: the pass had not fallen far behind, the subtraction was meaningless. The correction is recorded on B322.
  - **Not fixed here, and the reason is that both meanings are load-bearing.** The worker path's guard needs points; the cap-only path's writer has dabs. Repairing it means deciding what the field is *for* and giving the other reader its own value — which is a small change with a real chance of a silent regression in the pass-scheduling guard, and it is not what the branch that found it was doing. B322's fifth attempt therefore added `PostStampedDabs` beside it rather than touching it.
  - **The fix, when someone takes it**: name the two things separately — `PostStampedPoints` for the scheduling guard and `PostStampedDabs` for anything measuring the mark — and delete the ambiguous name entirely so no third reader can pick the wrong one. A test that runs a cap-only stroke and a worker-path stroke and asserts each field against its own unit is what closes it. Cost: S, and the risk is entirely in the pass-scheduling guard rather than in the arithmetic.

    | the stamp alone, 1195 dabs | 0.86 ms | **0.52 ms** | 1.65x, stable over three runs |
    | end to end, 400 events | 1.876 ms/event | 1.861 ms/event | 0.8% |
    | end to end, 800 events | 1.694 ms/event | 1.643 ms/event | 3.0% |

    In Debug the same end-to-end pair read 3.45 against 2.50 ms — a 27% win that does not exist.
  - **So the outline is not the bottleneck.** The stamp is a small part of a per-event cost that is dominated by the whole-mark *fill* (**B299**) and by the walk `WalkDabs` performs every event regardless (BR1). A cache of the outline buys 1–3% end to end, which is inside the noise of three repeats.
  - **Withdrawn rather than shipped** because the price was a public cache type, mutable state on `LivePaintSession`, and a resumable-walk refactor of the hottest function in the engine — for a change that cannot be distinguished from noise. Left open at P3 as a *finding* rather than a task: if B299 ever removes the fill, the outline becomes a larger share and this is worth re-measuring. `evidence: manual` because what is recorded here is a measurement, not a behaviour a test can assert.
  - The transferable half is in `docs/DESIGN-performance.md`: **measure a per-dab optimisation in Release or do not believe it.**

- [ ] **B101** `P3` `brush` A simulated medium's picker tile is too faint to read `evidence: manual`
  - Repro: open the brush picker and look at **Watercolor** beside **Watercolor (flat)**. Measured by `ChannelsMoved` in `BrushPickerTests`: the flat one moves 890 pixels against its ground, the simulated one **2**, at a threshold of 12 per channel.
  - **Not the same defect as B50, and worth separating because B50's fix did not move it.** The on-canvas mark now peaks at 96/255 at the brush's own size, and the medium holds up as the brush shrinks — swept at sizes 8/12/17/25/42/80/150 the peak runs 71/80/87/98/96/105/107, so there is no size cliff. The tile is faint at a size where a real stroke is not.

It is a contrast problem, not an empty render: `worst channel delta 12` over the entire tile, sitting exactly on the threshold.

- [ ] **B92** `P3` `brush` Smearing does not preserve detail, because it deposits a colour rather than moving pixels `evidence: manual`
  - Krita's two Color Smudge algorithms differ in *what* they lay down: smearing "copies the area underneath the previous position of the brush onto the new position, taking opacity into account", so texture and detail streak; dulling "picks up the colour underneath it, mixes it with its own colour, then paints with it", so detail dissolves and the brush shape is preserved.
  - `StampSmudgeDabs` implements **both** as a single averaged `SKColor` laid down through `LerpDab`. The two modes therefore differ only in how much of the local sample is blended into the carried colour — `deposit = carried` for smearing against `Mix(sample, carried, carryOver * 0.5)` for dulling — and neither can preserve detail, because a scalar colour has none to preserve.
  - The code says otherwise, which is the part that makes this worth an entry rather than a shrug: the comment above it reads *"Smearing drags a sample along the stroke and refreshes it as it goes, so detail smears into streaks"*. It does not streak; it cannot.
  - Fix is a translated patch rather than a colour — read the dab's neighbourhood from the previous dab position and composite it at the new one, weighted by the dab shape. That is a change to the deposit itself, so it collides directly with **B69/B89**'s preview work and should not be attempted alongside it. Cost: L
  - P3 because the brush is useful as it stands — it blends, which is most of what it is reached for — and because the gap is expressive rather than corrupting. Raise it if an artist asks for texture to survive a smear.

- [ ] **B71** `P3` `brush` Brush settings are lost when Lightbox closes `evidence: BrushSettingsPersistenceTests, BrushSettingsSurviveARestart, ABrushLeftAtItsDefaultsWritesNoKey`
  - Reported: individual brush settings are not kept for the session, and after closing and reopening they are back to defaults.
  - The per-document half of this is B67, and this is the other half: nothing is written at all, so even a single-document session loses tuning that took real time. **Q24 is answered: persistence is automatic and there is no save button**, so this entry is the whole of the work — one mechanism, no second one with a different lifetime, and the per-file/per-project scope question deferred with the button that would have forced it.
  - Whatever is stored must follow `AProjectThatNeverAsksForThisWritesNoBrushKey`: a brush left at its defaults writes nothing. Cost: M

- [ ] **B60** `P3` `brush` The brush engine assumes a read bitmap's origin is the document's origin `evidence: manual`
  - Found while fixing B59, and it is the reason B59's obvious fix made things worse rather than better.
  - `BrushEngine.SampleAverage` indexes the bitmap an effect brush reads using the dab's **document** position: `Math.Clamp((int)(pos.X + dx * spread), 0, pixels.Width - 1)`. `LerpDab` does the same, mixing `GetDeviceClipBounds` (device space) with `pos.X * outputScale` (document space). Both are correct exactly while the read bitmap covers the document from its own (0,0) — which every caller predating tiling did.
  - Nothing is broken today. `FrameRasterizer`, the live preview and the export all pass document-aligned bitmaps, so the assumption holds everywhere it is currently made. This is a latent constraint rather than a live defect, which is why it is P3.
  - What it costs is optionality: an effect brush cannot be rendered against any surface that is not document-aligned, so it cannot be tiled, cannot be rendered into a scratch around a region, and cannot be re-rendered for one viewport. `TiledRasterizer.CanTile` refuses effect brushes for exactly this reason, and that refusal is the B59 fallback.
  - Fix: thread a read origin through `StampSmudge`/`StampSmudgeDabs`/`SampleAverage`/`LerpDab` and the blur pair, defaulting to (0,0) so every existing caller is unchanged, and subtract it where the read bitmap is indexed. Mechanical, but it edits the hottest file in the repository on the path invariant 2 guards — so it wants `RuntimeDeterminismTests` green and the effect-brush suite unchanged as its evidence, not just a compile. Cost: M
  - Closing this is what lets an effect brush tile properly and retires B59's whole-frame fallback. `EffectBrushesAreRefusedByTheTiledPathUntilB59IsFixedProperly` is written to fail on that day and say so.
  - **The mechanism now exists, and this entry deliberately stays open.** Canvas resize needed the identical conversion, so `StampSmudge`, `StampSmudgeDabs`, `SampleAverage`, `LerpDab` and both blur paths now take an origin and subtract it wherever a bitmap is indexed — `DocumentOriginTests` proves it against a document grown left and up. What that origin currently carries is the *document's* top-left rather than an arbitrary read bitmap's, but the two are the same conversion and the same parameter: handing a tile its own document origin is what this entry asks for, and nothing further in `BrushEngine` stands in the way.
  - So what is left is no longer the engine. It is `TiledRasterizer.CanTile` still refusing effect brushes, the callers that would have to pass a tile's origin, and the evidence to replace `evidence: manual` — which is why this is not ticked. A latent constraint whose fix is written but not switched on is still a constraint.
  - One thing the origin work fixed on the way, worth recording here because it is the same class of fault: `DabShape` seeded rotation jitter from its **device** centre, so a tipped effect dab re-rolled its bristles at any output scale but 1. It now seeds from the document position, like everything else.
  - **Measured 2026-08-12, and it overturns the paragraph above: the origin is necessary and nowhere near sufficient.** Two experiments, both backed out.
    - **Passing the tile its own origin breaks the *paint* path, before effects are even considered.** `TheTileSizeDoesNotChangeTheRender` fails at all four tile sizes. The reason is the design that makes tiling work at all and is easy to miss: `RasterizeByTile` passes the **document** `info` and translates the canvas, so every stroke is computed over its **full document extent** and Skia clips the *drawing* to the tile. Handing it a tile-sized `info` instead makes `SegmentBounds` clamp the scratch to the tile — so the stroke-global passes (wet edge, medium, granulation, texture) compute over a tile-shaped fragment of the stroke, and the render starts depending on the tile size. **Compute whole, clip to the tile** is the invariant of this file, and an origin-sized scratch violates it.
    - **Removing the refusal and leaving the rest alone costs 3,214 px.** A smudge dragged through the seam at x=256 differs from the untiled render in 3,214 pixels, worst alpha delta 199, **100% of them inside the smudge's own footprint**. That confinement is the diagnosis: an effect brush reads the pixels *beneath* it, and a tile holds only the strokes that reach that tile — so a dab sampling past the tile edge reads **absent** content rather than shifted content. No coordinate conversion fixes absent content.
  - **So the real fix is a halo, and the origin is what makes it expressible.** Each tile carrying an effect stroke renders into a padded surface covering tile + halo, replaying the strokes that intersect the padded rect, and the centre is copied out; the padded surface's own top-left is what `origin` would carry. The halo has to be the effect's reach — smudge `radius × SmudgeRadius`, blur `sigma × 4` where `sigma = Flow × Size / 4` — and it has to exceed it rather than match it, because the padded rect still clips the stroke-global passes and the bar is bit-identity, not similarity.
  - The cost model changes with it: `(tile + 2·halo)²` per tile instead of `tile²`, and only for tiles an effect stroke reaches. Whether that beats today's whole-frame fallback is an open question and worth measuring before building — at a 40 px smudge and a 256 px tile the padded area is roughly 1.4× the tile, which is cheap; at a 147 px blur it is over 4×, which is not.
  - **Nothing here is a reason to weaken `AnEffectBrushAcrossATileBoundaryIsMeasuredRatherThanAssumed`.** It asserts equality and should keep asserting it: the numbers above are what it reports when the refusal is lifted without the halo, which is exactly the failure it exists to catch.

### canvas

- [ ] **B332** `P1` `canvas` A frame-cache miss re-renders the whole frame on the UI thread, and that is the jump the artist feels `evidence: AMissDoesNotRenderOnTheCallingThread, TheWorstBuildNamesItsOwnPhase, ACommittedStrokeDoesNotStallTheNextOne`
  - **FIXED 2026-08-28 01:1x by paying during the idle instead: `WarmWhatTheNextStrokeWillNeed`.** Two earlier attempts failed on the same point — **a miss during a stroke has no window to be warmed in**, because the next publish asks immediately. The capture of 00:50 is what named the right window: the two strokes reading `following: never` are the first of the session and the first after a thirteen-second pause, both beside the session's single 1131 ms build with two misses in it, while every other stroke began following in **28-39 ms**. **The freeze does not interrupt a stroke; it eats the first one after an idle** — and an idle is precisely a window.
  - **So the frames the next stroke will ask for are rendered off the UI thread while nothing is being drawn.** Only when no stroke is in flight, nothing is playing, and the prewarmer is not already busy; frames that `CanCache` refuses are skipped, because a warm of one is discarded on arrival. **It cannot become the fourth attempt** — that added work proportional to the mark *during* a stroke and took a frame build from 2.41 ms to 23.06 — because it never runs while the pen is down. The worst it can cost is a worker rendering a frame nobody needed.
  - **And unlike everything else tried on this entry, it has no visible trade.** Serving the last good render showed the frame one edit stale and was reverted; widening the repaint aimed at a call site that was not firing. Warming shows nothing stale because it shows nothing at all until the pixels exist. `WarmWhileIdleTests` pins the property the fix rests on — a warmed entry is pixel-identical to one the cache rendered itself, and the lookup that follows is served rather than rendered — plus the two ways a warm is silently wasted: stored under a key nobody asks for, or taken of a frame that is never cached.
  - **Unverified against a capture**, because it was built while the owner slept. The line that will say whether it worked is `following` in the stroke table: the first stroke of a session and the first after a pause should join the others at 28-39 ms instead of reading `never`.
  - **P1, and it is the symptom B322 has been chasing for three days.** Four captures on 2026-08-27, two arms of B322's fix, and the owner's verdict on both: *"for both arms the preview did still jump"* and *"I wasn't able to feel or see any discernable difference between A & B."* The tip was drawn on 90% of publishes in the best of them. **A preview that is present 90% of the time cannot fix a stall**, and the stalls are enormous:

    | capture | arm | building each frame, median | **worst** |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 22:52 | document | 2.30 ms | **4942 ms** |
    | 22:53 | document | 2.35 ms | **5015 ms** |
    | 22:57 | preview | 2.00 ms | **6354 ms** |
    | 22:59 | document | 2.74 ms | **3170 ms** |

    Three to six **seconds** on the UI thread, against a median of two milliseconds and a pen delivering every 5.1. That is what "it jumps" is: the mark freezes for seconds and then arrives in one step. Nothing about a tip, a budget or a dab's cost touches it.
  - **THE TWO FAULTS SEPARATED, 2026-08-28 00:01, and it took the owner's own suggestion to do it.** Asked to stop reading the worst build and look at every stall, and to define a stall by what the eye can see rather than by a round number. At **50 ms** — three refreshes, the point where the mark visibly stops following the nib — a whole session of the drawing the owner calls laggy contains **exactly one stall**:

    ```
    stalls (over 50 ms)      1   of which a cache miss was inside: 1
      time lost to them     7.62 s of 48.4 s drawing   (15.7%)
         at        ms   describing    points     dabs   misses
       17.9 s      7617         7617         0        0        2
    ```

    **One.** Seven and a half seconds, no stroke in flight, two cache misses, 100% describing. **B332 is a single freeze per session and it costs a sixth of the drawing time.** It is not the lag, and the old 100 ms threshold — round rather than meaningful — had been hiding the question by counting the same one stall.
  - **So the lag is elsewhere, and the same capture names it.** `building each frame` has a **median of 1.36 ms**; the frame build is not slow. What is late is the dam: **`publish held back 177 times, already drawn still held mean 8 ms worst 837 — 38% of the hold`**. The report's own line has said it all along — *"That share is not pacing, it is the dam finding out late. The frame was on screen and the publish went on waiting."* `event -> publish` median 18.35 ms against a pen delivering every 5.7, while `publish -> drawn` sits at the vsync floor and barely moves. **The continuous lag is B178's ground — a publish waiting after its frame is already on screen — and it is not the cache, the brush, the tip or the pass.**
  - **Which makes B322's three days, and this entry's evening, work on the wrong fault.** The preview arm, the budget, the dab cost, the stale serve, the repaint bounds: all real, all measured, none of them what the artist is feeling most of the time. The one thing that did land is the instrument, and it only landed once it was pointed at stalls rather than at averages — which is the owner's correction and belongs to them.
  - **THE REAL ROOT CAUSE, and both fixes aimed past it.** `dropped by: ClearLayerContent (no bounds)` is **correct** — clearing a layer changes the whole frame and there is no region to patch. Nothing is wrong with the invalidation. What is wrong is that **recovery from any whole-frame invalidation is synchronous on whoever asks next**, and mid-stroke that is always the UI thread. And the capture that followed says even that is not the freeze: `builds over 100 ms 1, of which a cache miss was inside 1`, worst **7090 ms**, `frame-cache misses in it: 2` — with `served stale, rebuilding 1`. **The two misses inside the giant build had nothing stale to serve, because they were first renders.** The freeze is the first publish of a document that already has artwork on it, rendering every layer from the stroke record on the UI thread before anything can be shown.
  - **Serving stale was built, measured on the owner's machine, and reverted the same hour.** It bought exactly **one** avoided stall in a session, left the 7-second build untouched, and the owner reported *"even medium strokes lag now"* — `publish -> publish` median 19 → 28 ms, `PEN -> SCREEN` median 46 → 57, `stamping the dabs` median 2.8 → 4.4. Whether the change caused that or the session did is **not established**, and it does not need to be: a fix that avoids one stall out of five and is suspected of a broad regression is not worth carrying while its premise — that the misses are refills — is already disproved. Reverted, instrumentation kept.
  - **What the evidence now points at, unbuilt.** The expensive misses are **first renders**, so nothing about refill strategy reaches them. A warm of the current frame's layers when a document opens and when the playhead lands — off the UI thread, through the prewarmer that already exists and already installs through `Drain` — is the only shape that helps a first render, and it has no visible trade because there is nothing stale to show. **Not built, because the branch that found it has been wrong three times about which path was firing** and this one deserves a capture that isolates it: a session that opens a document, draws one stroke, and writes a report before anything else.
  - **FIRST ROOT CAUSE FOUND IN THE CODE, and it explains the 0-of-1 repair rate exactly.** The capture of 23:21 reads `edits repaired in place 0 of 1   dropped whole 1` — when the invalidate path runs it never repairs. `MainViewModel.Documents.RebakeLiveSamples` is why: it calls **`InvalidateFrameRender(painted.Id)` with no bounds**, and `TryRepaintFrameRegion`'s first line is `if (repaintBounds is not { } bounds) return false`. **The repair is unreachable from that call site by construction**, so the frame is dropped whole and the next lookup pays a full render on the UI thread. It fires whenever a frame carries a stroke with `SampleSource.AllLayersLive`, on every edit — the document-wide guard in front of it was removed on measurement grounds, which is right and is not the problem.
  - **The misses are not one thing, and that is the finding rather than an obstacle.** Five misses, two key sizes, two frames:

    ```
    frame f_1a0451  960x540@1     cel 0   not held
    frame f_1a0451  960x540@1     cel 0   not held
    frame f_1a03dc  3840x2160@1   cel 0   not held
    frame f_1a0451  3840x2160@1   cel 0   not held
    frame f_1a0451  3840x2160@1   cel 0   not held
    ```

    The **same drawing at two sizes**, neither of which is the thumbnail path — `ThumbSource` and the navigator both ask at `Scene.Width, Scene.Height`. Who asks at exactly a quarter is not yet known and two rounds of grepping did not find it, so `Get` now takes a `[CallerMemberName]` and the miss log names the caller. **One defaulted parameter in place of a third round of guessing.**
  - **The owner's instruction, 2026-08-27, and it is the right one:** *"the most important part is to find the root cause. Without the root cause we are always circumventing which could bite down the line."* Offered three fixes — render off the UI thread (covers every cause), chase the causes one at a time, or widen the repaint alone — and refused all three in favour of finding out why. Recorded because two of those would have shipped while the quarter-size asker was still unexplained.
  - **CONFIRMED on the owner's machine, 2026-08-27 23:10, by the instrument built to refute it.** The worst build of the capture, attributed to the phase that one frame spent its time in rather than to a mean over every frame:

    ```
    the WORST build alone    3308.68 ms   — where that one frame went:
      describing it          3308.08 ms   (100%)   frame-cache misses in it: 2
      compositing it               0 ms   (0%)
      handing it over           0.01 ms   (0%)
      everything else           0.58 ms   (0%)
    ```

    **One hundred per cent of a 3.3-second stall, in describing the frame, with two cache misses inside it.** Two misses at the 797 ms measured on a lighter synthetic frame is 1.6 s; this document carries two layers and longer strokes, so about 1.65 s a miss. The mechanism, the cost and the attribution now agree, and the report's verdict line was written to be able to say the opposite.
  - **MEASURED 2026-08-27, and a miss costs 797 ms.** `FrameCacheMissCostTests` calls `FrameBitmapCache.RenderDetached` — the same render a miss performs, exposed for the prewarmer — on the owner's document size with five heavy strokes: **855, 797, 809 ms**, best of three **797 ms**. Against a typical build of **2 ms** that is **422x**, and against a pen delivering every 5 ms it is **159 events' worth of silence**. The synthetic frame is if anything lighter than the owner's, which carried two layers and longer strokes, so 3.2-6.4 seconds is a small multiple of this rather than a different phenomenon.
  - **That is the whole verdict on B322's three days.** The tip budget was argued down from 128 dabs to 3 milliseconds to 11 microseconds a dab, and the largest saving any of it bought was about **13 ms a publish**. One cache miss is **797**. Sixty publishes' worth of the entire optimisation, in one frame, on the thread the pen is waiting on.
  - **The mechanism, read off the code rather than inferred from the timings.** `FrameBitmapCache.Get` increments `Misses` and then calls `Render(source, ...)` **synchronously on the calling thread**. During a stroke that thread is the UI thread, inside the phase the report calls *describing it (pass list, stack fold, cel fetches)*. So a miss is a full frame rasterization from the stroke record — at 3840x2160, with wet-edge strokes whose post-process runs over the whole mark — in the middle of drawing.
  - **The counts line up and the coincidence is worth stating as a coincidence.** Every one of the four captures reads `had to render 5 (0.3-0.4%)` and `thrown out 1`, in a scene of **5 strokes**. One miss per committed stroke, and several multi-second stalls per session. That is consistent with a miss causing the stall and it is **not proof** — the report attributes phases by mean only, so no number in any capture says which phase the worst build spent its time in.
  - **The decisive next step is instrumentation, not a fix.** Attribute the *worst* build to a phase, the way B330 gave every phase of the chain a median. If the worst build is `describing it` on a publish that also missed, the mechanism above is confirmed and the fix is to render off the UI thread — `RenderDetached` already exists for exactly that and its own remarks explain why it is safe (rendering is a pure function of the stroke record, invariant 2). If it is not, this entry is wrong and something else stalls for five seconds.
  - **Why this is filed rather than fixed in the branch that found it.** B322's branch was finished and had a pull request open before this surfaced; the one-objective rule says the answer to finding something else is a new branch. The entry it came from cannot close on it either way, which is the more important point: **B322's tip machinery works and does not fix the reported symptom.**
  - Cost: M for the instrumentation and the move off the UI thread; the risk is entirely in what a publish does while a frame it wants is still rendering, which is B148's ground rather than new.

- [ ] **B255** `P1` `canvas` Hovering a menu with a pen tablet freezes the app for up to 6 seconds `evidence: manual`
  - **Measured, 2026-08-17, second `InputTrace` run on the reporter's Huion machine** — 56.7 s, 15,268 events, and this bug is the reason the stall watch was added to the instrument at all. The reporter had said the application "froze for a little while"; the first trace could not tell a freeze from a pointer resting over a menu, and the heartbeat that settled it found **22 UI-thread stalls, worst 6,103 ms**.
  - **The cause is not a correlation, it is an identity.** Every stall over three seconds is preceded by ~100 popup opens per second; the rate in windows away from any stall is **0.0/s**:

    | Stall | Popup opens in the prior 3 s |
    | --- | --- |
    | 3,227 ms | 296 (99/s) |
    | 3,827 ms | 289 (96/s) |
    | 4,354 ms | 303 (101/s) |
    | **6,103 ms** | 243 (81/s) |
    | 3,405 ms | 296 (99/s) |
    | 3,747 ms | 307 (102/s) |

  - **What is thrashing is the layer context menu.** Named by the trace, which is what the popup labels are for: `Submenu of “Follows the rig”` 612 opens, `“In exports”` 322, `“Linking”` 208 — all real `MenuItem`s in `MainWindow.axaml`. The Windows Ink echo stream (B126's diagnosis) makes Avalonia's own `MenuItem` hover logic open and close those submenus about fifty times a second, and building and destroying that many popup windows is what blocks the thread.
  - **This is why the fix could not be the one first proposed.** The canvas coalescing its own enter/exit — the recommendation made before this trace existed — would have fixed B126's ring flicker and *touched none of this*, because the thrash happens inside Avalonia's menu code, on a path no handler of ours is on. It would have shipped, the flicker would have improved, and the six-second freezes would have remained. **A fix aimed at the symptom you can see is not the same as a fix aimed at the cause.**
  - **The first fix attempt is disproven and reverted** — `PenEchoFilter` dropped nothing, because `Handled` at `PreProcess` does not stop Avalonia delivering a pointer event (proved headlessly; see B126). The trace after it read 1,163 "dropped" with the worst stall **rising to 18.9 s**.
  - Fix: **`OverlayPopups = true`** in `Program.cs`. It does not stop the submenu thrash — that is Avalonia's menu code reacting to an echo nobody in-process can suppress — it makes each cycle cost an in-window visual instead of creating and destroying a native window, which is the part the stalls actually tracked. The cost, recorded because it is a trade: an overlay popup is clipped to the window, so a menu near an edge lays out inside it rather than spilling onto the desktop.
  - **Measured after that fix, and it worked on the wrong axis.** Fourth trace, alpha.69: worst stall **18,926 ms → 849 ms** and total blocked time **63.5% → 29.3%** of the session — the app stopped seizing. But popup opens went **366 (10/s) → 2,763 (61/s)**, because making each cycle twenty times cheaper let six times as many fit, and the correlation came straight back: median **101 popup opens/s** in the three seconds before every stall over 400 ms. Treating the cost of a cycle is not the same as treating how often it happens.
  - **So the second half is a rate cap:** `Services/SubmenuCloseGrace.cs` refuses a submenu close that arrives within **250 ms** of the open — the half of the churn cycle nobody asked for — which caps it at about four a second instead of sixty. It never forces a submenu open and never resists a real dismissal; only the immediate close is refused, and the next one after the grace is honoured.
  - **The risk is recursion, not policy**, because it writes to the property it is handling. Removing the guard does not fail the suite — **it hangs it**, recursing until the run is killed, which is why the guard is the first line of the handler. `RefusingACloseDoesNotRecurse` pins it.
  - P1 rather than the P3 B126 carries: a six-second freeze while hovering a menu is not cosmetic, and folding it into B126 would have left the ledger claiming the worst consequence of this cause is an annoying flicker. Filed separately for that reason (the owner's call, asked before filing).
  - **`evidence: manual`, and the distinction is the point.** `PenEchoFilterTests` holds the *policy* — that a mouse move within 200 ms of a pen is dropped, that a pen-less machine can never engage the filter, that a button is never dropped, and that the reflected members still resolve. None of that is the *cure*: whether dropping those events actually stops Avalonia recomputing pointer-over, and so stops the submenu thrash, is Avalonia's behaviour on Windows with a tablet attached, and this repository has none of the three. Naming those tests here would tick the box on a freeze nobody has watched stop. What closes it is a traced minute on the reporter's machine showing `UI-thread stalls 0` with `echo events dropped` in the thousands.

That fix is wired and running: `compositor wake-ups asked 676, arrived 676` — every frame asked for arrived. So the old explanation does not fit this capture, and re-applying B164's fix would be treating a symptom that already has one.
  - **The report's own diagnosis prose is stale and asserts B164's answer as CONFIRMED.** It reads "frames wait until the CANVAS is invalidated, and only its own pointer handler does that" — written before `KeepPresenting` existed and never re-checked. Fixed separately; noted here because it is what a reader would otherwise act on, and it would send them to the wrong place.
  - **The wait still varies with pointer input, which is the clue worth keeping.** Pointer still: 241 frames, mean **236.5 ms**. Input on the canvas: 197 frames, mean **88.43 ms**. So something about canvas input still shortens the path even with the present loop running — but "nothing wakes the compositor" is refuted, so the mechanism is different from B164's.
  - **A hypothesis worth testing first, not a conclusion.** `PumpPresentLoop` keeps exactly one animation-frame request in flight and re-arms from inside the callback, so its rate is bounded by how long a callback takes. At a 38.47 ms draw that is ~26 Hz, and 676 wake-ups over ~35 s of playback is ~19 Hz — consistent with the loop running as fast as the draw allows rather than at display rate. If the loop is draw-bound then publishes at 12 fps should still be picked up within one draw, so a 176 ms mean needs a second cause; instrument where the wait accumulates before changing anything.
  - **The report's own counters give the mechanism, and it is a rate mismatch rather than a wake-up fault (2026-08-12).** Three rates over the same ~35 s capture, all from numbers already in the entry above:

    ```
    ticks that advanced   339   ~9.7/s   the playhead, at 12 fps with drops
    frames published      757  ~21.6/s   about 2.2 publishes per tick
    frames drawn          501  ~14.3/s   bounded by the 38.47 ms draw
    ```

    **Publishing outruns drawing by about 1.5x**, which is exactly the shape of the two anomalies: 256 replaced before being drawn is the surplus, and a 176 ms mean wait is the backlog that surplus creates. A frame waits ~4.6 draws because roughly that many are queued ahead of it.
  - **So the question is no longer "why is the compositor asleep" but "why are there two publishes per tick".** The present loop is not the constraint: it re-arms from inside its callback and `InvalidateVisual` only marks dirty, so it runs as fast as the render loop will let it — ~26 Hz at a 38 ms draw, comfortably above a 12 fps playhead. A loop that can present at 26 Hz and a playhead that advances at 9.7 Hz should never build a backlog. One does because something publishes when the playhead has not moved.
  - **What that reframes.** Every remaining compositing optimisation makes the draw cheaper, which raises the draw rate — and against a publish rate 1.5x higher it buys proportionally less than it looks. Finding and removing the surplus publishes is likely cheaper than making the draw faster, and it is the first thing that would show up as fewer dropped frames rather than as a smaller number in the report.
  - **Not attributed, and deliberately.** `PublishSnapshot` has 45 call sites; which of them fire during playback is a question for a counter rather than for a grep, and this entry has already been wrong once by reasoning from prose (its own stale B164 diagnosis). The next step is a per-caller publish tally during playback, not a change to the publish path.
  - Cost: M to diagnose, unknown to fix. **Do not start by changing the present path** — that is what B164 already did, and the counters say it is working.
  - **The per-caller tally shipped (2026-08-15), and it is the counter the bullet above asked for — no publish-path behaviour changed.** `PublishSnapshot` takes a compiler-stamped `CallerMemberName`, so all 45 call sites report themselves without being edited and the name cannot lie about where the call came from; `PublishTally` counts them during playback only, so the table is the tick's surplus rather than thousands of legitimate pointer publishes; and the render report's *who publishes during playback* section prints the table busiest-first and judges the total against the ticks — one publish per advance is the playhead's own, everything above that line is the surplus, whoever made it. `PublishTallyTests` pins the gating, the caller attribution and the report's wording, and is deliberately not this entry's evidence — the same split `StrokeToScreenTests` holds for B189, because these prove the instrument rather than the fix.
  - **What closes the diagnosis step: play for half a minute on the owner's machine, then Help ▸ Write a render report.** The section names the caller supplying the ~1.2 publishes per tick beyond the playhead's own, which is where the 176 ms backlog is being fed from — and the next fix goes at that call site, not at the present path.

- [ ] **B335** `P2` `canvas` Live ink arrives in clumps of 5.2 pen events: the publish cycle is a round trip, not a refresh `evidence: ThePublishCycleIsARefreshNotARoundTrip`
  - **The owner's remaining complaint after B189's two branches landed**: *"still better. But still lag with really fast long strokes."* Not the stamp and not the draw — the same capture (2026-08-28) prices the stamp as cheap and puts `publish -> drawn` at **28.59 ms**, which is B321's floor of one and a half refreshes plus the draw, and therefore not a cost at all.
  - **The number that is the fault**: `publish -> publish` **29.26 ms** against a pen delivering every **5.68**. Four pen events in five produce no publish, so the ink arrives five events at a time. **That is chunkiness, not latency** — every individual mark is prompt, and they come in clumps.
  - **Why it is a bug and not the pacing working**: the in-flight depth is **2**, and the cycle is one *whole* round trip. A depth of two exists precisely so a publish can go out each refresh instead of each round trip, and it was chosen on a measured A/B — 2026-08-26, cycle **35.44 → 17.16 ms** when the depth went one to two. The cycle has since gone back to a round trip while the depth stayed at two. Something other than the pacing is setting the rate.
  - **Filed rather than fixed in this branch, and the reason is written into B178 two entries down**: *"the next step is a per-caller tally, not a change to the publish path"* — an entry that had already been wrong once by reasoning from prose. There are three candidate mechanisms and they recommend three different fixes, and the existing report cannot choose between them. It says so itself, offering two explanations for the dam's own 27% in one breath.
  - **So this branch ships the counter that chooses.** Every `RequestSnapshot` is now attributed to the gate that turned it away: the dam, or a publish already posted at `Input` priority and not yet run. The report prints the split, the dispatcher's own `asked -> published` wait, and a verdict naming one gate rather than listing suspects.
  - **And the third bucket turned out to be unreachable, which is a finding rather than a tidy-up.** A request cannot be refused by both gates: the sequence number only advances inside `PublishSnapshot`, and the posted flag is already down by then, so a pending post always sees exactly the gap the dam saw when it let that post through. The counter stays as a tripwire with the report warning on any non-zero, and `TheTwoGatesNeverRefuseTheSameRequest` holds the reasoning — the test was written to prove the opposite and measured its own premise wrong.
  - **The mechanism this is expected to name, stated in advance so the capture can refuse it.** B73's coalescing posts the publish at `DispatcherPriority.Input`; on Windows, pointer messages are handled by the platform loop, so a job posted behind a continuous stream of them comes round about once a round trip — and while it is pending, `RequestSnapshot` refuses every further event at its first line. That would make the post a rate limit nobody chose as one, stacked in front of the dam, which is the pacer that *was* chosen on evidence. **Written down before the capture on purpose**: a prediction that can only be read after the numbers arrive is not one.
  - **`LIGHTBOX_PUBLISH=inline` is the second arm, so one session answers it twice.** It publishes straight from the pointer event and hands the pacing entirely back to the dam. It is deliberately not the default: it gives up the coalescing, and B189 measured what that costs when it goes wrong — 935 of 1921 publishes replaced before anything drew them at ~27 ms of UI thread each. A build is 1.25 ms now rather than 27, which is why it is worth trying at all, and `replaced before drawing` in the report is the number that would refuse it.

That is the false green this file exists to make impossible, and the same split `PublishTallyTests` and `StrokeToScreenTests` are already held to: **they prove the instrument, not the fix.** `ThePublishCycleIsARefreshNotARoundTrip` is what would close it — a cycle measured against the refresh period rather than against `publish -> drawn`.
  - **What closes this entry is not a green test.** It is a capture on each arm and the owner's own verdict on a fast long stroke, the only test that has ever found one of these faults. The evidence anchor above proves the instrument cannot lie about which gate said no; it does not claim the cycle is fixed, and the box stays open until the cycle is a refresh rather than a round trip.
  - **ANSWERED, on both arms, 2026-08-28.** The prediction written above held: **179** of the 309 refusals were events the pacing would have let through, turned away only because a publish was posted and had not run, against **130** by the dam. The counter named the gate the same day it was built.
  - **And the second arm moved it.** Same build, same brush, same fast strokes:

    ```
                                     posted     inline
      publish -> publish            28.84 ms   22.12 ms
      pen events per publish            5.4        2.0
      PEN -> SCREEN mean           103.68 ms   40.49 ms
      PEN -> SCREEN worst          479.05 ms   79.15 ms
      refused by a pending post           179          0
      replaced before drawing             11%        14%
    ```

    **The worst case is the finding, not the median.** Half a second of ink standing still is what a person calls stuttering; 40 ms of extra mean is not. The typical post waited **3.94 ms** and the worst waited **470.57** — and the report's own half-a-cycle check reads the median and stayed silent on it. That check now has a tail arm beside it, for the mirror of the reason `Tally` exists: there, a mean lied about a typical frame; here, a median lied about the only frames anybody feels.
  - **So the route is switched and the old one stays reachable** as `LIGHTBOX_PUBLISH=posted`, the same way `LIGHTBOX_INFLIGHT` survived its own A/B — it is how this was settled and how it would be re-settled. The cost was priced before the switch rather than after: frames built and then replaced went **11% to 14%**, against the **48.7%** that made B189 prevent them, at a build of 1.25 ms rather than 27.

Filed as **B336** rather than folded in here: this entry's title is about ink arriving in clumps, and that is answered.
