Two different questions, mixed. Both captures are now regression cases in `TheCycleVerdictNamesOneGateTests` with their real numbers.
  - **The switch was made, and reverted the same afternoon by the suite.** Making the inline route the default fails **eight** tests, two of which are guarantees this branch had no business overruling. Recorded here rather than quietly narrowed, because the measurement above is genuinely good and the temptation to ship it anyway is the thing to guard against:
    - **B73's coalescing.** A burst of fifteen already-queued pointer events becomes fifteen full composes rather than one (`APenBurstIsOneFrameNotOnePerEvent`). In the running application the dam bounds this — the owner's own capture is 111 publishes from 221 events, not 221 — but **a canvas that has never presented is deliberately never paced**, so there the burst is unbounded. A route that only behaves once a canvas exists is not a route. `TheInlineArmGivesUpTheBurstCoalescing` states it from the route's side so the next person to reach for the default meets the reason first.
    - **B69/B89's live-equals-commit bar — now CLEARED.** `builtin-smudge` and `builtin-blender` stopped matching their own commits, by 20 px and 13 px at 1/255. Filed as **B337** and since fixed: the smudge takes its own tail back and re-stamps it, which changes pixels *behind* the pen, and only the new segment was marked for repaint. Not the route, and not caused by this branch — the same divergence appears on the shipped route by publishing once per pen event instead of once per burst, and the committed pixels were bit-identical throughout, so the record was never at stake.
    - **So one blocker of the two is gone.** B73's coalescing is the one still standing.
  - **Why not just rate-limit the inline route to the refresh interval.** It would satisfy the first blocker and does nothing for the second, which is about *when* a publish happens rather than how often — and B337 has to be understood before any cadence moves, or the next attempt trades a reported stutter for a silently wrong preview. That is a worse bug than the one being fixed, because nobody sees it.
  - **So the arm ships opt-in, and it works today**: `LIGHTBOX_PUBLISH=inline` gives the owner the improvement they confirmed, on dry brushes, at the price named above. The default is unchanged and the entry stays open.
  - Cost: S to attribute (done), S to switch once **B337** is settled.

- [ ] **B326** `P2` `canvas` The live re-flatten of a taped-up sheet view never reaches the canvas: Register refuses an id it already holds `evidence: none yet`
  - Found while measuring B325, and it is the reason that measurement was pure waste rather than merely expensive. `RefreshLinkedReferenceStrips` ends in `ReferenceStripRegistry.Register([(strip.Id, strip.Png)])`; `Register` opens with `if (... Sheets.ContainsKey(id)) continue`, and the id went into that dictionary when the view was taped up. So the new bytes are dropped on the floor. `ScenePassBuilder.ReferenceSpecs` and `SequenceExporter` both draw from the registry, so the canvas — and an export — keep the picture the view had at tape time. It corrects itself on reopen, because the registry is populated fresh from `strip.Png` when the document loads.
  - **Measured, not reasoned:** after drawing on the sheet, `strip.Png` changes and the decoded `SKBitmap` the registry hands the compositor does not. Q69 chose "live" over "a snapshot with a refresh button" and the code has been paying live's price without delivering it.
  - **Filed rather than fixed, and the reason is a lifetime protocol that does not exist yet.** The obvious repair — `Forget` then `Register` — disposes a bitmap the compositor may be mid-draw on. That is B130's exact signature, and `CanvasControl`'s retirement queue documents the crash from doing it by a fixed-count heuristic: *"safe only for as long as publishes never outran renders"*. Strip bitmaps are deliberately outside the `PinPasses` protocol (`PinPasses` pins into the frame and flatten caches; a strip bitmap belongs to neither and passes through as a no-op), and today that is safe **only because `Register` refuses to replace** — the no-op is accidentally load-bearing.
  - So a real fix is one of: extend pin/unpin to the strip registry, or stop round-tripping through PNG for a view-linked strip and composite the view's layers as passes from the frame cache, which are already pinned and already live. The second is probably the right design and removes the encode entirely. Cost: M–L, and it needs measuring before building.
  - **The manual currently promises this works** — `docs/manual/08-onion-skin-and-references.md`, *"It stays **live**: draw on the sheet … and the taped copy on the canvas updates by itself"*, and the same claim for the reference board and for a projected board tile. Left alone deliberately rather than overlooked: correcting it is this entry's objective, not B325's, and whoever takes this one either makes the sentence true or marks it *Planned*. Until then the manual documents a feature that does not work, which is the thing `CLAUDE.md` says is worse than no manual.

- [ ] **B170** `P2` `canvas` Lightbox sometimes dies while erasing `evidence: manual`
  - Reported alongside B169 — "sometimes crashing the application" — and filed separately on purpose: B169 has a mechanism and a headless test, this has neither, and folding them together would let a fix for the visible half close the half that takes the work with it.
  - No repro yet. What is known: it is intermittent, it is during an erase rather than after, and B169 says the erase preview is already doing something to the shared composite surface that no other tool does. The compose paths are also where `B125`'s GPU residency lives, and a surface the driver refused falls back to CPU mid-stroke.
  - **First step is not a fix, it is a repro.** `CrashReporter` and `DiagnosticLog` are already in the tree; the next sighting should arrive with a log rather than a sentence.
  - `evidence: manual` because there is nothing yet to name. It stays manual only until a repro exists — an intermittent crash that gets a test is no longer intermittent.
  - P2 on blocks work × occasional. Cost: M, and mostly diagnosis.
  - **Diagnosis 2026-08-12, alongside B169's fix. Still not reproduced — what follows is a named hazard with a code path, not an established cause, and the entry stays open for that reason.** The live stroke's scratch bitmap crosses to the render thread with **no protocol at all**. `PinPasses` walks `passes[i].Bitmap` and nothing else, so `StrokeOverlay.Scratch` — which is `_liveScratch` or `_livePostScratch`, both owned and mutated by the UI thread — is handed to a `DeferredCompose` unpinned and uncopied. `Materialise` then draws from it on the render thread, whenever the draw op gets there, while the UI thread is free to stamp the next dab into it, `Clear` a region of it, or (`EnsureLiveScratch`, and the realloc in `RenderLivePostProcess`) **dispose it and allocate a replacement**. A read concurrent with a write is torn pixels; a read concurrent with a dispose is a native access violation, which is the shape of this report.
  - **Why it can fire mid-stroke at all, given the routing.** The deferred routes need `dirty is null`, and an ordinary pointer event marks a bounded region — so drawing normally takes the ring, which composes on the UI thread and is safe by construction. Two things break that: `RenderLivePostProcess` calls `InvalidateWholeCanvas()` whenever its pass returns no bounds, mid-stroke, which makes the very next publish whole-canvas and therefore culled; and with the unbounded canvas on, `tileNative` sends **every** publish down the deferred route regardless of dirty. So the window opens on exactly the publishes that are already unusual, which is what "sometimes" looks like from the outside.
  - **What this does not establish, and it is the part that keeps the entry open: nothing here is eraser-specific.** Every live stroke publishes an overlay the same way, so if this were the whole story the brush would crash too. Either the report's "while erasing" is incidental to what the artist happened to be doing, or something narrows it that has not been found. Recording a mechanism that does not explain the one detail the report is sure about would be exactly the "number was real and the attribution was not" mistake `docs/DESIGN-performance.md` warns about.
  - **The fix is a decision rather than a patch, which is why it is not in this branch.** A deferred compose must not reference a bitmap the UI thread still owns, so the publisher has to hand over a snapshot instead — a copy of the stroke's scratch, per publish, on the drawing path. That is precisely the shape invariant 6 forbids paying casually: at 4K a document-sized copy is the cost B39's comment measured at ~1 s. The affordable version copies only the stroke's used region, which means teaching the overlay a bounds, and that wants measuring against `LongStrokeCostTests` before it is chosen. **See the pull request for the question as put to the owner.**
  - Two cheap things that are *not* the fix and would make the next sighting evidence: have `CrashReporter` record whether a stroke was live and which route the last publish took, and assert in a debug build that a pass handed to `DeferredCompose` carries no overlay whose scratch the view model still owns.
  - **The owner answered the pull request's question (2026-08-15): diagnostics only, for now.** The bounded-copy fix — teach the overlay a bounds, copy only the stroke's used region per publish, measure against `LongStrokeCostTests` — stays on the table and unbuilt; what it costs is a copy on every live publish for a crash that has fired twice, and the decision is to buy evidence before buying the copy. Both diagnostics are in: `DiagnosticLog.NoteRender` stamps every publish with the stroke-live flag and the route (plain field writes, formatted only if a crash report is actually written, so the drawing path pays two stores), and the crash log's `render` line carries it. The debug assert guards the **culled** deferred route only — the tiled route sends every unbounded-canvas publish deferred, overlays included, so asserting there would fire on every unbounded stroke and be noise rather than a tripwire; that known crossing is exactly what the breadcrumb records instead.
  - **A neighbouring crash with this report's exact presentation was found and fixed meanwhile: B213**, a native use-after-free on any publish whose working set outgrows the frame cache — no managed stack, empty log, SIGSEGV. It is *not* established as this bug (B213 needs a deep or over-budget document, and nothing in this report says the erased document was one), but the next sighting's breadcrumb plus B213's fix being in will either clear it or leave this entry pointing at the scratch handoff alone.

- [ ] **B167** `P2` `canvas` Playback composites through the tiled path, which is entirely on the CPU and is 66–84% of the frame budget at 4K `evidence: manual`
  - **The route playback actually takes, and the one B125 never reached.** `tileModeOn = UnboundedCanvasOn || IsPlaying`, so pressing play changes the compositor: a 4K document paused goes through the ring, the same document playing goes through tiles. There is no resolution term in the decision at all.
  - Measured on the owner's machine, 4K at 300 dpi, 2 layers, not zoomed in: **Display quality 49.49 ms/tick Compose, 66% of budget, 3 frames dropped; Full quality 60.42 ms/tick, 84%, 47 dropped.** 100% of layer passes tiled in both, and **zero publishes reached the GPU path**.
  - **B125 stages 1–5 targeted the culled route, which playback never takes.** That was a real mis-aim rather than a wasted effort — the machinery (pin protocol, identity harness, `DeferredCompose`, `GpuComposite`, `LayerTextureCache`) is sound and reusable; it was pointed at the wrong compositor. `docs/DESIGN-tiled-compositor.md` points the same machinery at the right one.
  - **The blocker dissolves rather than needing to be confronted.** `_tileFrames` is owned by the view model and the draw op cannot reach it — but *after flattening, a tile pass is just a bitmap pass*, and `DeferredCompose` already carries those across the thread with a working pin protocol. The tile cache never has to move.
  - Six phases, each independently landable and none of them changing what an artist sees until the last changes how fast: **measure the flatten/blend split** (the report cannot currently tell them apart, and optimising the wrong half is the same mistake B125 made one level up), **cache the flattened bitmap**, **move the composite into the draw op** measured against `ComposeIdentityTests`, **GPU surface** (the gate — upload cost on integrated graphics decides everything after it), **resident tiles** only if that gate says so, then **retire** `ComposeUnboundedSnapshot` and the ring.
  - The ring stays CPU on purpose: it reuses three buffers and patches a dirty region, and B121 measured what breaking that costs — 1 232 px becoming 134 400 px, 0.26 ms becoming 76 ms at 4K. Drawing is already cheap; playback is not.
  - Cost: L, and the phases are the point — see the note rather than re-deriving them.

- [ ] **B165** `P2` `canvas` Every layer is recomposited on every frame, including the ones that did not change `evidence: manual`
  - **The layer-count axis, and the reason B125 alone does not reach the roadmap's own targets.** During playback the compositor blends every layer of every frame from scratch: a five-frame, two-layer capture shows **1138 layer passes over 568 ticks** — two per tick, every tick. A held background, a colour-hold layer, a locked BG plate and a static prop are all re-blended twelve times a second to produce pixels identical to the ones already on screen.
  - Why it survives B125 rather than being absorbed by it: compositing costs *area* × *layers*. GPU compositing divides the area term and leaves the layer term untouched, and they multiply. B125's own 8K measurement is **1344% of the playback budget for three layers**; a 20× GPU win makes that 67%, and the same frame at ten layers is **224% after the GPU**. Ten layers is an ordinary character rig, not a stress test.
  - The shape of a fix: cache the composited result of the contiguous run of layers below the lowest one that changed, and blend only from there up. The playhead moving changes which *drawings* are exposed, so the invalidation key is per layer per frame rather than per layer — which is the part to get right.
  - **The risk is stale pixels, and this codebase says in its own words that it is the failure it is least able to notice.** A wrong invalidation shows yesterday's art silently: no exception, no red test, and an artist who cannot tell it from their own drawing. Any implementation needs a test that changes a layer *under* a cached run and asserts the composite followed — the case a naive "did this layer change" key gets wrong.
  - **Measured 2026-08-10, and it is bigger than this entry guessed.** `UnchangedLayerRun` computes the saving from the exposure sheet rather than from pixels — whether a layer's drawing changes between two playhead positions is a property of the sheet, so the whole question is answerable before anything is composed. Over a 24-frame range: **2 layers 26.1% of blends saved, 6 layers 50.7%, 10 layers 59.1%.**
  - **The reason is holds, not background layers, and that is the finding.** This entry expected a two-layer scene to be "a rounding error" because a held paper under one drawing layer has depth 1 and saves nothing. It measured 26%. Both the entry's guess and mine were wrong the same way: **an artist working on 2s holds every drawing layer on every second frame**, so half the transitions have the *entire stack* unchanged rather than just the paper. The same two layers animated on 1s save exactly 0.0%. Working on 2s is the norm rather than the exception, so the fix is worth more on ordinary documents than on the stress case.
  - The rule the fix rests on: the run must be **contiguous from the bottom**, ending at the first layer whose drawing moved. Compositing is ordered, so a static layer *above* a changed one saves nothing — its pixels sit on top of pixels that changed. `AStaticLayerAboveAMovingOneIsNotPartOfTheRun` is the guard, and it is the case a naive "which layers changed" implementation gets wrong.
  - Foldability is `LayerStackBake`'s rule, shared rather than restated: correctness rests on premultiplied source-over being associative, so a Multiply layer ends the run whether or not it moved.
  - **`LayerStackBake` is most of the machinery already, and its own remarks name the gap:** *"the caller also skips folding outright during playback, where keys never repeat by construction."* That is true of its key — the whole segment — and false of the layers inside it. Same idea, different key.
  - Sized **S–M** rather than "unknown": the measurement is done, the invalidation key is settled, and the remaining work is wiring a bake whose key is the bottom run.
  - **The other half landed too: whole-frame reuse (2026-08-10).** If the playhead moves to a position where every visible layer exposes the same drawing, the composite would be identical and is not performed. `FrameFingerprint` carries everything outside the layer stack that a composite reads — frame index, compose scale, viewport, camera, visible layer count — so "nothing changed" is a decision rather than a hope, and adding an input to compositing without adding it there is a visible omission.
  - **Route-independent, which is why it matters more than the fold.** B125's GPU work only reaches the culled route and playback takes the tiled one; skipping applies wherever the composite would have happened. The owner's 4K report measured Compose at **62.76 ms of an 83.3 ms budget**, the largest single cost in the tick, and on 2s roughly half of playhead positions expose no new drawing.
  - **It uses `NothingExposedChanged`, not `Depth == VisibleLayers`, and the difference is real.** `Depth` stops at a blend that reads what is beneath it, because associativity is what licenses *folding*. Nothing about that applies to asking whether the picture moved — a held Multiply shadow is exactly as unchanged as a held SrcOver one — and conflating them would have excluded every document with a Multiply layer near the bottom from a saving it is entitled to.
  - **A camera is refused outright rather than compared**, because a keyframed camera moves every pixel while the drawings hold perfectly still, and telling that apart from a still camera is not a judgement this guard should make.
  - **Ten tests failed at once and were right to.** The first version also reused a republish at the *same* frame index. That looks free — identical pixels — and nothing in playback ever asks for one, because the tick always advances the playhead. What it actually did was refuse an explicit "publish this now" from everywhere else. The guard now requires the playhead to have moved.
  - The reuse guard rests on an existing contract: **anything that changes pixels already marks the canvas dirty**, or it would not reach the screen today either. `InvalidateWholeCanvas` also forgets the fingerprint, so the dependency is explicit rather than implicit.

  - **Wired 2026-08-10: `LayerStackBake.FoldHeldRun`, folding the run that holds still for the whole playback range.** The bake already had the key machinery — bitmap identity plus content version, seen twice before it pays for a bake — and its own remarks named the gap: *"the caller also skips folding outright during playback, where keys never repeat by construction."* True of the key `Fold` uses, the whole not-being-drawn-on segment, which changes the moment any layer exposes a new cel. False of the held prefix.
  - **The durable prefix, not the momentarily-unchanged run, and this is the correction to the sizing above.** `Depth` compares two adjacent frames, and on 2s its answer alternates — the whole stack on a hold, just the paper on a key. A bake keyed on that would rebuild every frame, which is the cost it exists to avoid. `HeldPrefix` is the layers holding still across the whole range, whose key is identical on every frame. **So the mechanism captures less than the 26/51/59% measured**: that figure includes the hold frames where nothing at all moved, which is whole-frame reuse rather than a layer fold and needs its own mechanism. `BakeableSaving` reports the half this delivers, and the two are kept apart on purpose rather than one number being quoted for both.
  - **Both folds are called every publish, including the one that will decline.** Each owns a "was I serving a bake" flag, and skipping the call leaves it stale — so stopping playback could miss a fold transition, and a missed transition is folded and unfolded pixels mixed on one surface by a dirty-region patch. Declining is cheap; not asking is not. That was a real bug in the first draft of the wiring.
  - **What the tests spring and what they do not.** The pixel tests hold: a folded playback frame matches a layer-by-layer one to within rounding, a mark on a layer that was inside the run shows on the next publish, and stopping playback does not leave the held bake serving. **Deleting the content version from the key leaves them all green** — checked by mutation, not assumed — which is the same limit `LayerStackBake` already records about its own version half: a re-render hands over a new bitmap instance, so the key misses on identity before it reaches the version. The version stays as defence against an in-place mutation path that does not route through active-layer segmentation, and the test says so rather than implying coverage it does not have.

  - **Not to be started before B125.** Not because it depends on it, but because the measurement that sizes it does: on a two-layer test scene the win may be a rounding error, and on a ten-layer rig at 4K it is the difference between playable and not. Measure the unchanged-layer share on a real scene first — cheap, and it decides whether this is S or M.
  - Cost: M, and unknown until that measurement.

  - Repro: a 3-layer scene, drag the playhead. Measured p95 **124 ms** at 720p against a 16 ms interaction budget — the cliff is at **12 frames**, which is well inside the cache, so this is not B28. Scrubbing is simply a full recomposite and a full recomposite is not cheap.

One cause, four symptoms — filed once, on purpose. Filing the symptoms separately would have four people fixing the same blend loop.

Linear in layers — measured **n^0.99**, so nothing is accidentally quadratic — and the constant is simply large: about 20 ms per 1080p layer on this container.
  - Why drawing does not suffer: `ComposeRing` repaints only the region a stroke touched, which is the whole reason that class exists. The gap is that **a frame change has no equivalent** — it always goes wide.

It had not: the sweep's paint is character-for-character what `SceneRenderer.DrawPass` builds. Timed at 1920×1080 on this container — **no paint at all 18.53 ms, an empty paint 18.60, `DrawPass`'s paint 18.80.** Under one and a half per cent between them. The blit itself is the cost, at about 9 ns a pixel, so there is no cheap fix hiding in the paint and the structural ones below are the only ones there are.

A miss is **worse than doing nothing**: 463 ms against 434 at 24 layers, and the cliff moves from **8 layers to 4**, because the cache pays to rebuild the side and then pays again to blend it. And onion ghosts still build as bitmap passes during a scrub — `FlattenTilePasses` converts the tile-native passes and leaves the rest, so a mixed list composes correctly and a scrub with onion on simply wins less. `AScrubStillDrawsItsGhostsAndTheyAreNotTilePasses` holds that, because a ghost silently vanishing mid-drag is the failure worth guarding.

  - **The layer axis is now swept to 100 (2026-08-14), and the side cache's case gets stronger with depth.** A hit stays flat the whole way — 34.8 ms p50 at 100 layers, `n^0.01` — while the plain recomposite is 1.04 s at 64 layers and **7.1 s at 100**, where a single frame's cels stop fitting the frame cache and every recomposite re-rasterizes what was just evicted (B198 owns that wall). So at working depths the candidate's win is the 12× above; past the residency wall it is the difference between usable and not, because two held surfaces also remove the need to keep every cel resident.
  - **Candidate 1 is built (2026-08-15), as the rework of `LayerStackBake` recorded under B198** — spec-keyed segments that skip the fetches they cover, invalidated through the render funnel, guarded by the change-a-layer-under-the-run test this entry asked for. What it delivers is what the measurement above promised and no more: the deep-stack cliff flattens and the residency wall dissolves, **and the entry stays open**, because a perfect hit still floors at two full-canvas blits (~35 ms at 1080p) against a 16 ms scrub budget. The remaining term is *area*, which is B82's — composite the visible rectangle rather than the whole document — and every other symptom row above (onion, playback at depth) now rests on that term too.

- [ ] **B137** `P3` `canvas` A baseline that will not decode crashes the render instead of being skipped `evidence: ACorruptBaselineIsSkippedRatherThanFatal`
  - Repro: give any frame a `PngBase64` that is valid base64 but not a PNG, then let the canvas publish. `FrameRasterizer.Materialize` calls `PngCodec.Decode` unguarded (`FrameRasterizer.cs:117`), SkiaSharp finds no codec, and `SKBitmap.Decode` throws `ArgumentNullException: Value cannot be null. (Parameter 'codec')` — out through `FrameBitmapCache.Get` and `PublishSnapshot`, taking down whatever edit triggered the repaint.
  - **Found sideways, and how is the interesting part.** A test in the frame-class collapse used three arbitrary bytes as a stand-in baseline. Under the old code the operation it drove — pasting a cel with pixels onto a vector layer — was *refused*, so nothing ever decoded them. The moment the refusal went, the same three bytes reached the renderer. The bad test data was mine; the unguarded decode is not new, and `git show 5855b80:src/Lightbox.Raster/FrameRasterizer.cs` has the identical call.
  - **The inconsistency is the argument.** `MainViewModel.ResampleBaseline` already treats this exact case as survivable — *"Corrupt baseline: leave it untouched rather than destroy pixels"* — so the write path, which runs once per transform, is defensive, and the read path, which runs on every repaint, is not. That is the wrong way round.
  - P3 because nothing in the application can currently produce a corrupt baseline: every writer re-encodes Skia's own output. It needs a file edited by hand, truncated on disc, or written by a future importer. That last one is why it is filed rather than shrugged at — import is the feature that creates baselines, and a half-written file is exactly what this does with one.
  - Fix: a decode that returns null and a decode that throws both mean "no usable baseline". Skip it and render the strokes, rather than losing the frame and the edit. Cost: S.

- [ ] **B126** `P3` `canvas` Windows draws its own pointer over the brush ring while a pen hovers `evidence: manual`
  - Reported as *"an annoying flicker between the brush tip and Windows' own pointer"*. **Mouse: none whatsoever. Huion pen tablet: constant.**
  - **The cause first recorded here was wrong, and the correction is the useful part.** This entry originally said the ring is composited in the same `DrawOp` as the artwork, so it only moves when the canvas redraws — a real coupling, and not this. That explanation predicts mouse and pen behaving identically, and the reporter's very next sentence was that the mouse is stable. **A cause that does not distinguish the cases the symptom distinguishes is not the cause**, and it survived a whole exchange only because nobody asked it to.
  - What it actually is, characterised on the reporter's machine rather than reasoned about:
    - the **ring stays put** — it is the OS pointer that appears and disappears over it, so nothing is wrong with what Lightbox draws;
    - it happens on **hover** and persists with the pen **held still**, so it is not driven by motion — a stationary pen still reports at the tablet's polling rate;
    - it **never happens while drawing**, which is precisely where `e.Pointer.Capture(this)` is in force. The flicker lives exactly where capture is absent.
  - So the working explanation is that the cursor is re-evaluated per hover frame and something in that path alternates between the canvas's `StandardCursorType.None` and the default arrow, while capture pins it during a stroke. **Stated as a hypothesis** — the mechanism is not proven, and this repository has already been embarrassed once today by a confident cause.
  - Not fixable by switching input path, checked rather than assumed: **`Avalonia.Win32` contains no WinTab support at all** (zero references in the shipped assembly), so Windows Ink / `WM_POINTER` is the only pen route. Disabling Windows Ink in the Huion driver would therefore not trade one working mode for another — `PressureOf` returns 1.0 for anything that is not `PointerType.Pen`, so **every stroke would paint flat at full pressure**. Confirmed the same way: the Windows "show cursor" and "show visual effects" pen settings were both turned off and the flicker survived.
  - Also worth recording: Avalonia never calls `SetWindowFeedbackSetting`, the per-window Win32 API that configures pen feedback, so Windows' defaults are simply left in place. That is the one documented, non-invasive lever nobody has pulled.
  - **Downgraded to P3.** It was filed P1 on the belief that it was the drawing latency an artist feels first. It is not: it is hover-only chrome that vanishes the moment a stroke begins, and drawing at 4K/300dpi is reported as responsive. It is annoying and it is cosmetic.
  - Options, none taken: `ShowCursor(false)` bracketed by pointer enter and exit works but is a process-wide counter and an unbalanced pair hides the cursor across every window; `SetWindowFeedbackSetting` is per-window and safe but may not reach the cursor at all; an upstream report to Avalonia is the right long-term route and this entry's characterisation is most of one. Nothing here is verifiable in this repository — there is no pen and no Windows — so any fix must be checked on the reporter's machine before it is believed. Cost: M
  - **New evidence, 2026-08-17, and a decided next step.** The same machine now also shows hover flyouts ignoring the pen and collapsing the moment they open (**B254**) — a second symptom the eventual cause must explain, and one that strengthens the enter/leave-churn / second-device candidates over anything cursor-specific. **Q115** chose to instrument before fixing: an input event trace on the diagnostics surface (device type and id, event kind, enter/leave, cursor decisions, timestamps), run for a minute of hovering on the reporter's machine, so the one round-trip a fix needs anyway is spent identifying the mechanism instead of checking a guess.
  - **The instrument is built** (`Services/InputTrace.cs`, `F9`, report beside the crash logs). What it settles, and how to read it — this is the protocol, so a later session does not have to re-derive it:

    | The report says | The mechanism | What to try |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | *Two pointer streams interleave* | The driver emits an emulated mouse beside the pen; each stream undoes the other's cursor and steals the popup's pointer | Suppress the echo stream while a pen is in proximity — in Lightbox if the ids are distinguishable, upstream if they are not |
    | *The pointer left and re-entered N times* | Proximity flapping. Every exit re-arms the window's default cursor and light-dismisses hover UI, which is both symptoms at once | `SetWindowFeedbackSetting`, or a short exit-debounce before the cursor and popups react |
    | *Lightbox … never changed its mind* | Not ours. One decision, one assignment, and the arrow still flickered | Upstream report to Avalonia, carrying the trace — the characterisation here is most of one already |

  - **How a fix is measured, rather than felt.** The counters are the before-and-after: `moves/s`, `stream alternations`, `canvas enter/exit`, `popups collapsed`. One traced minute of the same ritual on each side of the change — hover still, hover moving, draw a stroke, open a flyout — and the two reports go in this entry. **A fix that does not move a counter did not fix anything**, whatever it looks like; a flicker is exactly the kind of intermittent thing that both looks cured and is not. Note the trap the instrument itself fell into and now guards: a short trace extrapolates a per-minute rate from noise, so the comparison is only honest at a comparable duration, and anything under five seconds refuses to conclude at all.
  - **What the trace cannot see, said plainly so it is not over-read.** It starts when the event reaches Avalonia, so anything the driver or Windows does before that is invisible — which is precisely why the third row above is a *finding* rather than a failure. `InputTraceTests` pins the wording and the attribution; deliberately not evidence anchors here, because they prove the instrument rather than the fix, the same split `StrokeToScreenTests` makes for B189.
  - **MEASURED, 2026-08-17, on the reporter's machine. The mechanism is no longer a hypothesis.** 30.3 s, 4,395 events, Windows 10.0.22631, build `0.1.0-alpha.65`:

    | Evidence | Number |
    | --- | --- |
    | Devices seen | `Pen 1001` (2,389 ev), `Pen 1009` (1,002), **`Mouse 1000` (994)**, `Pen 1006` (9) |
    | Exit→Enter pairs | **663, of which 663 are a device switch and 0 are the same device** |
    | Which switches | 661 of 663 are Pen ↔ `Mouse 1000`; 2 are pen-to-pen |
    | Gap across the switch | median **0.5 ms**, p90 0.8 ms |
    | `Mouse 1000` coordinates | **0% fractional** — every sample on an integer pixel, pressure exactly 0.50, no tilt |
    | Pen coordinates | **89% fractional**, real pressure to 1.00, tilt reported |
    | Cursor | **1 decision (`start→Paint`), 0 reassignments** in 30 s across 3,055 hover moves |
    | Exits while the pen was down | **0 of 664**, across 4 strokes totalling ~11.5 s |

  - **`Mouse 1000` is not a mouse.** Integer-only coordinates, Avalonia's default 0.50 pressure and no tilt, interleaved with the pen at sub-millisecond spacing — it is Windows Ink's mouse emulation shadowing the pen, snapped to whole pixels. No human mouse produces 994 events perfectly alternating with a pen stream.
  - **So the chain is closed:** the echo stream makes the canvas fire `Exit`+`Enter` ~22×/s → each `Exit` nulls `_hoverPoint` (the ring is torn down) and light-dismisses hover UI (**B254**) → the canvas's hidden cursor stops applying while the pointer is "away", so the window's arrow shows for the length of the gap. That is the flicker. `Pointer.Capture` during a stroke suppresses the churn entirely, which is why the reporter always said it never happens while drawing — now measured as 0 of 664.
  - **The correction that matters most: this is fixable here.** The instrument's third verdict said that a trace where Lightbox never changed its cursor meant the fix belonged upstream, and that sentence is wrong — the *cause* is below the app, but Lightbox chooses how to react to the exits, and that is where the cure is. The wording is fixed; had it stood, it would have parked a fixable P2 as somebody else's bug. **A verdict that names a culprit must not also assume a venue.**
  - **Fixed, pending the reporter's confirmation** — `Services/PenEchoFilter.cs`, installed before any window exists. It marks a mouse event `Handled` at `IInputManager.PreProcess` when a pen event arrived within **200 ms**, which is ahead of the pointer-over recomputation and therefore ahead of the enter/exit pair that is B126, B254 and B255 alike. Three properties of the guard, each measured rather than chosen:
    - **200 ms against a measured median handoff of 0.5 ms** (p90 0.8 ms) — two orders of magnitude of headroom, sized for the fastest a person swaps pen for mouse rather than for the echo it has to catch.
    - **A machine with no pen can never engage it**: the clock is only ever set by a pen event, so with none the filter is a branch that is never taken.
    - **Buttons are never dropped, only moves and leaves.** A swallowed move costs a few milliseconds of position the next event corrects; a swallowed press costs a click the artist meant, with nothing to correct it. The churn is made entirely of moves and the enter/exit they imply.
  - **It is reflection, and that is a cost worth naming.** `IInputManager.PreProcess` and the `RawPointerEventArgs` members are public on Avalonia 12.1.1's *runtime* assembly and hidden by the *reference* assembly it ships, so the call compiles nowhere and works everywhere. There is no second lever: pointer-over is recomputed inside the input manager ahead of any routed event, and `PointerEntered`/`PointerExited` are `Direct`-routed, so no ancestor ever sees them to intercept. The failure mode is chosen to be safe — an unresolved member means nothing is filtered and the application behaves exactly as it does today — and `TheRawInputHooksStillResolve` fails the build rather than letting an Avalonia upgrade silently restore the freeze.
  - **The first fixed build did not install the filter at all, and the counter is the only reason anybody knows.** The reporter's confirmation trace (2026-08-18, alpha.67) read **`echo events dropped 0`** with every symptom untouched — 725 alternations, 318 of 323 popups collapsed, **10 UI-thread stalls, worst 6.9 s**. The fault was one line of reflection: the input manager was looked up in `typeof(Application).Assembly`, which is **`Avalonia.Controls`**, while `AvaloniaLocator` lives in **`Avalonia.Base`**. It resolved to null, `Install` recorded "no input manager (headless)" on a desktop, and stood down.
  - **The lesson is about where the untested part was, not about the typo.** The filter's *policy* had eight tests — the window, the pen-less guard, the button asymmetry, the move-like list, the resolve check — and the three lines deciding whether the policy ever ran sat in `App.axaml.cs`, which no test reaches. **The covered part was correct and the uncovered part was the whole feature.** The lookup now lives in `PenEchoFilter.FindInputManager`, `Resolve` checks the locator type, and `TheInputManagerIsFound` fails against the shipped bug — verified by reintroducing it.
  - **The counter now names the reason as well as the number.** `echo events dropped 0` could mean "declined to engage" or "never installed", and those want opposite responses; the report prints `(filter not installed: …)` when `Unavailable` is set. A counter that reads zero for two reasons has to say which.
  - **Seventh trace, alpha.72 — the stalls are largely solved, and the fix was the change nobody credited.** Blocked time **30% → 6%** of the session (19.3 s → 1.5 s), stalls **43 → 5** (0.68/s → 0.19/s), worst **600 ms → 363 ms**. The only thing that could have done that is dropping the enter/exit `InvalidateVisual` pair — which was landed explicitly as *waste removal, not asserted to be the stall cause*, because there was no evidence for it at the time. It was the fix.
  - **And garbage collection is exonerated by the counter added to catch it: `GC pause total 114 ms`, 7% of the blocked time.** The `DrawOp` retention theory — thirty-five captured fields, one allocated per repaint, matching an upstream report the owner found — was the most convincing hypothesis of the whole investigation and it is **wrong**. Had it been "fixed" on conviction, the work would have gone into restructuring the draw path while the actual cause (repaint *count*, not repaint *cost*) sat untouched.
  - **The pair is the lesson worth keeping.** The change with no evidence behind it did the work; the theory with a mechanism, a matching upstream report and a plausible profile did not. Across this bug the score is now: four fixes shipped on conviction, of which one worked, one regressed and two did nothing — against three measurements, all three of which were decisive. **Measure, then act; and when a measurement contradicts a good story, the story loses.**
  - **What remains: 5 stalls, worst 363 ms, 6% blocked.** Real but no longer the headline, and the cause is unidentified — not popups (zero), not GC (7%), not repaint count (already removed). The churn itself is unchanged at ~86 enter/exit a second, as expected, since nothing in the app can reach it.
  - **Sixth trace, alpha.71 — the popup theory is finished and two of B256's hypotheses died with it.** `SubmenuCloseGrace` had already cut popups to nothing; this session opened **zero popups** and still recorded **43 UI-thread stalls, 30% of the session blocked, worst 600 ms**. Whatever blocks the thread is not popups, not native windows, and not the submenu rate.
  - **What is left is allocation, and the shape of the code invites it.** `CanvasControl.DrawOp` is an `ICustomDrawOperation` whose primary constructor captures ~35 arguments as fields — a `RenderSnapshot` owning a full-canvas image, a `LayerTextureCache`, a `PresentedFrame`, several `SKPath`s and a dozen lists — while `Dispose` releases three of them. **One is allocated per repaint**, and the enter/exit churn was driving ~97 repaints a second. The owner found the matching report upstream (an Avalonia issue about a wrapper holding a `DrawingContext` past its call, needing two GC passes to free) which is the same pattern one level up.
  - **Measured rather than assumed, again.** `GC.GetTotalPauseDuration()` and the per-generation counts now ride the report. If the runtime's pause total is close to the heartbeat's blocked total, the stalls are collection and the fix is allocation; if it is a small fraction, garbage collection is exonerated and the next hypothesis gets its turn. **Two counters, one answer, no argument.**
  - **And the enter/exit repaints are gone**, which is waste removal rather than a fix: since the leave grace an exit changes nothing on screen, so its `InvalidateVisual` repainted an identical canvas ~97 times a second, and the enter repainted it back. Removing work that provably changes no pixel is right on its own terms — whether it moves the stall count is the next trace's to say.
  - **The whole approach is disproven, and the filter is reverted.** With the lookup fixed, the third trace (alpha.68) read **`echo events dropped 1163`** — the filter running at last — and the churn went *up*: 26 → **39 alternations a second**, worst UI-thread stall **6.9 s → 18.9 s**. A headless experiment settled why rather than a fourth guess: with the filter installed and engaged, a synthetic mouse move **still reached the control**. **Marking a raw pointer event `Handled` at `PreProcess` does not stop Avalonia delivering it**, so the filter was inert and its counter was counting events it had not prevented.
  - **`PenEchoFilter` is deleted rather than kept and annotated** (the owner's call). Dead code that increments a plausible-looking counter is worse than absent code: the next session to read `echo events dropped 1163` would reasonably conclude the echo was handled. The finding is what is worth keeping, and it lives here — **do not retry raw-input suppression in Avalonia 12.1.1.** There is no wndproc hook in `Avalonia.Win32` 12.1.1 either (`Win32Properties` is not exported), and `PointerEntered`/`PointerExited` are `Direct`-routed, so no ancestor can intercept them.
  - **What is fixed here instead is the app's own reaction, in two places, because there are two mechanisms.** `LeaveGraceMs` in `CanvasControl.Pointer.cs` makes a departure count only once it has lasted 50 ms — against a p90 churn gap of 0.8 ms and a longest genuine departure of 16 s — so the brush ring stops being torn down 39 times a second. And `OverlayPopups = true` makes a popup cost a visual rather than a window, which is the measured cause of B255's freeze. Neither stops the echo; both stop it mattering.
  - **Reverted, 2026-08-18: mirroring the canvas cursor onto the window did not fix the flicker and broke the mouse.** With a mouse the window kept the canvas's hidden cursor and the artist had no pointer to navigate the UI with — "near impossible", and worse than the bug. It also did not work: the flicker was reported unchanged. The idea was that the arrow appears because the window's cursor is the fallback when pointer-over leaves the canvas; that may still be true, but the fix's cost is unacceptable and its benefit is unobserved, so it goes back.
  - **The fifth trace kills the popup theory for the residual stalls, and that is the most useful thing in it.** `SubmenuCloseGrace` worked exactly as designed — popup opens **2,763 → 11**, with 1,258 closes refused — and the stalls did **not** improve: **39 → 54, worst 849 → 945 ms**. So popup churn caused the *huge* native-window freezes (18.9 s), and something else entirely causes the ~0.9 s ones. Do not spend more effort on popups.
  - **How the reporter confirms it**, since nothing here can: a traced minute on the fixed build, doing the thing that froze it. `UI-thread stalls` is the number that decides B255 — it was 12, worst 18.9 s. `stream alternations` and `canvas enter/exit` will **not** fall, because the echo is untouched; what should change is that the ring no longer strobes and the menus no longer seize. `popups are in-window overlays` on the counters line confirms the setting took.
  - Two instrument defects the same run exposed, both fixed: the popup hooks watched `FlyoutBase` and `ToolTip` and so recorded **"popups opened 0" for a session that opened a context menu and a submenu** — neither of which has an `IsOpenProperty`; `Popup.IsOpenProperty` plus `MenuItem.IsSubMenuOpenProperty` is what covers them. And a 16.4 s silence could not be told from the freeze the reporter described, because the trace watches only the canvas: a **dispatcher heartbeat** now records UI-thread stalls, so a silence is labelled *frozen* or *the pointer was elsewhere* instead of guessed at.

### colour

  - Reported: swatches appear not to be saved on creation in a project, and not saved or loaded for a standalone file either.
  - Distinct from **B10**, which was swatch *links* dying when a project was saved and reloaded and is fixed: this is the swatch itself never reaching the file. B10's guards (`ASavedProjectKeepsItsSwatchIds`) check that an id survives, which passes whether or not the palette entry behind it was written.

### export

- [ ] **B304** `P2` `export` A PSD import spends 97% of its time encoding canvas-sized baselines `evidence: BaselineRect, ALayerStoresOnlyItsOwnBoundsRatherThanTheWholeCanvas`
  - **Evidence.** Measured 2026-08-24, `PsdImportCostTests`, layers holding a
    300×300 patch on a large canvas:

    | Document | Parse | Baselines | On disk |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 1920×1080, 8 layers | 41 ms | 621 ms | 2 KB |
    | 1920×1080, 24 layers | 47 ms | 1,929 ms | 7 KB |
    | 3840×2160, 12 layers | 21 ms | 3,805 ms | 12 KB |

    Reading the PSD is 1–3% of the work. The rest is building one full-canvas PNG
    per layer — 8.3M pixels traversed at 4K to encode a picture that is almost
    entirely transparent.
  - **Not the reader's fault, and not a mistake either.** Baselines are
    canvas-sized by decision, because `FrameRasterizer.Materialize` draws a
    baseline stretched across the whole canvas, so a layer stored at its own
    bounds would be scaled up to fill the frame. The write-up of that decision
    claimed "only decode time and memory pay", which this measurement corrects:
    the *file size* half held up completely — 12 KB for a 4K import — and the
    *time* half did not.
  - **Filed rather than fixed, under the second exception.** The fix is a nullable
    rect beside the baseline, and that changes a serialized type read by
    `FrameRasterizer`, `ImageResize`, `MainViewModel.Crop`,
    `MainViewModel.Transform` and `LayerMerge`. It also changes what a `.lbx`
    contains, so it wants asking about rather than deciding inside a branch whose
    objective was reading PSDs. Cost M: the record and the rasterizer are S, the
    five readers and their round-trip tests are the bulk.
  - **Do not re-run the compression experiment.** PNG level is the obvious lever
    and is not one: zlib 1 saves about 20% of the encode, and zlib 0 takes the
    32 KB file to 32 MB. The work is proportional to canvas area whatever the
    encoder does, which is why only the rect helps.
  - Bounded, and only on import: nothing in the paint path does this, and a
    document already imported pays none of it again.

### project

- [ ] **B295** `P1` `project` `ids --fix` renumbers both entries of a duplicate filed inside this branch's own range, so the duplicate survives at the new number `evidence: _keeping_spots,cmd_selftest`

- [ ] **B300** `P2` `project` `ids` counts the branch's own remote ref as another branch, so rewriting a ledger entry you already pushed reads as a collision with yourself `evidence: cmd_ids,_ids_created_here`
  - **Editing an entry that is already on your own remote costs a spurious renumber.** `ids` takes "created by this branch" as *in HEAD but not in the merge base with the default branch*, and "created elsewhere" as *in any other ref but not in that merge base*. A branch's own `origin/<branch>` is one of those refs, so an id it filed and pushed is in both sets and reports as a clash against itself.
  - Reproduced on this branch 2026-08-24. B296 was filed and pushed; the entry was then rewritten in a later commit on the same branch; `ids` reported *"CLASHES ID B296 — another branch already took it"* quoting **this branch's own title**, and the pre-push autofix moved it to B299 and rewrote its citations. `origin/main` had no B296 at all at that moment, so nothing was actually colliding. **A postscript that reads as vindication and is not:** `main` acquired a B296 later the same day — a different bug, filed by a different branch (the `SimBaker` progress race) — so the renumber turned out to avoid a real collision. It avoided it *by luck*: the tool was comparing against this branch's own remote and quoting this branch's own title back, which is the defect regardless of what number somebody else took afterwards.
  - **The cost is exactly the churn the machinery exists to prevent** — a renumber on a branch whose objective is something else, plus every citation of the id going stale in commit messages and pull-request bodies that are already written. It also trains the reader to accept renumbers without checking, which is the habit B295 and B264 make dangerous.
  - The fix is to exclude the branch's own upstream from the "elsewhere" set, or to compare entry identity rather than bare presence so a rewritten entry is recognised as the same one. Filed rather than fixed because it is `project` domain on a `brush` branch, and because it sits beside two open bugs in the same tool (**B295**, **B264**) that want deciding together. Cost: S.

- [ ] **B283** `P2` `project` Removing or deleting a folder orphans the sheets filed in it `evidence: OrphanedSheetTests, RemovingAFolderReturnsItsSheetsToTheProject, DeletingAFolderDetachesTheSheetsFiledInIt`
  - **Evidence.** `ProjectFolders.Remove` re-homes a removed folder's *documents* to the project root (the orphaned list `RemoveFromProject` walks), and nothing does the same for sheets: no code path writes `SheetRef.FolderId = null` on folder removal (grep 2026-08-22), and `ProjectWindowViewModel.DeleteFromDisk`'s folder branch detaches contained documents only. A `SheetRef` whose `FolderId` names a removed folder is skipped by every listing — `Emit` walks existing folders plus null, `ProjectSheets.In` matches by id — so the sheet vanishes from the docker, the window and the reaching chain while its ref (and, for Remove, its file) still exists.
  - Delete permanently is the worse half: the folder's directory goes, taking the sheet's file with it, while the dangling ref survives in the manifest.
  - Filed rather than fixed because it was found while the Q150 branch (delete clears version history) was in hand — one objective per branch; this is the next branch. The fix mirrors the documents path: Remove re-homes sheets to the project (`FolderId = null`), Delete detaches their refs (and, with Q150, clears their histories). Cost: S

- [ ] **B269** `P2` `project` A full-solution test run sometimes executes hundreds fewer App tests than exist and still reports green `evidence: FullSuiteExecutionCountIsAsserted`
  - **Evidence.** Two `dotnet test` runs from the repository root on 2026-08-20,
    same container, trees differing only by additions: the first reported
    `Lightbox.App.Tests` as **3489 passed / 3489 total**, the second — after a
    merge that only *added* tests — **2889 / 2889**, exit 0, `Failed: 0,
    Skipped: 0`. Discovery on the same tree (`dotnet test --list-tests`) finds
    **3498**, and an immediate re-run of the assembly alone executed all
    **3498 / 3498**. So a full-solution run silently dropped ~600 tests and
    called the suite green.
  - **Why it matters more than a flaky failure.** A red flake wastes a re-run;
    this reports *success while proving less than it claims* — a regression in
    any of the missing 600 would ride a green suite to `main`. It is B259's
    condition (full-solution contention, four assemblies on the box at once)
    with the opposite symptom: there a test ran and failed, here tests never
    ran and nothing said so.

    very next solution run executed everything — and the fix is an

    is the guard the anchor names: assert the executed count against the
    discovered count (in CI or a wrapper), so an under-run turns red instead

It is not: outside a merge only one is ever in the tree, and inside one both are marked ours, so the filter is unreachable in every case. It was written, tested, shown to change nothing, and reverted rather than left in as an unguarded edit to merge logic.

- [ ] **B341** `P2` `transform` The first drag of a selection transform stalls for a third of a second `evidence: TransformSplitIsBuiltOnceTests, TheFirstDragOfASelectionTransformIsNotAStall, ACommitDoesNotRebuildTheSplitTheDragAlreadyBuilt, TracingAFullPageMaskIsLinear`

The overlay is fast throughout, which is the tell — the gizmo is not the slow part, the pixels behind it are.
  - **Measured on a 1920×1080 document, 60 strokes, one rectangular marquee, one drawing in scope.** With a selection: the first preview publish takes **346–389 ms** and every later one 12–14 ms; the commit takes **346–392 ms**. With no selection: 14 ms and 50–66 ms. So the whole of the difference is one piece of work, and it is paid twice — once lazily on the first pointer event of the drag, once again at the commit.
  - **Where it goes**, timed component by component on the same document: `FloodFill.TraceAllContours` over the inverted full-page mask is **240 ms** and returns ten points; `MaskFromContours` is **32 ms** and is called three times across the flow; `Doc.Clone` is 8 ms and each full-canvas rasterization 21 ms. The trace is the whole of it, and it is a breadth-first walk of 1.9 million pixels through a `Queue<int>` and a `yield return` neighbour enumerator, allocating a page-sized `bool[]` per component.

Preview-vs-commit divergence, the exact defect class `SceneRenderer.DrawStroke`'s own comment records.
  - Filed rather than fixed because the fix is not small: the carve has to apply in document space while the content moves in preview space, which means a shape matrix (or its inverse) plumbed through `RenderPass`/`PassSpec` and split from the parallax term that shapes *should* ride. Wrong only while the pen is down on a masked layer under the transform tool; every commit, export and still render is correct.

### ui

- [ ] **B281** `P1` `ui` The App suite sometimes runs a few hundred tests short and reports success anyway `evidence: manual`
  - **Measured 2026-08-17, on `main` at 28a2462 plus one small view change, same commit both times.** `dotnet test` on `Lightbox.App.Tests`, back to back: **2,779 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped, exit 0**, then **3,587 passed / 0 failed / 0 skipped, exit 0**. `--list-tests` discovers **3,587**. So the first run silently omitted **808 tests** and called itself green.
  - **Why this is P1 rather than a curiosity.** Every other guard in this project is built on the suite meaning what it says. A run that quietly covers 77% of itself and exits 0 makes "all four suites green" an unreliable sentence — in CI, in the pre-merge check, and in every entry above that cites a passing suite as evidence. It is worse than a red run, which at least announces itself.
  - **Related to B93 and not the same thing.** B93 is the headless harness *failing* a test at 1 ms with a native exception, and announces itself. This announces nothing. They may share a cause — both are the harness losing work it was given — and that is a hypothesis, not a finding.
  - **What is known, and what is not.** Known: it is non-deterministic across identical commits; the shortfall is large; no crash line, no skip count, exit 0. Not known: whether the tests are never *started* (a discovery or scheduling fault) or run and never *reported* (a logger fault), which is the first thing to establish because it splits the search in half. Nothing about the count 808 has been shown to be meaningful — one sample.
  - **First step for whoever picks this up**, and it is cheap: run the suite several times capturing `--logger "console;verbosity=detailed"`, and diff the list of test names *reported* against `--list-tests`. The set that goes missing — whether it is whole collections, one assembly-level fixture's worth, or scattered — is what names the cause. A `--blame` run is the second step if the first is ambiguous.
  - **Not caused by the change it was found on** (B282's drop fix, which touches drag-and-drop handling only): the two runs bracketing the measurement were the same commit, and the earlier of them was the short one.
  - **Not seen on CI yet, which narrows it.** The run for the pull request that found this executed **3,594 of 3,594** and passed. Both short runs were local, in this sandbox. So the next question is whether the shortfall is environment-shaped — core count, memory pressure, a container's process limits — rather than something in the suite itself, and a CI run is not evidence that the suite is sound. Two observations against one environment is not a pattern; it is where to look first.
  - **2026-08-27: the run now says what it is doing, and it is being killed.** Seen three times in one sitting on the B30 branch, and the line the earlier samples did not have is xUnit's own: `[FATAL ERROR] Xunit.Sdk.TestPipelineException` / `Catastrophic failure: Test process crashed with exit code 137` — and then, on the next line, `Passed! - Failed: 0, Passed: 3266, Skipped: 0`. **137 is SIGKILL**, which on a container with no swap is the out-of-memory killer. So the bullet above guessed the right half of its own list: it is *memory pressure*, environment-shaped, and the tests that go missing are the ones that were never reached because the host died mid-run.
    - **This narrows the first step rather than replacing it.** "Started but not reported" is now ruled out for these three samples — the process was killed, so the missing tests never ran — and the remaining question moves from *where do the tests go* to *what makes the host grow*. The counts are consistent with a walk that gets progressively further as the machine happens to be quieter: **2 367, 3 266, 3 510** across three runs of the same suite in one hour, against 3 587 discovered.
    - **The reporting fault is separate and is the P1 half.** Whatever the memory cause turns out to be, xUnit printing `Passed!` on the line after `Catastrophic failure` is the thing that makes a green run untrustworthy, and it would still do that if the crash had a different cause. A run whose host died must not exit 0.
    - **Not the B30 branch's doing, checked rather than assumed.** The same suite was run on the stashed tree — every checkpoint file removed, `git stash push -u` — and crashed identically at exit 137 with a *shorter* count (2 367 against 3 266). The branch is not implicated; it was the branch that happened to be in the tree when the machine was busy enough to show it three times running.
    - Machine at rest during these runs: **16 GB total, 15 GB free, no swap.** So whatever grows, grows fast and inside one process — which makes a `--blame` run, or `DOTNET_GCHeapHardLimit`, the cheap next probe.
    - **Settled the same hour by a counter-example on the identical commit.** PR #466's CI ran the App suite at `aaaf155` — the same tree that had just been killed at 2 368 locally — and got **4 053 of 4 053, zero failures, in Release**. So it is not the suite, not a test, and not the commit: it is this sandbox. That is worth more than the three local samples put together, because it is the same code on two machines with opposite outcomes, and it means **the reporting fault is the only half that can bite CI** — a runner that did run out of memory would print `Passed!` there too.
    - What that leaves for whoever picks this up is one question rather than two: not *why do tests go missing* but *why does this container run out of 16 GB running a suite CI runs inside a standard runner*. Release versus Debug is the obvious first suspect and is free to test — every local run above was Debug, every CI run Release, and Debug inflates exactly the per-test allocation a headless Avalonia session makes.

  - **A third sighting, 2026-08-25 — and it is a DIFFERENT failure with the same face, which is the useful part.** Debug build, `dotnet test tests/Lightbox.App.Tests` in the remote container (4 cores, 16 GB, no swap). The run printed **`Passed!  - Failed: 0, Passed: 3361, Skipped: 0, Total: 3361`** at 8 m 48 s — and then, at 9 m 54 s, `[FATAL ERROR] Xunit.Sdk.TestPipelineException` / **`Catastrophic failure: Test process crashed with exit code 137`**. An immediate re-run on the same commit executed **3,883 of 3,883, exit 0**, which CI independently confirmed as the full count on that commit.
  - **137 is SIGKILL, and that is what separates it from the two sightings above.** This entry's samples record *no crash line and exit 0*; this one announced itself. So there are at least two ways to arrive at "ran short, printed `Passed!`": the silent one this bug is named for, and an OOM kill. They are told apart by whether a fatal line follows the summary — which means the summary line alone does not distinguish them, and **`Passed!` with a low total is also what a killed run looks like.**
  - **A fourth sighting hours later withdraws the obvious explanation, and pins the exit code.** The first sample above ran concurrently with an Avalonia application under Xvfb, so "self-inflicted memory pressure" looked like the whole story — and one clean re-run seemed to confirm it. It does not survive the next one: on a **fresh, essentially idle container** (no Xvfb, no app, 14 GB free), the suite was killed the same way at **2,822 of a discovered 3,910 — 1,088 short — again printing `Passed!`, again `exit code 137`.** So the OOM is intermittent and is *not* reliably attributable to concurrent load. Whatever grows, grows on its own.
  - **And the exit code, captured properly this time, separates the two mechanisms cleanly: the OOM variant exits `1`.** `dotnet test` returned **EXIT=1** while its own summary line said `Passed! - Failed: 0`. This entry's silent samples record exit **0**. So a short run can be attributed without guessing — `0` is this bug, `1` with a fatal line is the kill — **provided the exit code is captured rather than piped away.**
  - **What it contributes to the open question.** "Is the shortfall environment-shaped?" now has to be asked twice, because at least one shortfall mechanism here demonstrably *is* (memory), and it is not the one this bug describes. Whoever picks this up should therefore separate the samples by whether a fatal line was present before reasoning about causes, or two mechanisms get averaged into one.
  - **One methodological trap, found by falling into it.** The first run above was reported as `exit 0` and was not: the command was piped through `tail`, so the exit code observed was the pipe's last stage rather than `dotnet test`'s. Anything claiming an exit code for this bug should say how it was captured — `PIPESTATUS`, a bare invocation, or `set -o pipefail` — because a piped run cannot see the one number that would settle whether a short run failed or "passed".
  - Filed rather than fixed because it is a research task into the test harness rather than a defect with a place to stand — B60's shape — and because guessing at a fix here would produce exactly the false confidence the bug is about. Cost: M to localise, unknown to fix.

A popup that dies within **500 ms** of opening is counted as *collapsed* rather than dismissed, and the report says how many of how many — which is this bug reduced to a number that a fix has to move. The read-out protocol and the before/after ritual are in B126's entry rather than repeated here.

This entry's fix is therefore the same fix, judged by the collapsed-popup counter rather than by the cursor one.
  - **Measured, second trace: 2,285 of 2,300 popups closed within 500 ms of opening.** Not the reporter dismissing menus — the echo opening and closing the layer menu's submenus about fifty times a second, which is also what freezes the application (**B255**, filed P1 off the back of it). So this bug's real cost is not "a menu is fiddly", it is that a menu cannot be used at all with a pen tablet attached.

The submenu hook is kept as a *label* rather than a tally, because `Submenu of “Follows the rig”` is what identified the culprit; `Annotate` records into the event list without touching a counter.
  - `evidence: manual` for B126's reason: no pen and no Windows exist in this repository, so nothing headless can hold the fix — diagnosis and verification both go through the owner's machine. Cost: M

- [ ] **B100** `P3` `ui` Undo history does not survive a save, and the owner wants it to — blocked on the step record becoming data `evidence: SerializableEditStep, UndoPersistence, UndoHistoryTests, UndoSurvivesAReload, RestoringUndoDoesNotMarkTheDocument`
  - Asked for 2026-08-06: *"undo history is always saved for the max amount of the buffer"*, and *"silently saved instead of showing a badge"* — so persisting it must not itself dirty the document, which B98's derived revision gives for free.
  - **Measured 2026-08-06, and it refuted the estimate above rather than confirming it.** I had said the stack holds commands rather than snapshots and would therefore be cheap. Both halves were wrong, and the class doc says so in its first line — *"snapshot-based undo/redo… snapshots are JSON clones"*.
  - **`SnapshotStep` holds a whole `Doc` clone.** Measured: a 20-stroke document is **45.9 KB**, so a full 64-deep stack is **2.8 MB — a 64× file-size multiplier**. A 60-stroke document is 126.6 KB, which puts the same stack near 8 MB. Growing from empty is gentler (**524 KB** over 64 edits) but that is the best case, not the working one. `Perform` is used 18 times in the editor and 10 more in the view models, so snapshots are the common step, not the exception.
  - **`DeltaStep` holds `Action<Doc>` delegates, which cannot be serialized at all.** This is the blocker rather than the size. Closures have no data form, and **a stroke commit is a delta** — deliberately, because snapshotting per pen lift caused a visible pause (the hot path B15/BR1 exist for). So the single most common thing an artist would want restored, *undo my last stroke*, is exactly the step that cannot be written to a file.
  - **So B100 is blocked on a prerequisite it did not name: `DeltaStep` has to become data instead of a pair of lambdas.** Each of the 16 delta sites has an apply/revert pair that is representable — "add this stroke to this frame" and its inverse — so the conversion is mechanical, but it is a discriminated set of step records and 16 call sites rather than a serializer, and it is the refactor `DocumentEditor`'s own doc comment already anticipates: *"to be replaced by command deltas when heavy raster editing arrives"*.
  - **Recommended order, and it changes what B100 is.** Convert the step record to data first as its own objective — it is worth having regardless, since it also removes the 64× snapshot cost from memory and makes Pillar 6's unbuilt undo-history browser buildable. Persisting it afterwards is then small. Persisting the *current* representation is not a smaller version of that; it is 2.8 MB of clones plus the half that cannot be written.
  - The owner's other requirement is already met by B98 for free: restoring history must not raise the badge, and it cannot, because the badge compares a revision rather than counting events.
  - Pairs with Pillar 6's unbuilt *undo history browser*, which wants the same records to navigate.
