A full run under it was started and abandoned after running far past the ~5-minute norm without finishing, which is unexplained and is exactly the shape a shared dispatcher blocked by one test would take.
    - So the change is **reverted rather than shipped**, and that is the recommendation to inherit: an isolation switch that hangs the suite would cost every pull request far more than B93 does, and B93 costs a re-run. B60's precedent — establish that the fix is a research project, write it up, leave the bug open on purpose — is the right shape here, and a green checkbox over an unvalidated switch is the thing these ledgers exist to refuse.
    - **What would settle it**, for whoever picks this up: run the App suite under `PerAssembly` to completion with a hard timeout, several times. Green and fast is a real candidate; a hang names the test that blocks the shared dispatcher, which is a deterministic bug and a better one to have than this. Either outcome is worth more than another sighting, and neither needs a lucky CI run.
  - Likely the same unnamed intermittent failure seen twice in full local runs and never captured; the local capture came back green five times running, which fits a bug this rare rather than proving anything.

  - **A candidate fix, landed 2026-08-10: run this assembly's collections one at a time.** Every frame of the stack is inside Avalonia's headless harness *starting an application* — `HeadlessUnitTestSession.EnsureIsolatedApplication` → `AvaloniaHeadlessPlatform.Initialize` → `ServerCompositor..ctor` → `DefaultRenderLoop.Add` → `VerifyAccess`. Nothing in it belongs to this codebase, which is why sixteen sightings across fourteen unrelated classes never converged on a defect in any of them. The collections that share mutable global state already disable parallelisation individually; everything else runs concurrently, and **every victim has been an `[AvaloniaFact]` class in a different collection from the last one**. Two sessions initialising at once is the one thing that explains a victim moving between classes on an unchanged commit.
  - **What settles it is that it costs nothing measurable.** App suite, Release, 4 cores, wall clock: **parallel 249/285/290 s, serialised 242/297 s** — indistinguishable, and note the ~20% spread *within* each configuration, which is larger than any difference between them. The first two runs read 242 against 249 and would have supported "3% faster"; that was noise dressed as a finding, and the extra runs are what stopped it being reported that way. That there is no cost reads as a contradiction and is not: 154 of the 203 test classes are `[AvaloniaFact]` classes and those already serialise on the headless dispatcher whatever xUnit does with the collections, so the parallelism was never overlapping the *work*. The only thing it overlapped was session creation, which is the race.
  - **Recorded as a hypothesis, not a fix, and the checkbox stays open until CI says otherwise.** B93 has never reproduced locally in any of its sightings, so there is no red test this turns green — claiming one would be exactly the assertion these ledgers exist to prevent. The proof is CI staying green across the next several PRs. **If B93 appears again with this in place, the parallelism theory is wrong and this entry says so** rather than the line being quietly deleted.

  - **Worse than a coin flip, measured over the next four runs.** Fails, fails, passes, then fails again on PR #143 (`SymbolScopeTests.DeletingASymbolStopsItResolving`) — **three of four**, and a fourth distinct victim class in four runs across two PRs. Nothing common to `ProjectWindowTests`, `DocumentTabTests` and `SymbolScopeTests` except that a headless session seated them. At this rate every PR costs one or two extra CI cycles, which is no longer a rounding error against the cost of fixing it.
  - What that costs, which is the part worth acting on: **a blind re-run is roughly a coin flip on this suite, not a formality.** Two runs to get past one commit is now the observed case rather than the worst case, and it is the argument for either fixing B93 or serialising the headless sessions — the bug has been "annoying but cheap" on the strength of single re-runs converging, and that assumption is now measured to be wrong.
  - The diff it landed on is the other half of the evidence: `SnapshotGeometry` and `ComposePlan` are pure arithmetic with no dispatcher, window, threading or UI in them at all, and both victim classes pass 46/46 locally in Release. There is nothing in the change for this to be about.

  - **Sighted again 2026-08-08, and briefly misfiled as its own bug.** `MarkerNotesTests.NotesAreListedInFrameOrder` failed at **1 ms** in 2 of 5 full App-suite runs on `perf/canvas/B125-playback-through-tiles`, passing every time in isolation and in a two-class run. It was filed as B145 with a DispatcherTimer-interleaving theory before the 1 ms signature was checked against this entry — a body that never ran cannot have been raced by a timer tick, and the owner is who caught the duplicate. Two lessons folded back in: the failure is not confined to tests that touch rendering (three sightings, three unrelated test classes — the victim is whoever the harness seats next), and **grep the ledger for the signature before filing the sighting**; this entry's whole third bullet is about rediscovery being the expensive part, and it still happened.
  - **Sighted again 2026-08-21, on PR #384 (`claude/timeline-ux-improvements-97279v`) — and it lands after the 2026-08-10 serialisation hypothesis, so that entry's own condition is met and the parallelism theory is not the whole story.** `PaletteHierarchyTests.TheHierarchyAndTheSwatchesReadAsTwoPanes` failed at **1 ms**, `Test Case Cleanup Failure`, the exact stack (`HeadlessUnitTestSession.EnsureIsolatedApplication` → `AvaloniaHeadlessPlatform.Initialize` → `DefaultRenderLoop.Add` → `VerifyAccess`), 3,540 passing either side. The diff was timeline UI and never touches the palette; the same suite passed twice in full locally on the same commit, and the single CI re-run came back green — one re-run converged this time, against the three-of-four rate measured on PR #143. Second time this class is seated (B180 records `RenamingARowRenamesTheModel`), consistent with victim-by-seating rather than victim-by-content.

---

## Fixed

Entries move here when `sync` closes them; the evidence stays so a deleted
test reopens the bug.
  - **Sightings nineteen to twenty-one, 2026-08-16 to 2026-08-17, on two unrelated pull requests.** `PaletteHierarchyTests.TheHierarchyAndTheSwatchesReadAsTwoPanes` twice — once per PR — and then `ProjectSheetAppTests.ASecondDocumentInTheProjectSeesTheSameSheet` on the very next run. All three at **1 ms**, stack unchanged, on branches that reach neither palettes nor project sheets; all three passed all four suites locally beforehand.
  - **The interesting part is the correction.** The first two looked like the first repeat in twenty sightings — a favourite class at last — and that was written down here as the new fact. The next run moved to a fifteenth distinct class and refuted it inside twenty minutes. Recorded rather than quietly edited out, because it is this entry's own lesson arriving on schedule: **the victim is whichever test the harness happened to be seating**, and any pattern read from two samples of that is noise. The one thing that has never varied in twenty-one sightings is the stack.
  - **Three consecutive red runs on one branch is a worse rate than this bug's own history** (B93 records roughly eight of nine green after `DisableTestParallelization`). Not attributed: the branch touches the canvas control, the reference record and the shortcut map, and the failures are in cleanup of tests that reach none of them. If it happens on a fourth run the rate itself is the finding and belongs here as a measurement, not another re-run.

### ai

- [x] **B195** `P1` `ai` `render_frame` fails with "Invalid Base64 string" on every frame of every document, blank or not `evidence: TheRenderedFrameTravelsAsBase64TextNotAsRawPngBytes, ABlankFrameMakesTheSameTripAndIsStillAPng, TheReferenceViewImageGoesThroughTheSameConversion`
  - Reported from an agent session: an empty fresh document at 4K still failed. That is the useful half of the report, because it rules out the theory it arrived with — the payload being too big. A blank 4K PNG is tens of kilobytes and nowhere near any cap, so a failure that is both **content-independent and size-independent** is not about the image at all.
  - `ImageContentBlock.Data` in the MCP SDK is **the UTF-8 bytes of the base64 text**, and the decoded image is the separate `DecodedData`. Both image tools read that name the other way round and assigned `Convert.FromBase64String(b64)` — the decoded PNG. It compiles, because `Data` is a `ReadOnlyMemory<byte>` and a `byte[]` converts implicitly, and the SDK then writes those bytes into the JSON string verbatim. Measured on a twelve-byte PNG: `{"data":"�PNG\r\n\n\0�"}`. (**The NUL in that example is written `\0` rather than as the byte itself, on purpose:** a literal NUL anywhere in this file makes `grep` report *"binary file matches"* instead of the matching lines, for every search of the whole ledger. Do not restore it.) The client base64-decodes that and gets the reported exception.
  - So it could never have worked, for anyone, once. A PNG's first byte is `0x89`, which is not valid UTF-8 whatever follows it, so the very first character was already destroyed before any pixel was considered.
  - Fix: pass the text through — `Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(b64)` — in one `LightboxTools.ImageBlock` helper both tools now call, since `render_reference_view` carried the identical line and the identical bug. The old decode also validated the string by accident; `Base64.IsValid` keeps that guard deliberately and without allocating a second copy of a 4K frame, and a bad payload now fails with a sentence the model can act on rather than a `FormatException` from inside the tool. Cost: S
  - **What let it ship is the shape worth remembering: the test stopped one assignment short of the bug.** `IpcTests.RenderFrame_ReturnsDecodablePng` covers the app half and passed throughout — the payload really was a decodable PNG. Nothing then checked what the MCP tool did with it, and `Data` holds bytes either way, so only *serializing the block* tells the two apart. `McpImageBlockTests` therefore asserts on the wire form, and needed `Lightbox.App.Tests` to reference `Lightbox.Mcp` so one test can drive both halves of a seam that spans two projects.

- [x] **B233** `P2` `ai` A cleared region reaches the AI as a brush stroke, and what it cleared is sent too `evidence: ClearedRegion_IsDropped_AndSoIsWhatItCleared, ClearedRegion_EmptiesItsInsideRatherThanItsOutline, ClearedRegion_LeavesWhatIsInsideItsHoles, ClearedRegion_DoesNotTouchInkDrawnAfterIt, AClearedRegionNeverReachesTheWire`
  - Found while answering the owner's rule for B232 — *"the AI should only see what actually is there"* — on the assumption that the AI surfaces needed fixing. They did not: `IpcDocumentApi.GetFrameStrokes` and the inbetween payload have both run `StrokeRecordCleaner.EffectiveStrokes` all along. The hole was one tool kind inside the cleaner.
  - **`EffectiveStrokes` dropped `Eraser` and not `ClearRegion`**, so clearing a selection left *both* halves of the erasure in the effective record: the strokes it emptied, and the clear itself. Two separate costs from one omission — tokens spent on artwork the artist deliberately removed, and the inbetweener matching against lines that are not on the page.
  - **The second half is worse than the budget.** `StrokePayload.ToWire` collapses six document tool kinds onto the wire's two, mapping everything that is not an eraser to `"brush"`. For a fill that is lossy and honest — there is a mark there, roughly here. For a cleared region it is a phantom: the model is told a brush stroke traces the outline of a space the artist emptied, and then asked to inbetween it.
  - Fixed in the cleaner, by the grouping `LayerMerge`, `MotionTrail` and `StrokePicker` already make: the two kinds are separate because they *render* differently — a path walked laying dabs versus a filled contour — and they are one thing to anything asking what is on the drawing. `Covers` reads a cleared region as an even-odd area with its holes, not as a path along its outline; reading the outline would only cover what sits near the edge, so a shape cleared out of the middle of a drawing would come back.
  - **The wire test is composed rather than a unit test**, deliberately: the fix *is* that `EffectiveStrokes` always runs before `ToWire`, so a test of `ToWire` alone would pass on the broken build and on this one.
  - Not fixed here, and named so it is not lost: `ToWire` still describes a fill and a gradient as brush strokes. That is lossy rather than false, it needs the art-director's judgement about what a model should be told a fill is, and it is a different objective — a separate branch.

- [x] **B31** `P2` `ai` Every AI call re-renders and re-encodes the reference views on the UI thread `evidence: ReferenceImagePayloadTests, ReferenceViewsAreEncodedOnceNotPerCall, TheEncodedViewIsReusedWhileTheSheetIsUnchanged, EditingTheDrawingThrowsTheEncodedViewAway, HidingALayerChangesWhatIsSent, TheLongEdgeIsCappedOnTheWayOutRatherThanOnTheView, ASmallViewIsNotUpscaledToTheCap, TheDownscaledReferenceStillHasTheDrawingInIt`
  - Repro: a document with two character-sheet views, then **✦ AI Inbetween** twice. `CollectReferenceImages` runs synchronously in `AiInbetweenAsync` before the request is built, and it composes, PNG-encodes and base64s each visible view every time.
  - Measured: **52 ms** to encode and base64 one 960×540 view (38 ms at 768×432), so the default two views cost about **100 ms of UI-thread stall before every AI call**. Timed on dense synthetic line art, which is the pessimistic end; a sparse sheet is cheaper but not free.
  - It is pure waste, not merely slow: the sheet has not changed between calls, so the bytes produced are identical every time. `_cache.Get` already memoises the *layer* render — what is uncached is `Compose` + PNG + base64, which is the expensive half.
  - Fix: memoise the encoded string per view, keyed on something that actually changes when the drawing does. Invalidate where `OnDocumentChanged` already funnels every edit. Cost: S
  - Two things fall out of the same measurement and belong in whatever commit closes this. **Cap the long edge** on the request rather than on the view — providers bill by area, so 768 px is 442 image tokens against 691 and 244 KB against 333 KB, and the artist's sheet stays whatever size they drew it. And **WebP halves the bytes but doubles the encode** (106 ms against 52); on the UI thread that is a bad trade, and once the cache exists it is free to reconsider.
  - Context and the rest of the payload arithmetic: `docs/DESIGN-ai-payload.md`. The images are ~87% of a request's bytes and ~5% of its tokens, which is why this is a latency bug and not a cost one.
  - Fixed: encoded views memoised per view, thrown away by `MarkDocumentEdited`. Measured **225 ms cold against 0.03 ms warm**, with both numbers printed by the test so "the second was faster" is never the whole claim. The long-edge cap landed in the same commit: a 1920×1080 view now sends 768×432, **7 KB instead of 115 KB**, aspect kept, and the view's own dimensions untouched.
  - **The fix above named the wrong funnel, and it was the dangerous half.** `OnDocumentChanged` takes an early return for scoped edits and a stroke commit is exactly that — so a cache invalidated there would have survived the edit it exists to notice, and sent a model a picture of art the artist had already changed. Nothing in the output says so; it reads as a worse inbetween. Hung off `MarkDocumentEdited` instead, which is the real per-edit funnel at 18 callers against 3, and `EditingTheDrawingThrowsTheEncodedViewAway` drives a real begin/move/end to pin it.
  - A cap needs the other direction asserted too, or it becomes a target: `ASmallViewIsNotUpscaledToTheCap` keeps a 400×300 sheet at 400×300, because enlarging one spends tokens on pixels the artist never drew.
  - **The first ink test was vacuous and it is worth recording why**, because it is the saturation trap wearing different clothes. It counted `Alpha > 40` on an opaque composite, reported **100.0%**, and would have passed just as happily on a blank sheet. Rewritten to count darkness against an empty sheet of the same size: **9720 dark pixels with art, 0 without**. The number was real and it was measuring the wrong thing.
  - **Gate G12: reviewed by the pair, and both changed the diff.** ai-engineer tried to break the invalidation across stroke commits, timeline edits, undo/redo, layer visibility and reorder, palette recolour, symbol copies, tab switch, project load and MCP writes, and could not — all of them reach `MarkDocumentEdited`. It found two things this now fixes: `AddReferenceSheet`/`AddReferenceView` wrote to `Doc.ReferenceSheets` without announcing the edit (inert today, and the path a future "duplicate view" would extend), and **ids are not unique across tabs** — `DocJson.Clone` preserves `ReferenceView.Id`, so a template and a new-from-template collide in one dictionary that lives on the view model. Both are covered now, the second by `TwoTabsWhoseViewsShareAnIdDoNotShareAPicture`, which fails when invalidation is removed.
  - art-director's verdict was **accept-with-condition**: the cache costs nothing in expression, and the 768 px cap measurably loses facial construction on a face close-up and on a naturally-small head. Recorded as **Q27** with the four ways out rather than settled by whoever ran last — and with the caveat that the fixture's thin lines were drawn at pressure 0.25–0.5, where pressure drives flow as well as size, so the cap made a marginal line invisible rather than a solid line marginal.
  - **The cap leaked onto a consumer nobody was thinking about**, which is the mistake this entry should be remembered for. Putting it in the parameterless `RenderReferenceViewPng` also shrank what the MCP surface answers `render_reference_view` with — an agent asking for a picture of a view should get the view. Caught by `RenderReferenceView_ProducesDecodablePng`, a test older than this work that asserts the authored width. The cap now lives at `EncodedReferenceView`, the one call site where "billed by area" is true.

### brush

- [x] **B314** `P1` `brush` The live post-process is queued below the pointer events feeding it, so a fast stroke starves it `evidence: APassQueuedDuringABurstIsNotLeftBehindByIt, DrainingToInputLeavesBackgroundWorkAlone`
  - **Reported from the hand, and the report's mean said nothing was wrong.** After B313 landed the owner tried it and was precise: *"especially speedy lines trail behind the pen. Short quick strokes not so much."* Their capture of 2026-08-26 puts the wait from queued to started at a mean of **7.5 ms** — unremarkable — beside a **worst of 3,126 ms**. Averages hide a tail, and nobody experiences an average. The two counters that found this were added for a different hypothesis and refuted it in the same line: `of the mark re-processed 1.3%` says B313 works exactly as designed.
  - **The mechanism is the same one B312 had just been fixed for, in another file.** `RequestLivePostProcess` posts at `DispatcherPriority.Background`, and Avalonia runs `Render > Loaded > Default > Input > Background`. So for as long as the hand keeps moving, every pointer event outranks the pass — which is the whole of a long fast stroke and none of a short one. That is precisely the difference the owner described, and it is why a mean taken over a session of mixed strokes reads fine.
  - **Being late compounds, which is what makes it visible rather than merely slow.** The pending region accumulates while the pass waits, so a starved pass is no longer a band: the same capture shows a **360 ms** pass over a region averaging 1.3% of the mark. And `ScenePassBuilder.OverlayFor` takes the whole live overlay from the processed buffer once any pass has landed, so a brush with an effect shows the mark **as of the last completed pass** — the paint simply stops there until the next one lands. A 3 px Pencil hides that; a 22 px flat does not, which is why only the flats were reported.
  - **The comment being deleted predicted this shape and did not recognise it.** It argued Background *"yields to pointer input, so during a fast drag the pass starts in whatever gaps exist"* — measured, during a fast drag there are no gaps — and it rejected a cost-based throttle because *"it blocked the pass that would have settled the preview, so the mark froze part-drawn until the pen lifted."* That is a description of this bug. Background priority is a throttle too.
  - **Input rather than Default**, for B73's reason: that queue is FIFO, so the pass lands behind the events already waiting — it sees all of them — and ahead of the ones after, so a continuous drag cannot starve it. Default sits *above* Input here and would jump the pen. `FinishLivePostProcess` has been at Input since B189 on the identical argument, which was never carried back to the start.
  - **Affordable only now.** The reasoning for yielding was written when a pass cost 45–143 ms. B293 and B313 took it under one, and a millisecond between pointer events is not a throttle worth having.
  - **Tested without a clock, because the claim is about order.** "Trails behind the pen" means events are queued and the frame does not contain them yet — the reframe `StrokeLatencyTests` makes for B73. Draining the dispatcher to `Input` and no further leaves anything at `Background` exactly where it sat, so the two priorities give different answers on a run with no timing in it. Proved sensitive: with the priority put back to Background the burst test fails, and the second test exists so a `RunJobs(Input)` that quietly ran everything could not make the first one vacuous.
  - **P1 rather than the P2 it was filed as.** It is unbounded — 3.1 seconds is not a budget overrun, it is the preview stopping — and it reaches every brush carrying an effect, which is Pencil, all three flats and every medium.

- [x] **B311** `P1` `brush` A silhouette brush draws a gentle curve up to 20 px away from where its own dabs are `evidence: tests/Lightbox.Raster.Tests/SilhouetteFollowsItsDabsTests.cs`
  - **Found 2026-08-25 while prototyping an alternative to the silhouette, by comparing three renders of one dab list.** On a gentle arc — 15.1 document px a step, heading turning 0.004 rad a step, so a radius of curvature of about 3,800 px — the per-dab path and a max-accumulated prototype both ink at the dab's own edge, and the shipped silhouette does not:

    | x | dab centre y | per-dab | silhouette | error |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 400 | 1085.7 | 1083 | 1098 | **15** |
    | 1200 | 1217.0 | 1214 | 1232 | **18** |
    | 2000 | 1540.9 | 1538 | 1559 | **21** |
    | 2800 | 2125.3 | 2122 | 2138 | **16** |

    The dab radius is 2.5 px, so the per-dab row is the dab's own top edge to within rounding, and the silhouette is six to twenty-one pixels below it. The error oscillates rather than accumulating, which is the signature of where the runs happen to break rather than of drift.
  - **The mechanism, read off `BuildSilhouette`.** The run simplifier keeps an `anchor`, and breaks the run when `pending` — the dab immediately before the current one — strays more than `Tolerance` (0.05 px) from the chord `anchor → pos`. **That samples the deviation at the one point on the run where it is smallest.** On a smooth curve the last dab is near the chord however far the middle of the run has bulged from it, so a run grows long and the capsule it finally emits cuts the corner by orders of magnitude more than the tolerance implies. A tolerance checked at the wrong point reads as tight and is not.
  - **Why nothing caught it.** `LiveMatchesCommittedTests` compares the live preview with the commit, and both take the silhouette — they agree with each other while both stand away from the record. The determinism fingerprints were re-recorded for hard-aa when #404 landed (Q156), so they pin the displaced render as the reference. Nothing in the suite compares a silhouette against the dabs it is made of, which is what the evidence anchor above has to do.
  - **P1, not P2 as filed.** Invariant 1 is that the stroke record is the document; a mark drawn twenty pixels from where the record puts it is lost work rather than a cosmetic fault, the same reasoning B256 carries. It reaches the whole hard round family — Ink, hard round, the eraser and any preset an artist builds from them — which is to say all line art.
  - **Interaction with B299, stated so the two are not fixed twice.** B299 is the same code being slow; this is it being wrong. The max-accumulated prototype in `tools/Lightbox.Bench/MaxCoverageProto.cs` costs **0.02 ms an event against 12.46 ms** and tracks the per-dab render to within a pixel across the whole arc — so it answers both, and the owner has already said the silhouette itself is on the table. Fixing the run test in place is the smaller change; replacing the mechanism is the one that also closes B299.
  - Cost: S to fix the run test (measure the maximum deviation over the run, not the last one), M to replace the mechanism.
  - **Fixed 2026-08-25 by replacing the mechanism** — `BrushEngine.StampSilhouette` accumulates coverage as a running maximum into an opaque layer (`Lighten` is exactly `max` when both alphas are 1) and reads it back as ink through a colour matrix. There is no run, no chord and no anchor, so there is no simplification to check at the wrong point. `SilhouetteFollowsItsDabsTests` asks the question the suite never asked — does the mark sit on its dabs — against the per-dab render rather than a remembered number, and is proved sensitive: against the old code it reports the silhouette standing **19 px** off. `hard-aa` re-recorded; `jitter` and `soft` byte-identical, which is exactly the set the predicate allows this to reach.
  - **Two invariant-7 faults were found on the way, both by `OutputScaleTests`.** Rasterising into a bitmap sized from the band — stroke coordinates — rendered the mark at document resolution and scaled it, so 4× resolved no more detail than 1×; a `SaveLayer` inherits the canvas transform and device resolution instead. And a ramp fixed at half a *stroke* unit is half a pixel at 1× and two at 4×, keeping the edge proportionally as soft at every scale, so it is read from the canvas matrix as half a **device** pixel. Recorded because both are the same mistake in different clothes: a length that must be in device units written in document ones.
  - **It cost, and B299's other half is what paid for it — they landed together.** Correct is not the same as ready. On its own the replacement took one whole-mark draw at 3840×2160 with Ink from **12.46 ms to 55.49 ms**, because twelve thousand individual `DrawCircle` calls cannot match one `DrawPath` over twelve thousand contours: Skia scan-converts the path once and pays the per-draw setup once with it. Reusing one shader across a run of equal radii took the *build* from 14.08 ms to 8.94 ms and left the fill where it was, which is per-draw overhead and does not tune away. The whole win of max accumulation was always that it is **incremental**, so the two had to ship as one change — see B299.

- [x] **B299** `P1` `brush` A silhouette brush's live fill covers the whole mark every pointer event, because the stamping cut is pinned at zero `evidence: ASilhouetteStrokeRestampsOnlyItsMovingTail, AHardRoundInkStrokeIsTheSameLiveAndCommitted`
  - `StampLiveDabs` pins the cut at zero for a silhouette brush, so `StampDabRange` is always called with `from = 0` and the band it writes — `RangeReach(dabs, 0, count)` — is the whole mark. **This is where a silhouette stroke's per-event time actually goes**, which B292 established by removing the other candidate and finding nothing moved: the outline derivation is worth 1–3% end to end in Release, and the fill is the rest.
  - **The pin is not gratuitous, and two ways of removing it are already known to be wrong** (both measured during #404 and #405):
    - Stamping a settled prefix separately writes the still-provisional tail's shape into the scratch *before* the tail backup is taken, so a tail that then moves leaves its old position behind — live 2.8% fatter than the commit, pixels 239/255 apart in both directions.
    - Bounding each draw's path by its own range caps the mark where the full list carries a capsule onward, and the band is inflated by `DabReach`, which is wider than the mark — so the band around every event straddles exactly that difference. 3.5% fatter.
  - **The shape that should work, not yet tried:** keep one draw an event, but give the settled part a band of its own that is *clipped away from anything the tail can reach* — `ClipRect(settledBand)` then `ClipRect(tailBand, SKClipOperation.Difference)`, which is a rect minus a rect and something Skia does directly. The settled region is then permanent and provably outside what a moving tail can touch, and the tail keeps the backup-and-replace it has now.
  - Filed rather than fixed because at this boundary a design that reads correctly has twice not been, and because the measurement that makes it the priority only exists now. Cost: M.
  - **Raised to P1 on 2026-08-25, because the price was measured in the wrong cell and is six times what was recorded.** #404's commit message put the live cost at *"3.19 ms an event against 1.50 ms at size 5 on a 400-event stroke"* and accepted it as a trade. `LiveStampSplit.Presets` (`tools/Lightbox.Bench`) re-measures it in the cell the owner actually draws in — 3840×2160, fit to window, and **15.1 document px of travel an event**, taken from their own capture rather than chosen — and gets **18.64 ms an event for Ink at 400 events**, 5.84 ms at 100. Every other shipped brush finishes a whole event in **0.20–0.66 ms**. Ink is the only shipped preset that satisfies the predicate.
  - **What makes it P1 rather than merely slow: it exceeds the gap between pen events, so the backlog is unbounded.** The owner's trace puts delivered moves at **112/s — one every 8.9 ms**. An event costing 18.64 ms can never be caught up on while the hand keeps moving, so the queue grows for the whole stroke and drains when the pen lifts. That is precisely the report: *"every stroke the entire stroke is not live but revealed on release"*, on a build where dabs are otherwise correct. Their render report agrees from the other end — `stamping the dabs` mean **13.42 ms** over strokes of two to ten seconds, which is where a session of mixed lengths on Ink lands.
  - **The travel figure is the part that was missing, and it is why 3.19 became 18.64.** Dab pitch is size × spacing in *document* pixels, so what decides the per-event dab count is how far the pen travels in document space — and a 4K document viewed fit-to-window has a compose scale of 0.375, which turns one view pixel of hand movement into 2.67 document pixels. A measurement taken at 1:1, or on a shorter stroke, understates the cost of the one configuration this brush is for: line art on a big canvas.
  - **The other candidate was eliminated rather than assumed, again.** The same harness times the whole-stroke dab walk separately: linear in stroke length exactly as BR1 implies (**exponent 0.94**), and **0.49–1.16 ms** at 400 events — 1–6% of the total. That independently reproduces what B292 found by withdrawing the outline cache, from the other direction.
  - **A citation to fix while here:** #404's message says the live cost was *"filed as B290"*. B290 is the region-transform erasure bug, long closed. This entry is the one it meant.
  - **The shape above was tried on 2026-08-25 and does not work. Third attempt at this boundary, and the first to say why rather than what.** `ClipRect(settledBand)` then `ClipRect(tailBand, Difference)` is necessary and not sufficient: with it the ink case of `LiveMatchesCommittedTests` drifts **10.17/255 mean, worst 195, ink ratio 1.001** — the live mark carrying ink the commit does not, which is the 2.8% defect in its original form.
  - **The reason it cannot work as stated: `StableCount` answers about positions, and a silhouette's pixels are not a function of positions alone.** `BuildSilhouette` is a greedy run simplifier — it holds an `anchor`, accumulates while dabs stay within 0.05 px of the chord, and emits a capsule only when the run **breaks**. While a run is open, the path carries one capsule from that anchor to the tip. So the geometry that can still change reaches back to the **current run's anchor**, not to the last dab that moved — and on the straight and gently curved marks Ink exists for, the run stays open for most of the stroke. There is no prefix of the dab list whose pixels are settled while that is true, which is why every cut derived from the dabs has failed.
  - **What that leaves, and it is geometry rather than a clip.** The only thing that actually changes between events is the terminal capsule: it extends at the far end always, and its near end moves only when the chord **rotates**. A straight run therefore has a genuinely settled near end even though the path object changes every event. Bounding the redraw by the capsule's *swept* region — the area between its edges at event *n* and at *n+1* — rather than by its whole area is the version that would pay, and it degrades gracefully: exactly nothing is saved on a stroke that curves hard, which is the stroke that was never the problem. `BuildSilhouette` would have to report the open run's anchor for any of this, which it does not today.

The mechanism had to go, and B311 — the same code drawing curves 6–21 px off its own dabs — said so independently.

Max is also order-independent and idempotent, so a cached prefix plus a fresh tail is exactly the whole — the property the union could not offer.

What max cannot do is take a dab back, so the moving tail keeps the same backup-and-replace the scratch already used, moved one level down onto that buffer; a cut that went backwards rebuilds from black rather than trusting `StableCount`'s monotonicity, which is true in practice and is not an invariant.

The silhouette route is no longer mirrored at all: it calls `BrushEngine.AccumulateCoverage` and `CoverageToInk`, and only the bookkeeping being measured stays in the harness.

  - **Kept rather than deleted because it carries evidence B298 does not**, and the evidence is what rules out a rendering change as the cause. Both strokes walk **98 dabs** with and without B307's subdivision — probed, `maxFidelity=1`, because the control's spacing of 0.08 is already finer than the 0.09 fidelity target — and the absolute costs are identical on both trees to within a millisecond: on `main` at 081acd8a, 720p medium 113.5 ms against plain 126.9; on the branch, 114.4 against 125.5. At 4K, 118.0 against 165.4 and 115.8 against 164.0. So the plain control is simply the dearer stroke, because it pays the footprint ceiling — a pixel pass over the stroke's region, which grows with the canvas — while the medium is excluded from that ceiling and simulates on a bounded lattice.

Both were guesses that fitted the symptom; neither survived being measured. The number was real and the attribution was not, which is the lesson `docs/DESIGN-performance.md` already records.

    | 50 | 7.93 ms | 0.20 | **7.73** | 126 |

    | 400 | 52.12 ms | 12.23 | **39.89** | 19 |

    | **n^** | **0.77** | 1.51 | **0.69** | |

    | points | rebuilt | carried | **cap-only** | events/s |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 50 | 7.11 ms | 0.87 | **0.15** | 6,549 |
    | 200 | 33.82 ms | 23.70 | **0.02** | 55,249 |
    | 800 | 59.63 ms | 31.92 | **0.02** | 45,249 |
    | **n^** | 0.75 | 1.30 | **−0.84** | |

  - **So both halves of this entry are one fix: accumulate the footprint incrementally and cap only the band that changed.** The footprint is a running maximum, which is monotone — B292 worked that out — so a persistent buffer stamped with only the new dabs answers the stamping cost, and a `StableCount` cut with a tail rollback answers the objection `PostProcessRegion` records. `LivePaintSession` already holds exactly such a buffer for B299, and the two are **mutually exclusive by construction**: `NeedsFootprintCap` requires `!DrawsAsOneSilhouette`, so one buffer with one lifetime serves both routes and only the accumulating shader differs. Once the footprint is band-local the region copy follows it, which is the second half without a second mechanism.

    | size | without | with |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | 12 | 25.7 ms | 39.9 ms |
    | 30 | 33.0 ms | 47.4 ms |
    | 80 | 46.4 ms | 87.0 ms |

    So 1.44–1.87×, and the reason is that every dab is drawn twice — once for the mark, once for the footprint — plus one span pass. Too much for the per-event fast path, which is why it went where the other stroke-global passes are.
  - **The fix is to make the footprint cheap rather than to move it.** A footprint is the falloff as a function of distance from the centreline, so it does not need one draw per dab: the stroke's path stroked at a handful of decreasing widths, outermost first, describes the same field in ~32 draws instead of ~2000, with no max-accumulation needed because the bands nest by construction.   - **Narrowed on 2026-08-24, not closed, and the two attempts are worth having written down** (`BrushEngine.CanOutrunItsFootprint`, `FootprintCapTests.SkippingTheCeilingWhereItCannotBindChangesNoPixel`).
    - **Skipping the ceiling where it cannot bind is exact and lands.** Overlap is what makes it bind: at a pixel where one dab's shape is `s`, `n` overlapping dabs at flow `f` reach `1-(1-f·s)^n` against a ceiling of `s`, so it binds only when `n·f > 1`. And `n` is bounded — a pixel is covered by at most one diameter of travel, a diameter holds `1/spacing` dabs — so **`flow ≤ spacing` cannot reach the footprint however the dabs fall**. Verified on pixels rather than argued: two brushes one ulp of flow apart, either side of the predicate, render **0 differing pixels over 2 990 partial ones**, where a real flow change moves 2 998 of them by up to 196/255.
    - **It reaches two shipped presets, and they are the two that matter most.** **Smudge** (flow 0.08 against spacing 0.10) and **Blender** (0.06 against 0.06) both fall under the line, and the cap was the *only* reason either was on the deferred path — measured across all fourteen built-in presets, both go from `deferred True` to `deferred False`. So the two brushes `docs/manual/03-tools-and-strokes.md` promises are "exact now — the same pixels, live and committed" are exact under the pen again, and they stop drawing every dab twice. What it does **not** reach is the paint brushes: Airbrush is flow 0.25 against spacing 0.08, Soft round is flow 1 against 0.15, and the default hardness 0.8 brush the entry is about is untouched.
    - **A question this raised and did not answer:** for an effect brush, `Flow` is not paint density — the Smudge preset's own comment says it is "how hard each dab pushes", and for **Blur** it is the sigma (`sigma = Flow × Size / 4`). So a footprint ceiling on an effect brush may not describe anything, and Blur is still capped at flow 0.35 against spacing 0.12 for no reason anyone has stated. Not guessed at here; it wants asking.
    - **Bounding the pass spatially was tried and reverted: it culls nothing.** The idea was to stamp only the dabs that can reach the post-process region. Measured on a 1920-px stroke: region `{81,81,1838×438}`, **446 dabs, reach 19.0 px, 0 outside**. `PostProcessBounds` *is* the whole stroke's bounds, so both callers already pass the whole mark and there is nothing to exclude. Recorded because it is the same mistake as the withdrawn silhouette cache (**B292**) one step earlier — a plausible optimisation with no measurement in front of it.
    - **The untried candidate is the per-dab shader.** `StampFootprint` builds an `SKShader.CreateRadialGradient` for **every dab** — ~446 allocations on the stroke above — where one unit-radius gradient per stroke drawn under a translate-and-scale would be arithmetically identical for a radially symmetric gradient under a uniform transform. That is where the 1.44–1.87× most likely lives, and it wants pixel-equality evidence before it is believed.
  - **Filed rather than fixed** because it is a second objective on a branch whose first was the hardness defect. Cost: M.

  - **Attempted 2026-08-24 alongside B292 and stopped, with the two candidate fixes costed rather than guessed.** Both are real work and neither is safe to bolt onto another branch:
    - **Cache the settled footprint**, the way B292 caches the settled outline. It is the same monotone-prefix idea and it would work arithmetically — max-accumulation is monotone, so a cached prefix plus a fresh tail is exactly the whole. But `PostProcessRegion` runs on a **worker** (`LivePostRunner`, B189), and that pass is thread-safe precisely because *"the worker touches only its copies"*. A cached Skia surface reaching across that boundary is the shape of hazard that produced B130's native crash, so this needs the ownership designed rather than a field added. It would also have to grow-and-blit as the mark's bounds grow, which is `EnsureScratch`'s problem again.
    - **Quantise the falloff into nested bands** — the original note's suggestion. Reusing the silhouette walk at scaled radii gives variable-width bands, which is what a pressure-varying brush needs; ~24 cheap path builds against ~4000 gradient-shaded dab draws. But it is an approximation of the falloff rather than the same shape, so it changes pixels and would re-baseline the same seven fingerprints Q157 just re-recorded — and that is a decision about art, not a refactor.
  - So the honest state is: the ceiling is correct and it is off the path the pen waits on (measured at 5.88 ms against 5.80 ms per event, hard against soft), and what it costs is exactness under the pen for the default brush. Making it exact needs one of the two above, chosen deliberately.

- [x] **B250** `P2` `brush` The weight brush reads a mouse as half pressure, so influence builds at half strength `evidence: AMouseDabsAtFullStrength, APenKeepsItsPressureAxis`
  - Owner's report, 2026-08-17: "I needed to paint many many times to turn it red." The weight path had its own pressure helper (`raw <= 0 ? 1.0 : raw`) that passed a mouse's ~0.5 straight into the dab, while the paint brush's `PressureOf(PointerPoint)` has always treated any non-pen pointer as full pressure. Half strength into the 0.35 per-dab rate roughly doubles the passes to saturate a region.
  - Fixed by giving the weight brush the paint brush's rule, as a pure function (`CanvasControl.WeightPressure`) the tests can hold without synthesizing pointer events.

- [x] **B226** `P2` `brush` A performance test divides by a three-microsecond measurement and fails on CI at random `evidence: FillCostFollowsTheRegionNotTheCanvas`
  - **Found by it failing a pull request that could not possibly have caused it.** `PaperFieldTests.FillCostFollowsTheRegionNotTheCanvas` went red on a branch that touches nothing in `Lightbox.Raster`, which is what made it worth root-causing rather than re-running.
  - **The measured cause, not a guess.** The test asserts the 1024×1024 fill is at least 20× the 64×64 one, proving cost tracks the region rather than the sheet. Instrumented locally it reads **93–121×**. On the CI runner it read **9.3×** — and both halves moved: the small side went **0.0031 → 0.0174 ms (5.6× slower)** as scheduler noise landed on it, while the large side went **0.3370 → 0.1616 ms (2× faster)** on a quicker CPU. A denominator inflated and a numerator deflated is how a 100× margin becomes a failure.
  - **The real defect is the sample size.** One 64×64 fill is ~3 µs, and the loop timed 200 of them — **~0.6 ms of work**, comparable to a single scheduler slice on a shared runner. A ratio whose denominator is three microseconds is not measuring the code, it is measuring the machine's mood. `SmallFills = 5,000` puts ~15 ms on the clock and `LargeFills = 30` puts ~10 ms, so both totals are large against the noise instead of inside it.
  - **The 20× floor is deliberately unchanged**, and that is the whole judgement in this entry. The obvious fix is to loosen the assertion until CI stops complaining, which keeps the flake — it only makes it rarer — and weakens the invariant-6 guard the test exists for. The honest fix for a measurement too small to trust is a bigger measurement.
  - **Detection power was proved rather than assumed.** `PaperField.Fill` was mutated to evaluate a whole 1024×1024 sheet per call — the exact rewrite this test guards against — and it fails at **ratio 0.9×**. The fixed test still catches what it was written for.
  - Costs nothing: the whole test runs in ~45 ms, because five thousand three-microsecond fills is fifteen milliseconds.

- [x] **B193** `P2` `brush` A failed settings write leaves every brush control silently dead for the rest of the session `evidence: BrushWorkingSetTests, AThrowInsideTheApplyStillLowersTheGuard, TheGuardIsRaisedOnlyForTheDurationOfTheApply`
  - Found while extracting `BrushWorkingSet` from `MainViewModel`, not from a report — nobody has hit it, and the entry says so rather than inventing a symptom.
  - **The mechanism.** Applying a preset assigns the bound brush properties, and every one of their setters writes back into the working settings — so the assignment has to be fenced or picking a preset immediately edits it. The fence was `_applyingPreset = true; …; _applyingPreset = false;`, written out **nine times, none of them in a `try`/`finally`**. Three of those regions reach `Settings.Save()`, which is file I/O: a full disk, a locked file, a profile directory that has gone away.
  - **What one throw costs.** The flag stays raised for the life of the view model, and from then on every bound brush property no-ops: the size slider moves and the mark does not change, the hardness dial turns and nothing happens, and there is no error anywhere to connect it to. It is B39's shape exactly — a stale flag that suppresses behaviour quietly — and the recovery is restarting the application, which an artist has no reason to think of.
  - **P2 rather than P1**: *blocks work* × *rare*. It cannot corrupt anything already drawn, and it needs a write to fail; but when it does fire it takes the whole brush with it and gives no clue why.
  - Fix: the raise and the lower are one method with a `finally` (`BrushWorkingSet.Applying`), and the flag has no public setter, so a caller cannot leave it up without writing a loop on purpose. Re-entrant calls run the body without re-raising, because nesting is not an error — lowering the guard early is.
  - Cost: S. The extraction it came out of is the expensive part and was happening anyway.

- [x] **B177** `P2` `brush` Pencil and the flat texture brushes lag while Ink stays responsive — and the cost badge calls all three Fast `evidence: BrushPresetBudgetTests, TheEverydayPresetsAreAllInsideTheStrokeBudget, GranulationCostsWhatTheBadgeSaysItCosts, TheBadgeFollowsTheCostTier`
  - Reported from the hand rather than a stopwatch: "ink is really responsive; flat medium and pencil lag."
  - **The reason to take this seriously is what the three presets have in common.** `Ink` is `Size = 5, Hardness = 1, Flow = 1, Spacing = 0.1` and nothing else. `Pencil` adds `Granulation = 0.15` and a tighter `Spacing = 0.12`; the flat brushes are the texture-only pair, "no simulation, just the rim and grain effects". So the two that lag are the two carrying per-dab texture work, and the one that does not is plain.
  - **And `BrushCostOf` badges all three `Fast`**, because it counts only a simulated medium, smudge/blur and cross-layer sampling — with a written argument that scatter, jitter, tips, paper texture and pressure curves "change how a mark looks without changing what the engine has to go and fetch, and calling them expensive would make the badge meaningless by putting it on everything." That argument is sound and this report is evidence against its conclusion, which is the whole point of a badge derived from settings: it can be checked, and here an artist has checked it.
  - **So there are two candidate outcomes and the entry must not prejudge which.** Either the badge is honest and the lag is somewhere else entirely — spacing, the live-preview repaint region, the stroke path rather than the dab — in which case this is a `canvas` bug wearing a brush's name; or granulation and grain really do cost enough to feel, and `BrushCostOf` needs a third answer between Fast and Expressive. Measure per-preset before touching either.
  - **Measure it the way `CLAUDE.md` says to measure a brush**, and note that the saturation trap does not apply here — this is time per stroke, not alpha along one — but its general form does: ask what else is in the measurement before asking what is wrong with the code. A `Spacing` of 0.12 against 0.1 is 20% more dabs on its own, and attributing that to granulation would be the same mistake in a new place.
  - P2 rather than P3: this is the drawing floor, on the two presets an artist reaches for without thinking, and the charter has budgets for exactly this. Cost: M, mostly measurement.
  - **Measured 2026-08-12, and the report is right: the badge is wrong.** `BrushPresetSweeps` sweeps the one axis nothing else did — *which brush* — and reports live cost and commit cost separately, because drag while drawing and a pause on pen-lift are different faults with different fixes. A 40-event stroke at 1920×1080, median of 7: **Ink commits in 7.8 ms, Pencil in 17.9, Gouache (flat) 37.0, Watercolor (flat) 39.6.** Live cost is 1.4–2.0 ms/event for everything, so this is a commit-time fault, not a per-event one.
  - **Attributed by removal rather than by elimination**, which is the part that makes it a finding instead of a suspicion. Turning one setting off and re-measuring: **Pencil 21.6 → 9.3 ms with granulation off (granulation is 12.4 ms, 57% of its commit)**; Watercolor (flat) 40.9 → 11.9 with wet edge and granulation off (**71%**); Gouache (flat) 37.9 → 10.0 (**74%**). With the texture effects off all three land at 9–12 ms, beside Ink's 7.8. **So the texture effects are the cost, and `BrushCostOf` calling them Fast is wrong.**
  - **Two predictions in this entry and in the plan that measurement refuted, recorded because they were the obvious ones.** The spacing/size confound this entry warned about does not exist: `WalkDabs` gives Pencil and Ink **the identical 2349 dabs** despite Size 3/Spacing 0.12 against Size 5/Spacing 0.10, so dab count explains none of the gap — and why spacing does not move the count is worth its own look. And the per-dab `SKPaint` allocation in `StampDab` is not the cause either: live cost separates the two presets by only 0.56 ms/event.
  - **The manual is wrong in two places as a result**, and both are promises rather than descriptions: `04-brushes.md:324` lists Pencil under *"**Fast** — stamps dabs and stops"*, and `:343` says every simulated medium has a flat counterpart *"for none of the cost"* — while **Gouache (flat) at 37.0 ms is 33% *slower* than simulated Gouache at 27.9**, and Oil (flat) at 29.3 is only 16% cheaper than Oil at 34.8. The flat counterparts are not, today, the cheap option they are sold as.
  - **Where the time goes is located, not guessed.** `ApplyWetEdge` (`BrushEngine.cs:1314`) allocates three `SKSurface`s and does about eleven full-region draws over the stroke bounds — four to saturate the silhouette, three more with `DstIn` to raise it to the fourth power, plus blur, carve and darken. Granulation already caches its grain tile, so its 8–12 ms is in the draw rather than in the noise.
  - **The obvious fix was tried and rejected, and the rejection is the useful part.** Both repeated-draw groups are exact per-alpha functions — `1-(1-a)^4` and `a^4` — so each is expressible as one `SKColorFilter.CreateTable` in a single draw, turning seven full-region traversals into two. The tables were built by replaying the eight-bit arithmetic rather than evaluating the formula, precisely so the rounding would match. **It still moved the pixels**, on exactly the two shapes that run the pass and neither of the two that do not: `9F85DAE8… → A54E82E2…` and `5FED81B4… → C4724B2A…`. `CreateTable` works in unpremultiplied colour, so the round trip rounds differently from repeated premultiplied compositing however carefully the table is built. Reverted.
  - **All 492 raster tests passed through that change**, because the wet-edge tests assert the rim is darker than the centre and that stays true when every pixel shifts by a unit. So it would have shipped, and every document already drawn with a wet edge would have re-rendered differently on load — the silent-pixel-change failure invariants 2 and 4 exist to stop. `BrushPresetRenderFingerprintTests` is the guard that was missing and now hashes the render of four brush shapes.
  - **Next candidates, none of which change a pixel by construction:** pool the three `SKSurface`s across commits rather than allocating per stroke; do the saturation on a smaller surface, since the silhouette only needs the stroke's own bounds; or skip the pass entirely below a `WetEdge` at which the rim is invisible — a threshold is a behaviour change but a *declared* one, unlike a rounding drift. Measure each against `BrushPresetSweeps` and the fingerprints.
  - **Resolved on the badge's side, which the measurement said was the honest one, plus the one free draw.** `BrushCost` has the third answer this entry asked about: **Textured**, between Fast and Expressive, derived from `WetEdge > 0 || Granulation > 0` the same way everything else on the badge is derived — the picker shows ◇ against Expressive's ◈, the tooltip names the pass and that pen-lift pays for it, and a medium outranks it so a brush never wears two badges. The original "per-dab arithmetic" argument is corrected in `BrushCostOf`'s own remarks rather than deleted, with the measurement that refuted it. The manual's two wrong promises (Pencil under Fast; flat counterparts "for none of the cost") now tell the truth.
  - **One of the eleven draws was dead and is gone:** `ApplyWetEdge` drew the raw stroke image into the rim surface on creation and then `Clear`ed it before the carve. Removal is pixel-identical by construction and the fingerprints pin it. The other candidates above remain candidates — they are improvement work, not this defect.
  - **What closes it:** the report was two claims — the lag is real, and the badge denies it. The first was confirmed and attributed (the commit-time texture passes, 57–74%); the second is fixed, so the cost is now *chosen* the way `CLAUDE.md` says costly options must be. `TheEverydayPresetsAreAllInsideTheStrokeBudget` guards the everyday four through the real pipeline at an order-of-magnitude budget, so a texture pass gone quadratic fails the suite rather than an artist's hand.

- [x] **B96** `P2` `brush` Selecting a brush marks the document unsaved; changing its settings does not `evidence: DirtyRevisionTests, ChoosingABrushDoesNotMarkTheDocument`

- [x] **B73** `P2` `brush` Fast strokes trail behind the pen `evidence: StrokeLatencyTests, TheFirstFrameOfABurstIsNotStale, APenBurstIsOneFrameNotOnePerEvent, WhenTheBurstHasDrainedTheMarkReachesThePen`
  - Reported for ordinary brushes and for media brushes, with the stabiliser on and off — so it is not stabilisation lag, which is the obvious suspect and would be the wrong fix.
  - `evidence: manual` originally, and the reasoning was half right: the existing budgets do all pass. `LivePreview_PlainBrushSegment_StaysCheap` is 7 ms and `APointerEventStaysInBudgetDeepIntoALongStroke` holds well inside a frame, so this was never the per-event cost those measure. The entry then concluded that a test "would have to measure *latency from input to pixel*, which Xvfb cannot supply honestly".
  - **That is true of latency in milliseconds and false of latency in pointer events**, which is the reframe that made this testable. "The ink trails the pen" is a statement about *order*: events are waiting in the queue and the frame on screen does not contain them yet. Whether a published frame includes the events already queued when it was published needs no clock, no compositor and no display — it is a fact about dispatcher priority, and it is exactly reproducible.
  - Cause, and it was the first place the entry said to look. **Avalonia runs `Render > Loaded > Default > Input > Background`** — `Default` is *above* `Input`, the reverse of WPF, where it sits below. `RequestSnapshot` posted at `Default`, so a publish jumped ahead of every pen event already queued:
    - the frame drawn was **already behind**, published before a single queued `MoveStroke` had run, so the ink stopped where the pen had been several events ago;
    - and because the publish ran *between* events rather than after them, a burst produced one publish per event. Measured: **11 queued events → 11 publishes**. A publish is the expensive half, so the faster the stroke the more the work multiplied and the further the lag compounded — which is why the report was about *fast* strokes specifically.
  - Fixed: post at `DispatcherPriority.Input`. That queue is FIFO, so the publish lands behind the events already waiting — one frame covers the burst and is current — and ahead of events arriving afterwards, so a continuous drag still renders. Measured after: **11 events → 1 publish**, and the first frame reaches the last event. `Background` also drains a burst and can be starved by continuous input, which is the state an artist is in for the whole of a long stroke; `Render` is forbidden for an older reason recorded at the call site. Cost: S
  - **What this does not explain**, so nobody closes the artist's report on the strength of it: the reporter saw it with media brushes too, and a medium may simply cost what it costs — that would be a different bug with the same symptom. Three things are now guarded and were not: staleness, work amplification, and that the mark reaches the pen at 12, 40 and 147 px once the burst drains. Stabilisation is measured separately in the same file so its designed lag can never be mistaken for this.

- [x] **B69** `P2` `brush` An effect brush changes what it painted when the pen lifts `evidence: EffectPreviewMatchesCommitTests, ASmudgePreviewMatchesItsCommit, ABlenderPreviewMatchesItsCommit, TheAffectedAreaDoesNotChangeOnRelease`
  - Reported for blur, smudge and blender together: "click and release changes the effected area. The strokes seem to settle on release. What we paint should be what we see. No post-processing settling of any kind."
  - **Related to B54 and deliberately not merged into it.** B54 is the measured blur instance — the draft snapshot is cropped per segment, so the live blur over-covers by ~88 px — and it is `P3` because the number is smaller than what was reported. This entry is the artist-facing statement of the whole family, across all three effect brushes, and it is the one that says what "fixed" means: the preview and the commit produce the same pixels. B54 can close without this one closing.
  - The mechanism is the split path: `StampBlurDraft`/the live composite run while the pointer is down and `StampBlur`/`StampSmudge` run on release, and they are different code. Anything that makes them agree fixes this; anything that only narrows the gap does not. Cost: L
  - **The stated mechanism was half right, and the half it missed is the one that mattered.** There is no `StampSmudgeDraft` — the smudge case in `StampStroke` ignores `draft` entirely, so the same code ran live and on release. The split was not in the *engine*, it was in the **feed**: `MainViewModel.FlushLivePreview` handed the smudge `points.Skip(stamped - 1)`, the newest segment, while the commit walked the whole stroke in one pass. Four things restarted every pointer event — the dab walk's spacing phase (BR1, fixed for paint in B45 and for blur in B54, left true here), the **carried colour**, the heading, and the one-point overlap where segments join, re-smeared because a smudge is not idempotent. The code said so out loud: *"Left on the segment feed deliberately; its own live-versus-commit fidelity is a separate question from B54."* It was the same question.
  - **Fixed with blur's treatment plus the one piece blur does not need.** The caller walks the whole stroke with the shared densify cache and stamps only the unsettled range, exactly as B54 does. A blur can stop there because its dabs read the pre-stroke pixels and are independent; a smudge's are a chain, so two more things travel between events: a `SmudgeCarry` checkpoint (the colour a single pass would be carrying at the settled boundary) and a backup of the pixels under the provisional tail, taken back before the range is replayed. That last part is what stops a re-stamped dab compounding its own previous deposit — a smudge reads the bitmap it writes.
  - **Exact, not merely closer**, which is what the entry demanded. After the restore the composite holds precisely "pre-stroke pixels + dabs 0..settled-1" and the carry is what a single pass would hold there, so replaying the rest *is* the commit's sequence. Reads reaching outside the restored region can only touch settled pixels. Measured through the real pipeline at four sizes and both modes, horizontal and diagonal: **0 px differ, worst 0** — where the blur's equivalent still carries a bounded rim residue because its dabs cannot be replayed this cheaply.
  - Before, on the same harness: **7,215 px for the smudge and 4,730 for the blender**, worst 13/255 and 8/255.
  - **Guarded in two places on purpose.** `EffectPreviewMatchesCommitTests` proves the engine's resumable range reproduces a single pass; `LivePreviewPixelTests.AnEffectStroke_LooksTheSame_LiveAndCommitted` drives BeginStroke → five MoveStroke events → EndStroke and proves the *application* feeds it that way. The engine was always correct when handed a whole stroke, so an engine test alone would have passed against the bug. Cost: L

- [x] **B55** `P2` `brush` No determinism evidence survives leaving the process `evidence: RuntimeDeterminismTests, TheFingerprint_MatchesTheRecordedBaseline, TheBaseline_IsStillRecorded`
  - Repro: not a failure to observe, an absence to check. `EffectBrushes_AreDeterministic_AcrossRerenders`, `FillStroke_SurvivesDocumentSerialization_PixelForPixel`, `ClippedStroke_ReRendersIdenticallyFromJsonAlone`, `WithoutACamera_TheExportIsByteForByteWhatItAlwaysWas` and `OutputScaleTests` all compare exactly — and both sides of every one of them are computed in the same process. Change the render by one bit between runtimes and all of them still pass.
  - What they prove is worth having and is not this: that the engine is a function, consulting no clock, no RNG and no uninitialised memory. Invariant 2 asks for that. It does not follow that the function is the same function it was on another runtime, because nothing compares against a value produced by one.
  - `Hash01` is not the exposure, which is the part that misdirects. All three copies — `BrushEngine`, `PaperField`, `TipGenerator` — are FNV-then-avalanche over `uint`/`int` seeded through `BitConverter.SingleToInt32Bits`, so the language specifies every bit and a runtime cannot change what they return. The exposure is the float arithmetic around them: scatter turns a hash into an angle and moves the dab by `Math.Cos`/`Math.Sin`, and transcendental results are not guaranteed bit-identical across runtime versions. One ULP moves a dab a fraction of a pixel, which changes an antialiased edge, which changes the file — and looks like nothing at all until two machines disagree about one document.
  - Fix: `tests/Lightbox.Raster.Tests/RuntimeDeterminismTests.cs` is the instrument and it was already in the tree; what closed this is its `Baseline` constant being filled in from a real run. Cost: S
  - P2, and it is the ordering that earns it rather than the severity. The baseline has to be recorded on the runtime being left behind; recorded after a TFM bump it captures the new runtime as the reference and destroys the only evidence that would have shown a change. So this was cheap now and impossible later. See `docs/DESIGN-net10-upgrade.md`.
  - Fixed: recorded on **.NET 8.0.29 / SkiaSharp 3.119.4, linux-x64**, with the runtime named in the constant's remarks because three hashes with no provenance are not evidence — a future mismatch is only diagnosable against a stated starting point. Debug and Release were checked to agree, so the guard does not depend on configuration.
  - **The reason it was `evidence: manual` is now closed rather than tolerated**, and that is the part worth keeping. `bugs.py sync` can see that a file exists and cannot see whether a constant inside it is still empty, so naming the fingerprint test alone would have ticked this box while the guard was inert — and emptying the constant is the cheapest way to silence a real pixel regression, because the test goes back to logging and passing. `TheBaseline_IsStillRecorded` asserts the constant is non-empty, so the blanking route is red instead of quiet, and the evidence list means what it says.
  - Blanking it was never needed to re-record either: `TheFingerprint_MatchesTheRecordedBaseline` writes what it computed *before* it asserts, so a failing run already prints the block to paste.

It is read only inside `WriteBack`'s `canMix` branch, which needs `PhysicalMixing` *and* existing paint underneath, so on bare paper it is inert by construction. The entry named it first and it is not a tuning knob for this at all; it is the pigment's hiding power *when layered over something*.

With the watercolour simulation on: **peak 51 over 17,680 px, total 469k**. The mark spreads to 1.7× the area — which is what a wash should do — but the total falls to **51%**, and spreading alone would leave it near 80. So it is not only spread: something between seeding and write-back is dropping about half of what it was given. (Darkening is not linear in pigment mass, so "half the pigment" is the shape of the claim rather than the number.)
    - The knobs that do move it, one at a time: `PigmentDensity` 0.5→0.95 gives 96, `Opacity` 0.55→0.95 gives 87, `Wetness` 0.85→0.5 gives 61, `FlowSteps` 16→6 gives 60. Together, 0.9 / 0.85 / `PressureWater` 0.5 reaches 141 — about where the unsimulated brush already is.

Whoever picks this up should reconcile the two numbers before tuning to either.

  - **The lattice loses nothing, and the "two things" above collapse to one.** Swept properly: `PigmentDensity` 0.25 / 0.50 / 0.75 / 1.00 gives total darkening **313,020 / 615,830 / 918,339 / 1,220,860** — linear to 0.1% — and at 1.00 the simulated brush lands within **0.46%** of the same brush with the medium switched off (1,220,860 against 1,215,215). `FluidLattice` conserves pigment exactly, as its own `TotalPigment` tests already claimed. The whole of the missing half was the preset's `PigmentDensity = 0.5` multiplying the seed at `SeedFromCoverage`, and the earlier sweep listed "0.5→0.95 gives 96" without connecting it. `Hiding` is confirmed byte-identically inert on bare paper, which the entry suspected. The 9/255 did not reproduce with or without `tip-builtin-wet-edge` registered — **54 either way**, so the tip is irrelevant to peak and the headline number should read 54.

Replaced with Beer–Lambert, `α = 1 − exp(−3·mass)`.

Three consequences, all of them the character of the medium rather than fidelity for its own sake: a thin wash reads (mass 0.1 gives α 0.26 against 0.10); **glazing works** — three passes give 96 → 168 → 210 where the old map was a flat wall above unit mass, and that is the single most characteristic thing watercolour does; and it approaches opacity without reaching it, while body media stay solid (Gouache 225, Oil 238). `PigmentDensity` now saturates — 0.25/0.5/0.75/1.0 give 62/96/115/126 — which is what a concentration does.

  - The doc comment on `MediumSettings.PigmentDensity` says "pigment carried per unit of **water**" and the code applies it per unit of **coverage**, independent of water. The code is the sane half — coupling it to water would make `Wetness` double as a darkness knob, backwards for a medium where more water means paler — so the comment is what is wrong. - [x] **B49** `P2` `brush` The shipped Blur brush does not blur `evidence: BrushPickerTests, TheShippedBlurBrushActuallySoftensWhatItPassesOver, EveryBuiltInBrushLeavesAMarkOnItsTile`
  - Repro: pick Blur and scrub over a hard edge. Nothing happens, and nothing ever will — not with a longer stroke, not with more passes.
  - Cause: `Flow` is the blur sigma (`sigma = Flow × Size / 4`), and the preset shipped at `Flow = 0.1` — a 0.6 px sigma on a 24 px brush, which is below what a pixel can show. The comment beside it justified the value on the grounds that the blur is "applied at every dab" and would therefore build up. **It does not build up.** `StampBlur` snapshots the layer once before the stroke and draws that one snapshot per dab with `SKBlendMode.Src` — deliberately, because stacking a semi-transparent blur per dab is what B37 was. So the sigma an artist gets is exactly the sigma of a single dab, and a value chosen on the assumption of accumulation is off by however much it expected to accumulate.
  - **Found by the picker preview, not by using the brush.** Three tiles came out blank because smudge, blur and the blender deposit nothing on clean paper; giving them a test pattern to work on fixed two of them and left the third visibly untouched, which is what made a brush nobody had complained about worth measuring. A sweep across `Flow` 0.1 / 0.4 / 1.0 at true size showed the first doing nothing and the other two working — so the path was fine and the number was wrong.
  - Fix: `Flow = 0.35`, a 2 px sigma at the default size, and the comment corrected to say why accumulation does not happen. Safe for existing art by invariant 4 — a stroke carries the settings it was painted with, so no drawing changes.
  - Still open: the same reasoning error may be sitting in the smudge presets, which were tuned in the same pass. Not touched here, because that is a second brush and a second measurement.
  - Cost: S

N passes of sigma s reach like s·√N, and each pass drags colour in from three sigma further out, so the mark spread well past the brush as the drag went on.

- [x] **B26** `P2` `brush` Paint load thins the whole stroke instead of running out along it `evidence: LoadAt, ALoadedBrushStartsFullAndRunsOut, AFullBrushNeverRunsOut, ItWorksWithoutASimulatedMedium, LoadIsNotAppliedTwiceWhenAMediumIsOn, ABiggerBrushCarriesFurther`
  - Repro: paint with Oil, which ships `PaintLoad = 0.6`. The mark is 40% transparent from the first dab to the last, evenly. Measured interior alpha 0.600 against 1.000 for the same brush with no medium — exactly the load, applied as a flat multiplier.
  - Cause: `PaintLoad` says "paint on the brush at the start of a stroke. Below 1 the brush runs out as the stroke lengthens, which is what dry-brush is", and `MediumSimulator.SeedFromCoverage` reads it as `pigment = density * c * load`. There is no arc length in that expression, so there is nothing for the brush to run out of. It is a transparency slider wearing a dry-brush label.
  - Consequence: oil and gouache are body colour and they render translucent, which is half of "gouache and oil have no height". It also means the one control that would give a stroke a *beginning and an end* — the loaded start, the dragged-out tail — currently gives it neither.
  - Fix: `BrushEngine.LoadAt` — remaining paint decays exponentially with distance travelled, measured between dab centres so it is the path the paint took after spacing and smoothing have had their say. It lives in the dab walk because that is where arc length is; `MediumSimulator` works off the scratch surface's coverage on purpose and never learns how the stroke was drawn. A side effect worth having: it now works for a brush with **no medium at all**, which is what a dry brush actually is.
  - The length scale is in brush diameters, so resizing a brush does not silently re-tune its load. Load 1 returns exactly 1 and is a byte-for-byte no-op, so nothing already drawn moves. And `MediumSimulator` no longer multiplies pigment by it — with depletion in the dab walk that would have applied it twice, and there is a test for exactly that.
  - **Dab overlap is what made this hard to tune**, and it is worth writing down. At the usual spacing a dozen dabs land on any given pixel, so the mark's alpha is `1-(1-a)^12` and saturates: at the first setting tried, a load of 0.35 faded from 1.000 to 0.858 over seven hundred pixels — not a brush running out, a brush thinking about it. The per-dab curve has to fall much further than the visible mark does, which is why the reach constant looks aggressive read on its own. Measured after: 1.000 → 0.214 → 0.000 across the same stroke. Cost: M

Above roughly 0.5 the rim comes out *lighter* than the interior, the opposite of a wet edge. **The Watercolor preset ships `EdgePull = 0.7`**, so the flagship wet brush sits on the wrong side of the peak.
  - Re-measured on a dried disc once B25 was in, rim over middle across EdgePull 0 → 1: **0.50, 0.50, 0.49, 0.48, 0.46, 0.44**. Worse than reported, and simpler: the response was not a peak that fell off after 0.5, it fell the whole way, and the rim was never darker than the middle at any setting. EdgePull made the edge *lighter*, monotonically. The number the original repro caught was a different band on a pipeline that was throwing most of the pigment away.
  - Cause: the potential, not the rate. The term climbed the gradient of film thinness, `1/(1+water)` — and inside a wash that field is bumpy, because the paper's tooth is in it and so is every eddy the flow left behind. So it was local gradient ascent on a surface covered in local maxima, and every one is a trap. Pigment walked a cell or two, found a dip, and stopped. Measured: interior roughness (scatter around the radial mean, so a smooth fade does not count) went **0.13 → 2.04** from EdgePull 0 to 1. Sixteen times the mottling and no rim — which is precisely the artist's "it still only looks like a texture created from noise".
  - Fix: make the potential the **distance to dry paper** instead. A chamfer field has no local extrema by construction, so pigment that starts moving keeps moving until it arrives; two raster sweeps, less than the smoothing pass the old comment here feared, and 242 ms against 238 ms on the 400×400×12 budget. Water depth moves from *defining the direction* to *gating the rate*, which is where it belongs: deep water carries pigment, a film about to dry pins it, so the drift stops at the rim on its own. `EdgeRate` 0.25 → 0.9, because a term that no longer traps pigment two cells from where it started needs to advect a whole cell per step to reach a boundary twenty cells away.
  - After: rim/middle **0.50, 0.81, 1.28, 1.97, 2.89, 4.03** — monotone, and a real ring at the top. Roughness 0.13 → 0.25 instead of 0.13 → 2.04. Through the stroke path, wet edge over centre at the shipped `EdgePull = 0.7` is **1.71**, against 0.97 with pooling off. The preset needed no re-tuning after all. Cost: M

No height buffer, so no per-layer state outside the document and no threat to invariant 1; the price is that two crossing strokes do not build a ridge where they meet, each being shaded from its own coverage. Evidence: `ThickPaintIsModelled_AndFlatPaintIsNot`, `TheRaisedEdgeCatchesTheLight`, `PaintWithNoBodyRendersExactlyAsItAlwaysDid`, `ShadingPaintsNoExtraCoverage`, `ReliefIsAsRepeatableAsEverythingElse`.

That does not close this entry: it is a different control in a different place, and `BristleDrag` on `MediumSettings` still reads by nothing.

That is the half that would have survived merely hiding the sliders, because it lives in the document rather than in the panel.

- [x] **B4** `P2` `brush` Blur, smudge and blender brushes only update on pen lift `evidence: SmudgeShowsMidDrag`
  - Repro: pick smudge or blur, drag across existing paint. The smear appears only when the pen lifts.
  - Cause: `FlushLivePreview` appends the draft into `_liveComposite`, but `PublishSnapshot`'s overlay branch only ever reads `_liveScratch`. The composite is computed every event and never shown.
  - Fix: for the active layer, a blur/smudge drag **replaces** the layer bitmap rather than overlaying a scratch — these tools modify pixels that are already there, so an overlay is the wrong shape.
