- [x] **B70** `P3` `brush` A brush tip has no effect on smudge, blur or the blender `evidence: EffectBrushTipTests, ATipChangesWhatAnEffectBrushTouches, AFollowingTipTurnsWithTheStroke, AnUntippedEffectBrushIsUnchanged`
  - Reported: setting a brush tip does not change these brushes. `StampSmudge` builds its dab from `RadiusAt` and a hardness falloff in `LerpDab`, and the blur path draws a blurred snapshot through a radial gradient — neither consults `BrushTipRegistry`, so a chisel or a bristle tip is silently ignored where a paint brush would use it.
  - It is `P3` rather than `P2` because the mark is still a legitimate mark and nothing is corrupted; what is wrong is that a control the artist set does nothing and says nothing, which is the same silence as B63. Cost: M
  - Fixed for all three. Smudge and the blender share one path — the blender *is* smudge in `Dulling` mode, not a `BrushKind` of its own — so a `DabShape` sampler multiplies the tip's own alpha into the per-pixel weight `LerpDab` already computes. A tip contributes a **weight** rather than a shape to blit here, because these paths composite per pixel: the deposit is a weighted move toward a colour.
  - Blur needed a layer and the reason is worth keeping. What is wanted is `dst = lerp(dst, blurred, tipAlpha)` and Skia has no blend mode for it against an existing surface; drawing the tip with `DstIn` straight onto the target would erase everything the tip does *not* cover, which is the artist's painting. So the blurred content is built in a layer the size of the dab, masked there, and composited over. The layer is the dab's own bounds, never the canvas or the stroke, so invariant 6 holds — and it is only taken when the brush *has* a tip, so a round blur still uses the cheap circle clip and nothing that works today pays for this.
  - **The first attempt made it worse and the number said so**: masking by drawing the tip image with `DstIn` only masks the pixels that image covers, so the ring between the tip's rect and the dab's bounds kept its blur — 19,646 px touched against the round dab's 9,823, the opposite of the fix. A `Decal`-tiled tip *shader* over the whole bounds reads as transparent outside itself, so one `DrawRect` masks the whole layer. After: 3,132 px with 396 above the tip's band, which is the blur's own spread and not the tip being ignored.
  - Measured with a tip no falloff can imitate — one horizontal bar across an empty square, so "the tip worked" cannot be confused with "softer" or "smaller". Smudge and the blender go from 9,740 px touched (2,450 of them above the bar's band) to 1,924 px with **none** above it.
  - `AngleFollowsDirection` reaches these brushes too, which it could not before: they iterate positions rather than the dab walk, so heading is computed from consecutive dabs using the walk's own rule that a stalled pen keeps its last heading. A chisel that ignores direction is a chisel at a fixed angle, which is a different tool.
  - **`AnUntippedEffectBrushIsUnchanged` is the guard that matters most.** This threads a shape sampler through the hottest pixel loop in the engine, and every document already drawn uses the untipped path — a refactor that shifted a round smudge by one 255th would be a silent change to existing art. `RoundnessAt` was extracted rather than duplicated for the same reason: a paint dab draws roundness as a canvas scale and an effect dab now samples it per pixel, and two copies of that rule would drift.

- [x] **B57** `P3` `brush` A Smudge dab renders at outputScale² instead of outputScale `evidence: ASmudgeAtHigherOutputScale_LandsInTheSamePlace`
  - Found while eliminating causes for B39. `StampSmudge` wrapped its dab loop in `target.Save(); target.Scale(outputScale);` — the pattern every other stamp path (`StampBlur` included) uses to keep dab geometry in document coordinates under a canvas transform. But `LerpDab` does not follow that pattern: it writes through raw pixel spans on both the read bitmap and the target, so it needs device pixels to index memory correctly, and it already converts every coordinate by hand — `cx = pos.X * outputScale`, device-space bounds from `GetDeviceClipBounds`, a device-pixel-sized patch. Scaling the canvas *as well* multiplied the final `target.DrawImage(image, left, top)` a second time, landing a dab at `outputScale²`.
  - Invisible at `outputScale = 1`, where a squared factor is still 1 — which is what B39 reproduces at, so this is not that bug. It is dormant today because nothing in the app renders an effect brush at any scale but 1: `FrameBitmapCache.Get` and `FrameRasterizer.Materialize` are called from every App call site with the default. It would surface the moment a high-res export or a camera push renders a smudge stroke above 1x.

Measured at 88 px of over-coverage and `maxDiff` 89 after B33, against 672 px and 255 before it.

Padding the subset would have changed nothing measurable, which is this ledger's recurring lesson in a new hat: the number was real and the attribution was not.

The dabs landed where the commit never puts them: **1148 px the preview blurred that the commit does not**, and 610 the other way, at 147 px. Twelve frames of a 60 Hz budget is not a preview, so invariant 6 wins and the residue is written down instead: up to 127 of 255 over a few hundred pixels at the mark's rim, where a pixel the commit reached with three overlapping dabs is reached here by one. `ADraggedBlurMatchesTheCommittedOne` bounds it so it cannot grow unnoticed.

- [x] **B46** `P3` `brush` The live preview re-densifies and re-walks the whole stroke every pointer event `evidence: IncrementalDensify, IncrementalDensifyTests, EveryPrefixMatchesDensifyExactly, OnlyTheTailIsRecomputedWhenAPointIsAppended, APointerEventStaysInBudgetDeepIntoALongStroke`
  - Not a defect an artist can see today; a scaling one, and recorded because it was introduced knowingly. Fixing B45 required the live preview to walk the whole stroke rather than the newest two points, which turned O(1) work per pointer event into O(n).
  - Measured, and attributed rather than guessed: 0.41 ms over the first fifty events of a 600-event stroke and 1.70 ms over the last fifty. `GeometryOps.Densify` is 0.84 ms of the 1.15 ms walk at 600 points, so it is the majority of it and it is pure re-computation — appending one point changes only the last two spans of its output.
  - Fix: densify incrementally. `Densify` already works span by span, and a span's geometry depends only on one point behind and two ahead, so the cached output can have its tail recomputed and everything before it reused. That also makes the walk resumable, since the settled prefix's dabs are already cached.
  - Accepted for now because the budget holds with room: a pointer event 550 events into one stroke costs well under a fifth of a 60 Hz frame, and `APointerEventStaysInBudgetDeepIntoALongStroke` guards that line and prints the growth so this can be measured against something.
  - Fixed: `IncrementalDensify` caches the densified path and recomputes only the spans an edit can reach — **3 of 199 on an append**, because a span is interpolated from one point behind and two ahead. `GeometryOps.AppendSpan` is now the single implementation both it and `Densify` call, so the live preview and the committed render cannot interpolate differently. Cost: S
  - **Faithfulness was the hard requirement, not the saving.** These points decide where dabs land and every dab dynamic is seeded from where its dab is, so a cache one interpolated point off would move a dab, re-roll its scatter and change the mark. `EveryPrefixMatchesDensifyExactly` asserts value-identity against `Densify` for *every prefix* of three stroke shapes — a fast arc, a crawl short enough that densification never fires, and a zigzag whose corners it must refuse to round off.
  - Derived rather than assumed, too: a stabiliser can rewrite points already seen and undo can shorten the list, so each call locates the first differing index instead of trusting that the list only grows. Both are tested.
  - It landed with **B54**, which needed the same machinery for a different reason: the effect path has to walk the whole stroke to get the commit's dab positions, and that is only affordable if densifying it again is nearly free.

Fixing that alone changed nothing, which is what pointed at the real wall: **`MediumSimulator` runs inside the region `DabReach` computed, and `DabReach` is the geometry of the stamps.** It knows nothing about fluid. A bug is closed by something that can fail, and a private method is invisible to the thing doing the resolving. `bugs.py check` now reports `PARTIAL EVIDENCE` when some of an entry's names resolve and others do not, which is the shape this had and the shape a half-landed fix has too.

- [x] **B25** `P3` `brush` A simulated medium paints three to five times fainter than the same brush without one `evidence: Drying_PutsEveryGrainOnThePaper, HowLongTheSolverRuns_DoesNotDecideHowMuchPaintLands, DryingAMarkThatNeverFlowed_LeavesItExactlyWhereItWasStamped, FlowStepsDecideWhereThePaintGoes_NotHowMuchOfItThereIs, AMediumThatNeverFlows_StillPaintsTheStroke`

The tell was that the *flow* control set the *opacity*: measured interior alpha 0.06 at 2 flow steps, 0.18 at 8, 0.29 at 24, and 0 at 0.

Bound in place rather than by running the solver down to dryness, because a cell with no water has no velocity, so the extra sweeps would move nothing. Measured after: ink mass 3034 at 0 flow steps and 2785 at 24 (the 8% is faint fringe falling under the visibility threshold), against roughly 5× before. `FlowSteps = 0` now paints the stamped mark at the medium's pigment density. ### canvas

- [x] **B334** `P1` `canvas` A band-local pass claims every dab below it, so ink outside the band is shown by nothing `evidence: InkThePassClaimedButNeverCoveredIsStillShown, WhereThePassHasCoveredTheProcessedResultReplacesTheRawInk, BeforeAPassLandsTheRawScratchIsStillTheWholeMark`
  - **The artist's words, and no instrument in this repository could see them.** *"On fast long strokes, the first dabs are visible but stop and disappear soon thereafter. They stay hidden for quite some time as long as I am drawing, but will jump into view at some point. It seems/feels like lifting the pen does let the strokes appear slightly faster."* Said while the same session's report read `live tip drawn 505 of 505`, `too far behind 0`, `stalls 0`, `time lost 0%`. **Every counter measured WHEN something happened; ink vanishing is a question of WHETHER IT IS THERE**, and that had never been asked.
  - **Measured 2026-08-28 09:20, with an audit written for the purpose.** Comparing the ink the stroke stamped against the ink the compositor shows, one publish in eight, every fourth pixel: **3 of 11 audited publishes were missing ink, worst 4.5% of everything stamped.** Not late. Absent.
  - **The mechanism, and the dab arithmetic is what hides it.** A live pass writes only the band it processed (B313) and then records `PostStampedDabs = dabsAtPass` — every dab that existed when it was queued. The tip begins exactly where that claim ends, so **no dab falls between the two**: the accounting is airtight. The pixels are not. A dab below the claim whose pixels no band ever wrote is carried by **neither the body nor the tip**, and stays invisible until some later pass happens to cover that region. Both paths do it — the worker path at `MainViewModel.Painting.cs:2860` and the cap-only path at `:2481`.
  - **Why pen-up appears to help.** The commit re-renders the stroke from the record, which has never been band-local. Nothing is recovered; the whole mark is simply drawn properly for the first time.
  - **The fix is strictly additive, which is the whole argument for it.** The raw stamped scratch now travels beside the processed body instead of being replaced by it, and the compositor draws raw ink first, then the processed result over it with `Src` **clipped to what the passes have covered**. Inside that rectangle the output is what shipped before, pixel for pixel. Outside it, what shipped before was nothing — so this can only add ink that was already stamped and can never alter a pixel a pass produced. `Src` rather than `SrcOver` because an effect usually *reduces* alpha, and blending over would let raw ink show through a mark the pass deliberately thinned.
  - **The test was seen to fail before it was believed.** With the fix disabled in place, `InkThePassClaimedButNeverCoveredIsStillShown` fails on the orphaned region and `WhereThePassHasCoveredTheProcessedResultReplacesTheRawInk` fails the other way; with it enabled all three pass. That check exists because this branch has twice written a test that could only pass.
  - **Measured after the fix, by the audit that found it: 1 publish in 17 still loses ink, worst 1.6%, against 3 in 11 at 4.5% before.** The box is ticked because the regression tests exist and hold, and that is what the checkbox means here — not that the audit reads zero. **Most of it, not all of it.** What is left is small enough that no capture has produced a description of it from the owner, and large enough that it is not nothing; whoever picks it up should start by asking the audit which region went missing rather than by re-deriving the mechanism above, which is settled.
  - **What it does not fix.** The ink is now always present, which is not the same as being under the nib: `PEN -> SCREEN` is about 45 ms, of which 28 is B321's vsync floor and 18 is the app's own publish cadence. **B334 is about absence; the remaining trail is latency, and they are different faults** — a distinction this entry's neighbours took two days to draw.

- [x] **B327** `P1` `canvas` Undo re-stamps every stroke on the drawing, so a finished drawing costs seconds per Ctrl+Z `evidence: UndoRegionRepaintTests, UndoingAStrokeLeavesExactlyThePixelsAFullRenderWould, RedoingItPutsBackExactlyThosePixelsToo, UndoingAnEraserRestoresWhatWasBeneathIt, RepeatedUndosDoNotDriftFromTheRecord, UndoPatchesTheDrawingRatherThanDroppingIt, ASmudgeOnTheDrawingSendsUndoBackToTheWholeRender`
  - Reported as *"undo is really slow in a reference sheet drawing"*. The reference sheet was a red herring: a plain document with the same amount of ink measured the same (463 ms against 471 ms at 300 strokes). What is true is that **a model sheet is one dense finished drawing**, so every stroke lives on the cel being undone, while an animation spreads the same work over many sparse cels. The reporter's fast "single file" was a lighter drawing, not a different code path. The reference-sheet-specific half of the complaint is **B325**.
  - **The asymmetry was exact.** Committing a stroke is bounded work — `AppendToFrameRender` stamps the one new mark onto the cached bitmap, invariant 6's shape. Undoing it was not: `ApplyEditScope` called `InvalidateFrameRender`, the cache entry went, and the next publish re-entered `FrameBitmapCache.Get` → `Render`, replaying **every stroke on that cel**. Drawing O(1), taking it back O(n), at ~1.9 ms per stroke with no knee — 50 strokes 79 ms, 400 strokes 729 ms, 800 strokes 1 498 ms, **1 600 strokes 3 092 ms**.
  - **Fixed by running `Append` backwards.** A `DeltaStep` now carries the rectangle its revert can repaint (`GeometryOps.BBox`, supplied by `BrushEngine.CommitBounds`), `EditScope` hands it to the view model, and `FrameBitmapCache.RepaintRegion` clears that rectangle on the cached bitmap and replays only the strokes that reach it, in record order.
  - **Invariant 2 is what makes the replay exact rather than approximate.** `Hash01` seeds every dab dynamic from the IEEE-754 bits of its position, so a stroke replayed under a clip lands the dabs it landed the first time. The clip is on the **canvas**, never on the geometry — invariant 7's rule, and the same reason output scale is a surface transform. `StampStroke` still receives the whole-document `info`, so the stroke-global passes compute over the whole stroke and Skia clips the drawing: *compute whole, clip to the region*, which is what `RasterizeByTile` already does.
  - Measured after, same probe and machine:

    | drawing | before | after |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | 200 small marks spread over the canvas | ~324 ms | **4.6 ms** |
    | 800 small marks spread over the canvas | ~1 498 ms | **6.7 ms** |
    | 200 long strokes all crossing one band | ~324 ms | 450 ms |
    | 800 long strokes all crossing one band | ~1 498 ms | 1 435 ms |

  - **It is the drawing being undone that costs, not the document.** 300 strokes sitting on layer 1 while a stroke on layer 2 is undone costs **21.8 ms** — layer 1 stays cached. That is what says the fix has a narrow target rather than needing the whole render path rethought.
  - **The last two rows are the honest limit and they are not a defect.** When every stroke crosses the reverted mark's footprint, repainting that footprint *is* repainting the drawing, and there is nothing to save. The first two are the case that matters: undo stops growing with the drawing — four times the strokes moves it 4.6 → 6.7 ms instead of 4×. Worth recording that the first measurement of this fix showed **no gain at all**, because the probe drew every stroke through one narrow band; a probe that only measures the worst case will report that the fix does not work.
  - **What it refuses, falling back to the old whole-drawing render:** a frame carrying a baseline PNG, a frame with symbol placements, a posed frame (`PoseResolver` means the held pixels came from a *substitute* frame), strokes that sample the layers live, and any **smudge or blur** reaching the region. The last is the interesting one: an effect brush reads the pixels it sits on, and outside the clip the bitmap holds the drawing as it stands *now* — including strokes painted after it — where a full render would have shown it only what came before. A smudge sampling across the region edge would drag future ink into the past, and no coordinate conversion fixes that. It is the same shape as B195's tiling finding, arrived at from the other side.
  - **Declared per commit path, never inferred.** The brush, shape, pen and fill commits pass their stroke's footprint; the text commit does not, because it removes and reinserts several strokes and its footprint is a union rather than a mark. A path that says nothing gets today's behaviour, which is why adding one is safe: `MainViewModel.FrameRenderDrops` is the counter that makes a forgetful new path visible as something other than a mystery.
  - **The bar is bit-identity, not similarity**, because a patch that merely looks right shows ink the document no longer describes, and only where marks overlap. Detection power proved with three mutants: dropping the clear kills four tests, reversing the replay order kills three, and removing the effect-brush refusal kills the smudge test. Cost: L
  - **Two holes stay open on purpose, and `Q167` answers them.** Replaying the record is what makes both the overlap case and the effect-brush refusal unavoidable here. Measured after this landed, restoring a saved copy of the patch instead costs **0.045 ms where this replay costs 7 497 ms** on a hatched 800-stroke drawing, and has no sampling problem at all — so the next step is Photoshop's and Krita's, filed as a roadmap item under *Editing*. Nothing in that supersedes this entry: the replay path stays for steps that name no footprint.
  - Sibling: **B325**, the reference-sheet-specific tax that rode on top of this one, fixed on its own branch.

A 10.9-second block inside a 15.2-second trace that never stopped answering for more than a twentieth of a second. The verdict said *"the application really did stop answering, and any silence in the event list around that point is the freeze"* — which is the sentence a reader acts on, and it was wrong.
  - **P1 rather than the P2 it was filed as, because of what rests on it.** B255's entire diagnosis is this counter: *"the heartbeat that settled it found 22 UI-thread stalls, worst 6,103 ms"*. An instrument that manufactures blocked time sends the next session after a freeze that is not there — and B126's history is three wrong causes chased in exactly that way. A false number is worse than no number, which is the rule `InputTrace` already states about its own popup counter.

Avalonia orders `Render > Loaded > Default > Input > Background`, so the beat yields to every pointer event and every render — which is precisely the state it exists to measure, and it cannot measure a state it is in. At 112 delivered moves a second the beat simply never got a turn, and every missed turn was reported as the thread being dead.

What survives is genuine unresponsiveness: one long operation, a blocking wait, a render that will not end. No headless test can prove that half; it is a fact about a real dispatcher under real input.
  - **The half that can be pinned is that the entries now arbitrate.** A stall of *d* ending at *t* asserts nothing ran in `(t - d, t)`; any pointer event delivered inside that window is a thread that was demonstrably answering, and the claim is refused. Refused claims are **counted, not dropped** — a report that quietly showed fewer stalls would look like a fixed application, where `late beats overruled` says the thread was *busy* rather than stuck, which is a real finding with a different fix. Only delivered input counts as evidence: a `Note`, a cursor decision or another `Stall` is written by this file and would let the instrument overturn its own measurement with its own bookkeeping.

B255 remains open and its evidence needs re-taking on a build with this in — the stall count it rests on was measured by the instrument this entry repairs, so it has to be read again before it means anything. That is the cost of the defect rather than an excuse for it.

- [x] **B201** `P1` `canvas` Moving the canvas floods it with the onion tint, because the culled route tints with Multiply and the ring tints with SrcIn `evidence: DeferredComposeTests, TheTintMatchesTheSceneRenderer`
  - Repro: turn onion skin on with any ghost showing, then zoom or drag the canvas. The whole canvas goes solid `#d04040` — the previous-ghost tint — with the current drawing still on top of it. Reported by the owner with two screenshots, one moving and one still.

Measured rather than reasoned: the same pass composited `empty=#808080` through `SceneRenderer` and `empty=#d04040` through `DeferredCompose`.

The two routes are meant to be pixel-identical and were not, on the one property nothing compared.
  - **Why the existing test could not see it.** `DeferredComposeTests` compares `DeferredCompose` against a literal copy of the publisher's culled compose — and that copy carried the same `Multiply`, so the two agreed perfectly while both disagreed with the path that decides what onion skin looks like. Two implementations copied from each other are one implementation with two names. The new assertion compares the moving route against `SceneRenderer` instead, and asserts on the *empty* region: the mark differed too, but only in shade, and comparing marks would have read as a near miss when the flood is the whole of what an artist saw.
  - P1 — wrong output × always, and it makes the canvas unusable during the two gestures an artist uses most. Cost: S.

- [x] **B191** `P1` `canvas` Dragging the reference opacity slider on a painted-on document freezes the app, then kills it with no crash report `evidence: ADragTickDoesNotRebakeLiveStrokes, ADragCoalescesIntoOnePublishInsteadOfOnePerTick, TheDialStillLandsAndStillShows`

Structural reference edits (import, remove, cell assignment) keep the full funnel. Cost: S
  - The tests were shown to fail without the fix: twenty ticks used to produce twenty publishes and twenty fresh bakes; they now produce one publish and none. What no headless test can show is the crash itself — that needs the 4K document and the machine, the same boundary B179 records.
  - The sibling found on the way is **B192**: the canvas *drag* of a reference goes through `PerformDelta` and is worse per event, plus an undo entry per pointer move — filed rather than folded in, because its fix is a drag session, not a funnel skip.

That is a crash rather than a slow frame, so it outranks every performance item open against this area.
  - **The report taken at the same time says nothing is wrong, and that is the most useful fact in it.** Frame cache 284 MB of 4008, flattened tiles 93 MB of 501, resident textures 93.4 MB, nothing thrown out anywhere — roughly **470 MB accounted for against 12 GB held**. So the growth is not in any pool the report tracked, and four reassuring lines actively pointed away from it.
  - **Two pools were tracked and never printed, and they are the first place to look.** `FrameBitmapCache.AwaitingUnpinBytes` and `TileFlattenCache.AwaitingUnpinBytes` — bytes a cache has evicted and cannot free because a published snapshot is still reading them. They are excluded from `CachedBytes` deliberately (they are not cache contents) and they are **unbounded by construction**. A third, `TileFrameCache.AllocatedBytes`, was budgeted and also never printed: the tile section counts passes, not bytes.
  - **Why that shape fits.** A pin is dropped when a published snapshot is released. B178 measures snapshots waiting a long time to be drawn and 256 of 757 replaced before drawing — so if any release path is missed, pins accumulate, and *a pinned bitmap is one eviction cannot free whatever the budget says*. The budget then stays green while memory grows, which is exactly what was observed.
  - **Not yet attributed, deliberately.** Every candidate above is a hypothesis; the machine that reproduces it is not this one, and shipping a speculative fix for a leak nobody has localised is how the wrong thing gets "fixed" twice. The instrumentation lands first: a `what memory is held` section printing the working set, the managed heap, every pool including the three that were invisible, and the **difference** — so the next capture distinguishes "the caches are fine" from "the caches are fine and the process is not".
  - **Suspicion falls on the recently changed code and that is not evidence.** B167 phase 2 turned flattened bitmaps from owned-and-disposed into cache-owned-and-pinned, and the residency wiring fix turned on a texture cache that had never run. Both are the right places to look first; neither is implicated by a number yet.
  - Cost: M to localise with the new section, unknown to fix.
  - **First capture with the section in (2026-08-12, alpha.28) refutes the leading hypothesis.** `process working set 2958 MB`, `managed heap 52 MB`, `accounted for by caches 596 MB` — and **`evicted, still in use  0 MB`** with `pinned by live snapshots 3 frame bitmap(s), 3 flatten(s)`. So the pin protocol is working exactly as designed, nothing is stuck awaiting an unpin, and the unreleased-snapshot theory this entry led with is **dead**. B167 phase 2 and the residency wiring are not implicated by any number.
  - **2362 MB is native, unpinned, unmanaged and outside every budget the application owns.** That narrows it to something nobody had measured rather than something mis-sized.
  - **Skia keeps two caches of its own, and neither was ever asked.** The GPU resource cache holds textures and render targets against a byte limit and **purges to that limit rather than on dispose** — a texture handed back is *purgeable*, not freed — and the CPU cache holds decoded images, masks and glyphs on the same principle. Either can be gigabytes with no application code wrong. `SkiaMemory` now samples both; the GPU one is only reachable from inside the draw op, because the `GRContext` lives in the render thread's lease and the report runs on the UI thread. **That is why it was invisible: the number was never unavailable, it was unreachable from where anyone thought to ask.**
  - **Skia is not the leak either (2026-08-12, alpha.29). Second hypothesis refuted.** `gpu resources 113 MB`, `cpu images and glyphs 0 MB` — 113 MB against a **1905 MB** gap. So the missing memory is not in any cache Skia keeps, nor any cache we keep, nor the managed heap (50 MB), nor awaiting an unpin (0 MB).
  - **One real finding falls out of it, smaller but its own bug: `gpu resources 113 MB of 28 MB`.** Skia's GPU resource cache is **four times over its own limit**, which it can only be when the excess is *referenced* — purging only reclaims unlocked resources. So something holds ~85 MB of GPU resources that Skia would otherwise free. Not the leak, and not nothing.
  - **What remains is the candidate this entry named in advance, and the arithmetic fits both captures.** `GpuComposite.CreateSurface` asks for `SKSurface.Create(gpu, budgeted: false, …)`, which **deliberately opts out of Skia's accounting** — so a compose surface is invisible to Skia's numbers *and* to ours, by construction. This capture: 133 GPU composites × 7.9 MB ≈ 1050 MB against a 1905 MB gap. The crash capture: compose scale 1.0, 31.6 MB a surface, and 12 GB is ~380 of them. Same shape at both sizes.
  - **`budgeted: false` is not an accident and must not be flipped casually.** Its comment gives the reason — *"a budgeted surface can be recycled underneath a snapshot that is still being read"* — which is B130's failure mode. Any fix has to keep that property, so "make it budgeted" is a hypothesis to test rather than a patch to apply.
  - **The cheapest decisive test is not another instrument, and it costs one playback: turn GPU compositing OFF and play the same file.** Flat memory means the growth is in the path the toggle controls, and `budgeted: false` is the specific line to examine. Still climbing means the GPU path is exonerated entirely and three rounds of instrumentation have been aimed at the wrong half. Asked twice and not yet run; it outranks any further measurement.
  - **ATTRIBUTED (2026-08-12): the leak is in the GPU compositing path, established by removal.** Same document, same playback, toggle off: **working set 894 MB and stable between 680 and 710 MB, never higher** — against 2537–2958 MB climbing to 12 GB with it on. Not an inference from a settings list; the one experiment that could refute it was run and did not.
  - **The corroborating line is Skia's own cache, which flips either side of the toggle.** On: `gpu resources 113 MB of 28 MB` — four times its limit, so the excess is *locked*. Off: `21 MB of 28 MB`, comfortably under. And `layer textures` goes 93 MB → 0. So switching the path on both fills the texture cache and leaves ~85 MB of GPU resources Skia cannot purge, on top of the 1905 MB it never sees at all.
  - **Two candidates remain inside that path, and they are distinguishable by one more experiment.** Either the unbudgeted compose surfaces (`GpuComposite.CreateSurface` asks for `budgeted: false`, so they are invisible to Skia's accounting *and* ours), or `LayerTextureCache`'s uploads holding more GPU memory than the CPU-side figure it reports. The first fits the arithmetic at both sizes; the second is bounded at 93 MB here and cannot explain 1905.
  - **A fact worth having before anyone reaches for a fix: nothing in this codebase ever calls `GRContext.Flush`, `Submit` or `PurgeUnlockedResources`.** Only `SKCanvas.Flush`, which pushes draws into a surface and is not what reclaims GPU resources. That is *suggestive rather than damning* — Avalonia flushes the context to present each frame, so pending deletions should be reclaimed a frame later — but it is the first thing to check, because a resource freed into a queue nobody drains is exactly the shape of memory that grows while every counter reads healthy.
  - **Two switches now separate the remaining candidates, one playback each, and neither can be tested here — this repository has no graphics context, which is why every finding in this entry came from the owner's machine.** `LIGHTBOX_GPU_BUDGETED=1` asks Skia to account for the compose surfaces instead of opting out; `LIGHTBOX_NO_RESIDENCY=1` keeps GPU compositing on and takes the texture cache out. Play the same file with GPU compositing on and one of them set:
    - **Budgeted on, memory flat** → the unbudgeted surfaces are the cause, and the fix has to keep the property `budgeted: false` was chosen for (Skia must not recycle a surface underneath a snapshot still being read — B130).
    - **Budgeted on, still climbing; residency off, memory flat** → the texture cache is the cause, and its 93 MB CPU-side figure is understating what it holds on the card.
    - **Both flat, or neither** → both are wrong and the next suspect is whatever else the GPU path allocates per publish.
  - **A capture taken with either switch says so in its own report**, under `diagnostic mode`. Without that line two runs get compared as though they came from the same build, which is the mistake this bug has already made twice with stale prose.
  - **The switch lived on `CanvasControl` for one commit and turned every render-report test red.** Reading a member off an Avalonia control forces its static initialisation, which registers styled properties and cannot run headless. Both switches are on `GpuComposite` now: **a flag the report has to read belongs on a type the report can touch.**
  - **Severity in practice is lower than 12 GB suggests, and that should not be lost.** GPU compositing is opt-in, off by default, and reached through Configure ▸ Performance — so no artist meets this without switching it on to help measure something. **The toggle is the mitigation**, and it works: turning it off returns the process to 894 MB.
  - **Also worth holding: memory is not monotonic across these short captures** — 2958 MB then 2537 MB. The 12 GB was reached over a longer session, so a capture taken early says little about the slope. The next one should be taken *after* memory has climbed, not at the start of playback.
  - **The bisect reproduces on alpha.30, which is the first build carrying the switches (2026-08-12, two captures 29 seconds apart).** Off: `working set 893 MB`, `layer textures 0 MB`, `gpu resources 21 MB of 28`, gap 447 MB. On: `2813 MB`, `93 MB`, `113 MB of 28`, gap **2182 MB**. Third independent confirmation, and the same corroborating flip in Skia's own cache.
  - **Neither of those two captures discriminates**, because neither prints `diagnostic mode` — the build had the switches and no one set them. The experiment above is still outstanding and is still one playback each.
  - **A false signal came out of the pair and is worth recording, because it was plausible.** The GPU-on capture read `of the publishes that could use the card: 160 did, 207 fell back`, where every earlier capture read none — which looks exactly like GPU surface allocation starting to fail under memory pressure. It was not: `GpuComposite`'s tallies never reset, so the 207 were the CPU composites of the *previous* capture taken with the toggle off. The tell is that `RefusedAllocations` prints its own `!!` line and did not. Fixed as **B184** (filed as B182 and renumbered on merge — `main` had taken B182 for the tile-cache scan).
  - **And one finding that survives the pair unambiguously: with GPU compositing on, playback is better.** Mean lateness **7.85 ms against 13.06**, worst **96 ms against 1326**, `Compose` 0.01 ms/tick against 0.3. So the path is not a mistake to be reverted — it earns its place and leaks, and the fix has to keep the speed.
  - **The discriminating experiment ran (2026-08-12, alpha.31) and answered in both directions at once.** With `LIGHTBOX_GPU_BUDGETED=1`, memory climbed a little, then **dropped** — Skia purging the compose surfaces it was finally allowed to account for, which is what proves **the surfaces are the growth** — and then the app froze and crashed: a purged surface recycled underneath a snapshot still being read, which is B130's use-after-free arriving exactly as the `budgeted: false` comment predicted. One run confirmed the candidate and refuted the easy fix. The second switch was never needed: `Budgeted` touches only the compose surfaces, so the drop exonerates the residency cache as the leak.
  - **The mechanism, once the surfaces were confirmed: the frames were freed on the wrong thread.** The composed frame is an `SKImage` snapshotted from the unbudgeted surface — the image owns the render target. The retirement queue disposes it on the **UI** thread; the `GRContext` lives on the render thread, inside the lease; and a GPU resource released off the context's thread is *parked* on the context's deferred-free queue, not freed — and nothing in the codebase ever drained it (the earlier bullet about `Flush`/`PurgeUnlockedResources` never being called was this fact, seen from the other side). So every publish leaked one render target: invisible to Skia's accounting (unbudgeted, by design), invisible to ours (already "disposed"), ~7.9 MB per publish at a 1080p compose and 31.6 MB at 4K/Full — the measured slope at both sizes. The CPU path frees through the identical code and stays flat because raster memory does not need a context to die.
  - **Fixed by moving the free to where the context is: `GpuImageReaper`.** `RenderSnapshot.Dispose` hands a GPU-backed image to the reaper instead of disposing it; the draw op drains the queue once per frame on the render thread with the lease's context current, then sweeps the context's own deferred-free queue (`PurgeUnusedResources`, Skia's `performDeferredCleanup`, with a two-second grace so warm scratch survives) — which also covers anything *else* released off-thread, such as a resident texture evicted on the UI thread. B130's guarantee is untouched twice over: the surfaces stay unbudgeted, and the reaper only adds delay after the retirement queue has already decided a snapshot is unreachable.
  - **Open until a capture on the fixed build shows it, and the report now has the line to look at**: `gpu frames reaped N freed on the render thread, M waiting`. Flat memory with `reaped` tracking the publish count and `waiting` near zero closes this; a growing `waiting` against a still `reaped` means the drain is not running and the fix is wrong. What the suite pins meanwhile is the routing (`GpuImageReaperTests`) — no test here can watch driver memory fall, for the same reason every number in this entry came from the owner's machine.
  - **Closed on the owner's confirmation (2026-08-12, the build carrying the reaper): the leak no longer reproduces on the machine that found it.** `evidence: manual` stays, honestly — the routing has `GpuImageReaperTests`, but the thing this bug *is*, driver memory returning to baseline, is only observable where a graphics context exists, and that machine said yes. A worthwhile follow-up if a local GPU workstation ever joins the loop: a `[Trait("Category","Gpu")]` suite that runs the compose → snapshot → dispose → drain cycle against a real context and asserts the baseline, which would turn this checkbox from a confirmation into a regression test.
  - **What the investigation cost, for the next leak like it: five report round-trips, three refuted hypotheses (the pin protocol, Skia's caches, per-dab allocation was never even in it), two false signals (stale diagnosis prose, the B182 counter), and one discriminating experiment.** The shape worth remembering: when every budget reads healthy and the process still grows, the memory is not in a cache anyone owns — ask *which thread frees it* before asking who holds it.

- [x] **B168** `P1` `canvas` Deselect does nothing while the Select tool is active `evidence: ToolSelectionFillTests, DeselectClearsAMarqueeWhileTheSelectToolIsActive, SelectAllTakesTheWholeCanvasWhileTheSelectToolIsActive`
  - Repro: pick a Select variant, drag a marquee, press Ctrl+D — or click the on-screen Deselect. The marching ants stay. Reported as "not by shortcut, not by on screen buttons", and the two share a cause: both routes run `DeselectCommand`.
  - `MainViewModel.Deselect` branches on the active tool. Under `ToolId.Select` it calls `_selectionManager.ClearAllSelections()` and returns; only the `else` branch clears `_selectionContours`. So the one tool that *makes* a marquee is the one tool whose deselect cannot clear it — the branch was written for the Arrow's object selection and catches the region tool by tool id.
  - **`SelectAll` has the identical shape three methods above**, and it is the same defect wearing the other key: Ctrl+A with the Select tool active selects all *objects* rather than taking the whole canvas. Filed here rather than separately because one branch condition is wrong in both and a fix that corrects one and not the other would be indefensible.
  - There *is* a workaround, and it is worth writing down precisely because nobody would find it: switch to the brush first, then Ctrl+D. That is the `else` branch, and it clears the contours the Select tool could not.
  - P1 on blocks work × every session: a live selection clips painting, so an artist who cannot clear one cannot paint outside it, and the symptom they see is "the app stopped drawing" rather than "there is a selection up". Cost: S — the branch should ask what kind of selection is live, not which tool is in the hand.
  - **Fixed, and the two commands ended up answering differently.** `SelectAll` still needs to know what *all* means, so it asks one property — `ObjectSelectionIsTheSubject`, true for the two arrows — and both commands read the same one, so a fix to either cannot drift from the other. `Deselect` asks nothing at all: it clears the marquee, the polygon in progress and the object selection unconditionally, because "none" means none and a deselect that leaves one kind of selection live is the bug rather than a subtlety.
  - **The entry said "the wrong branch condition" and the truth was blunter: it named the wrong tool.** `ToolId.Select` is the marquee — the tool whose entire job is making the region the command then refused to touch — while the tools that pick objects are `Arrow` and `DirectSelect`, as `ToolId.Arrow`'s own documentation says. So the condition was not close to right; it was inverted in effect, which is why Ctrl+A took the objects and Ctrl+D left the ants up.
  - `DeselectClearsAMarqueeWhicheverToolIsHeld` sweeps all four tools rather than pinning the one from the report, so the next tool added cannot quietly reintroduce this.

- [x] **B164** `P1` `canvas` The compositor only ticks when something invalidates, so playback ran at the scene's frame rate with nothing between the frames `evidence: PresentLoopTests, TurningItOnAsksForFramesWithoutAnythingElseHappening, TurningItOffStopsTheLoop, TurningItOnTwiceDoesNotStartTwoLoops, ACanvasThatIsNotPlayingAsksForNothing`
  - **The seventh answer to "playback is smooth only while the pointer moves over the canvas", and the first that survives the owner's own experiment.** `CanvasControl` asked for one animation frame per publish, so during playback the compositor ran **at the scene's frame rate and in lock-step with it** — twelve ticks a second, each triggered by the publish it was meant to show. Nothing ran between them, so every wobble in when a publish landed went straight to the screen with nothing to absorb it. Moving the pointer fixed it by accident: pointer motion invalidates the canvas at pointer rate, which keeps the compositor ticking at display rate, and a published frame is then picked up within a vsync instead of waiting for the next publish to drag the compositor awake.
  - **The experiment that identified it is the one every earlier hypothesis got wrong**, and it was the owner's, not mine. Mashing Ctrl (the eyedropper toggling on and off), mashing Space, and switching tools quickly all smooth playback. **Holding a key down does not** — tried with Space, the arrow keys and Ctrl. A held key repeats about thirty times a second, so events are arriving in quantity and it makes no difference. Everything in the working list **repaints a control**; nothing in the failing list does. That pair kills "input wakes the dispatcher" (B152, B153) outright, kills "the canvas's own invalidate is not producing a render" (B156), and explains the docker case that broke all of them: hovering a docker changes nothing visible.
  - Fix: while the transport runs, the frame request re-arms itself from inside its own callback, so the compositor ticks at display rate the way it does under the pointer. One request in flight at a time, so a publish arriving mid-loop joins it rather than doubling it; the last callback simply declines to re-arm when playback stops, so there is no timer to cancel and nothing spins while the artist is drawing. Cost: S
  - **What the tests can and cannot do.** They pin the loop's contract — it re-arms while playing, keeps one request in flight, stops dead, and is off by default. They cannot show the screen looks smoother: that needs a compositor against real hardware, which is precisely why this survived six rounds of headless measurement and why every one of those rounds measured the wrong side of the boundary.
  - **Unproven until the owner plays a scene with the pointer still**, and worth saying plainly after six wrong answers: the mechanism explains all four of the observations that previously contradicted each other, which none of the others did — but the confirmation is a person watching a sequence, not a number in the report.

- [x] **B161** `P1` `canvas` The report measures drawing the frame and throws it away, which is why the arithmetic never closed `evidence: WorkOutsideTheTickTests, TheDrawIsReportedBesideTheTickAndAddedToIt, NoHeadroomIsSaidPlainlyRatherThanLeftAsArithmetic, PlentyOfHeadroomSendsTheReaderElsewhere, NothingIsClaimedWhenTheDrawWasNeverMeasured`
  - **Four rounds of captures could not be reconciled, and this is why.** The tick breakdown measures *compositing*. Drawing the composited frame to the screen happens **outside the tick**, is timed on every render by `CanvasControl`'s draw op, lands in `PerformanceMonitor.FrameMs` — and was printed only inside a section guarded on `Presents > 0`, a counter that **only the durable-frame path increments**. B130 turned the durable frame off by default. So on every real machine the number was collected and discarded, and the report showed half the budget while asking the reader to explain the whole of it.
  - **The codebase already warned about this exact mistake, in the summary of the property being dropped.** `FrameMs`: *"on a large document it is usually the larger of the two … Reporting headroom from compositing alone said 'smooth' while the canvas ran at 34 fps."* That is a description of the defect, written before it happened, sitting on the field the report was failing to read.
  - The shape it produced: a capture with the tick at **40.91 ms against an 83.3 ms budget** — comfortable — beside a clock **100% late by a mean of 197 ms with 488 frames dropped**. Two facts that cannot both be true unless something unmeasured is spending the rest, and nothing in the file could name it. B158 concluded exactly that and could go no further.
  - Fix: the tick section now prints the draw beside the tick, **adds them**, and states the sum as a share of the frame period — with three verdicts, so a capture says "no headroom" or "comfortable, look elsewhere" rather than leaving arithmetic to whoever reads it. Absent when nothing was drawn, rather than a confident zero. Cost: S
  - **This is still instrumentation and not a fix**, which is the fifth time in a row on this bug. What it buys is that the next capture cannot be ambiguous: either tick + draw fills the budget — and then the target is whichever half is larger, with B160 having just made the composite the cheap one again — or it does not, and the time is somewhere neither number covers.

- [x] **B160** `P1` `canvas` A scaled composite costs 2.5× per pixel, so compositing *smaller* can cost more than compositing everything `evidence: ComposeScaleCostTests, AScaleThatWouldCostMoreThanNotScalingRoundsUp, CompositingJustUnderFullSizeIsNotCheaperThanCompositingAllOfIt`
  - **The third answer to one question, so the method matters more than the number.** B156 blamed the composite; B157 retracted it on four field captures where a *smaller* compose surface cost more; B158 "corrected" the retraction with a controlled measurement. **B158's measurement was clean and controlled on the wrong variable** — it varied the *document size* with the compose scale pinned at 1.0, so it only ever exercised the unscaled path, found it perfectly linear at 16 ms/Mpx, and concluded the field data was session noise. The captures differed in **compose scale**, which that experiment held constant.
  - Holding the document at 1920×1080 and varying only the compose scale — the thing that actually differed:

    | compose scale | Mpx | ms/tick | ms/Mpx |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 1.0 | 2.07 | 34.00 | **16.4** |
    | 0.75 | 1.17 | **45.92** | 39.4 |
    | 0.625 | 0.81 | 33.00 | 40.7 |
    | 0.5 | 0.52 | 20.85 | 40.2 |

  - **0.75 composites 44% fewer pixels and takes 35% longer.** That is the field observation reproduced exactly, after being dismissed twice. The owner's own capture at `Display` quality — 0.81 Mpx, **40.33 ms** — is the same result on their machine, and it arrived *because I advised them to switch to `Display`*, which moved them off the cheap path onto the dear one. **The advice made it worse**, and it was given with more confidence than a single controlled experiment could carry.
  - Cause, and it is not a bad sampler: at 1.0 the layer blit is a straight copy; below it every tile is drawn through `canvas.Scale` and interpolated. The filter is already `SKFilterMode.Linear` — the cheapest sensible choice, with `SceneRenderer.Downscale` explaining why — so this is simply what interpolation costs.
  - Fix: cost is `40·s²` against `16.4` for the whole document, crossing over at `s = √(16.4/40) ≈ 0.64`. `ComposeScale` now rounds anything above **0.7** up to 1.0 and takes the cheap path; below it, scaling genuinely pays (0.5 is 21 ms against 34). Threshold above the crossover rather than on it because the ratio is one machine's measurement and the penalty is asymmetric. Nothing about what is drawn changes — only how many pixels it is drawn into, which invariant 5 already makes view-only. Cost: S
  - **What this does not do is make 12 fps.** The owner's capture still shows the tick at 40.91 ms against an 83.3 ms budget with **100% of ticks late by a mean of 197 ms and 488 frames dropped** — which remains the reported symptom, since dropped frames are exactly the playhead "skipping to random frames". A 40 ms tick inside an 83 ms period should not produce that, so B158's real finding stands and is now the whole question: **something outside the tick is spending the rest of the UI thread.** `CanvasControl.Render` is still unmeasured.

- [x] **B158** `P1` `canvas` The composite is 40% of a 12 fps frame, so it cannot be why every tick is 50–170 ms late `evidence: ComposeCostScalesWithAreaTests, TheCompositeGrowsWithTheSurfaceAndTheHandoffDoesNot`
  - **First, a correction: B157's retraction was wrong, and B156's original attribution was right.** Measured properly — one process, one scene, three sizes, forty ticks each, warmed — the composite is **linear in area at ~16 ms per megapixel**: 8.56 ms at 960×540, 33.90 ms at 1920×1080, 76.43 ms at 2880×1620. The handoff B157 split out is **0.07 ms**, which is what made the split worth doing even though its conclusion was wrong: it is the thing that proves the cost is not there.
  - **Why I talked myself out of it.** Four captures showed the run with the *smallest* compose surface spending the most time in the phase, and "a cost that does not fall when the surface nearly halves is not paid per pixel" is sound reasoning about numbers that could not carry it. Those four came from three sessions with wildly different stalling — the 1440×810 run reported **56 dropped frames and three clock re-bases** against 4 drops and one re-base in the run beside it, over 76 ticks with a 55.82 ms worst. That is a machine having a bad minute. **Comparing means across sessions with uncontrolled stalls is exactly the trap `docs/DESIGN-performance.md` records**, and I walked into it while quoting it.
  - **The finding this leaves is better than either.** At **12 fps the frame period is 83.3 ms** and the whole tick — every phase — costs **~35 ms at 1080p**. That is 40% of the budget, with 48 ms to spare. **So the composite cannot be why the clock arrives 52–168 ms late in every capture.** The tick is now fully accounted for and it does not add up: something outside it is spending 50–130 ms of the UI thread between ticks.
  - The prime suspect, untested: **`CanvasControl.Render` is not in the tick profile at all.** It scales the composited image to the viewport on every present, on the same thread, and nothing anywhere measures it. That is the last unmeasured stretch of the UI thread in the playback loop.
  - **The artist-visible symptom is already named in the report and I read past it four times.** *"frames dropped to keep up: 70"* on a five-frame scene is not a rendering artifact — `Pace` is deliberately dropping frames because it believes it is behind, which is precisely the "playhead skips frames, jumps around" the owner describes. Fix the lateness and the skipping stops; the drops are a symptom of the clock, not a second fault.
  - **A mitigation exists today and costs one setting.** Canvas quality `Full` at a display scale of 0.625 still composites at scale 1.0 — the full 1920×1080 — because Full means *twice the screen, capped at the document*. `Display` would composite at 0.625 (0.81 Mpx, ~13 ms), a **2.5× cut** in the dominant phase. Worth trying before any of the above lands.
  - Cost: S to measure the render; the composite itself is B125.

- [x] **B157** `P1` `canvas` The tick's 35 ms is not the composite, and one number for two costs is why it looked like it `evidence: PublishPhaseSplitTests, ComposeAndHandoffAreReportedApart, TheFramePeriodIsPrintedSoTheBudgetCanBeRead, ThePeriodFollowsThePlaybackSpeedRatherThanTheScenesNominalRate, ATinyCohortGetsNoVerdict, AnAmpleCohortStillGetsOne`
  - **The measurement that refutes the attribution I put on B156.** I read `Publish 32.13 ms/tick` as B125's CPU composite at 1080p, on the strength of B144 pricing compositing at 55.7 ms for three layers at that size. Four captures later that is not supportable.
  - **A run at a 1440×810 compose surface spent MORE time in that phase than the three at 1920×1080 beside it** — 40.22 ms against 34.83, 36.64 and 35.52. That is 1.8× less area for 15% more time. **A cost that does not fall when the surface nearly halves is not paid per pixel**, so whatever dominates the phase is not the composite. Every other input was constant: same build, same machine, same 5-frame/2-layer/11-stroke scene, every frame a cache hit, 100% of passes tiled.
  - Cause of the confusion rather than of the cost: `Phase.Publish` timed **two** things — compositing the frame, and handing it to the canvas (the snapshot swap, the retired-image disposal, the invalidate). The enum's own summary said so in as many words and nobody read it as a warning. `Performance.RecordPublish` measures only the first half and is printed nowhere in an ordinary report, so the two could never be compared.
  - Fix: `Compose` and `Handoff` are separate phases, timed as siblings so `ALL PHASES` still sums. Whichever dominates, the next report names it.
  - **Two report defects found by these captures and fixed with it.** The tick breakdown says *"compare that with the frame period for this scene's fps"* — and never printed the fps or the period, so the one comparison the report asks for had to be done from memory; it now prints both, derived from the **playback speed** rather than the scene's nominal rate, because a scene at half speed has twice the budget. And the cohort verdict had no minimum sample: it announced "any input helps" — the verdict that points at the dispatcher — off four frames and one stall, while three captures with 31, 52 and 53 quiet frames said the opposite.
  - **What this does not do is fix the stutter**, and the entry should not be read as claiming otherwise. It replaces a wrong attribution with a measurement that can produce a right one. The open question it hands on: 35–40 ms a tick that does not scale with area, on a scene where nothing is rasterized and every pass is tiled.

- [x] **B144** `P1` `canvas` Playback re-rasterizes most of the scene every pass above 720p, because the frame cache budget is a fixed 512 MB `evidence: MemoryBudgetTests, TheCachesTakeTheirDefaultsFromTheDerivation, TheFloorsAreAffordableOnTheMinimumSpec, TheDerivedBudgetsAreInRangeHere, MoreMemoryMeansMoreBudget`
  - Repro: a 24-frame, 3-layer animation, played in a loop. Measured on the **second** pass, so the first-pass rasterization every document must pay is excluded. `AnimationSweeps.PlaybackCanvasSize`, budget 83 ms at 12 fps:
  - **Mostly defused for playback on 2026-08-08, and deliberately not closed.** Playback now goes through the tile store (Q62's first increment): while frames flip, a cel costs its ink rather than its paper, so the working set that thrashed a 512 MB budget as full-frame bitmaps stays resident as tiles. `AnimationSweeps.PlaybackSparse`, same scene both ways: **145 → 14 ms at 1080p, 334 → 39 ms at 4K** — inside the 83 ms budget at both sizes. What keeps this open: the budget is still a literal (tiles thrash too when dense ink at 1440p+ wants more than 512 MB, and tile thrash measured *worse* than bitmap thrash, 277 vs 186 ms, because `TileFrameCache` has no scan-aware eviction the way `FrameBitmapCache.EvictionOrder.MostRecent` is); scrubbing and the paused canvas still ride full-frame bitmaps; and a frame with baseline pixels, placements or an effect stroke still falls back. Budget-from-installed-memory remains the fix this entry names.
  - **The fallback now says which one it is, because "still stuttering at FullHD" could not be attributed without guessing.** The measured 14 ms at 1080p is what a *tiled* pass costs; a pass that falls back pays the old ~137 ms, and falling back was silent — so a document slow because it carries a camera and a document slow because the machine is slow produced identical evidence, which is none. `TileFallback.Reason` is now the gate itself rather than a `bool` beside a separate explanation, so a wrong reason and a wrong decision are the same bug instead of two that drift apart. `TileFallbackTally` counts them and `Help ▸ Write a render report` names the dominant one in the artist's terms — *the scene has a camera*, *frames place symbols*, *frames contain smudge or blur strokes* — each of which is something they can act on.
    - **Counted per layer pass, not per frame**, and the label says so: the gate is asked once per layer per publish, so a two-layer document reports two for every frame shown. The first version called them frames and a one-layer-of-two fallback read as half the sequence being broken.
    - **`Dominant` names the largest fallback rather than the one that beat tiling**, which was the first rule and was wrong in the ordinary case: paper tiles, paint does not, the split is exactly 50/50, and the tally announced that nothing was wrong on a document paying the old cost for half of every publish. How *much* it matters is a separate number (`FallbackShare`), and keeping the two apart is what stops either one lying.

    | canvas | p50 | p95 | resident | needed | effective fps |
    | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
    | 720p | 24.3 ms | 27.4 ms | 72 of 72 | 265 MB | 41 |
    | 1080p | 136.7 ms | 188.2 ms | 64 of 72 | 597 MB | **7** |
    | 1440p | 181.3 ms | 229.2 ms | 36 of 72 | 1.06 GB | **6** |
    | 4K | 314.6 ms | 356.7 ms | 16 of 72 | 2.39 GB | **3** |
  - **`n^2.25`, and the exponent is the tell.** Compositing is `n^1.03` — linear in area, as it must be. Playback is squared because two costs multiply: each frame costs more *and* fewer frames fit, so the miss rate climbs with the same area that makes each miss dearer. A budget expressed in bytes against bitmaps that grow with area gives a frame count that falls as the square.
  - Cause: `FrameBitmapCache.ByteBudget` is `512L * 1024 * 1024`, a compile-time constant with a preference beside it. A cached bitmap is `w * h * 4`, so the budget buys 141 frames at 720p, 62 at 1080p and 15 at 4K, against a scene that wants 72 — one per layer per frame. Above 720p the LRU evicts frames the next pass needs, and `EvictionOrder.MostRecent` (the scan-resistant flip, which is right) cannot help when the working set simply does not fit.
  - **Distinct from B29 and B125, which are the other half of the same stall.** Subtracting `CanvasSize` (3 layers, 1 frame, every access a hit) from this scenario splits it: at 1080p, 55.7 ms is compositing and **81 ms is re-rasterizing**; at 4K, 215.0 ms is compositing and **100 ms is re-rasterizing**. So B29/B125 own the majority at 4K and this bug owns the majority at 1080p, and fixing either alone leaves playback over budget at both. Filed separately because the fixes are unrelated — a budget that reads available memory, versus compositing that is not full-canvas CPU raster.

The cache stores full-document bitmaps either way — `_cache.Get(frame, scene.Width, scene.Height, …)` — so the miss cost transfers unchanged.
  - P1 rather than P2 on the strength of the number: 1080p is not an exotic size, 7 fps is not playback, and flipping drawings is the pillar-1 activity the application exists for. B29 and B125 stay P2 because each is a ceiling; this one is a constant that can be raised.
  - **Fix, and the first part is nearly free**: size the budget from installed memory rather than a literal, with the preference as an override rather than the only lever — a machine with 32 GB can hold a 1080p scene several times over and is currently held to 512 MB. That alone should take 1080p from 137 ms to about 56 ms, inside budget. 4K needs 2.4 GB for a 24-frame scene and cannot be solved this way at every length, which is where the checkpoint (B30) and the tile path stop being separate work.
  - **Closed 2026-08-12, and it had been fixed for some time without being ticked.** The named fix — *"size the budget from installed memory rather than a literal, with the preference as an override"* — is `Services.MemoryBudget`, and `FrameBitmapCache.ByteBudget` reads it rather than the constant this entry was filed against. `FrameCache()` takes an eighth of installed memory, floored at 256 MB and ceilinged at 4 GB: **1 GB on the 8 GB minimum spec, double the old literal, and 4 GB on a 32 GB machine, eight times it.** The floor is a production decision rather than a guess (Q64), and the artist's setting is still the last word.
  - **What kept it open was the evidence line, not the code.** `evidence: manual` cannot be resolved by `bugs.py sync`, so an entry carrying it stays red however thoroughly it is fixed — and this one names real tests now. That is worth recording beyond this bug: **17 of the 32 open entries carry `evidence: manual`**, so more than half the open list is incapable of closing itself. Some of those are genuinely open; some are B144.
  - **What remains is not this entry's.** 4K still needs about 2.4 GB for a 24-frame scene and cannot be bought with a budget at every level — that is the ceiling B29, B125 and B167 own, and the tile store already took playback from 334 ms to 39 ms at 4K independently of the budget. This entry was *"a constant that can be raised"*, and it has been raised.

  - **The measurement gap that hid this is worth more than the bug.** `AnimationSweeps.Playback` has always existed, times the identical operation, and never saw it: it runs at 720p and sweeps *frame count*, which is the one axis playback is flat on. Every recorded playback row sat inside budget while the application was at 7 fps on an ordinary document. A sweep is evidence about the axis it sweeps and about nothing else, and a scenario that fixes the axis an artist would name is not measuring their workload.

- [x] **B130** `P1` `canvas` Lightbox died on the first input after the splash, and wrote no crash report `evidence: PresentedFrameTests, AnImageHandedOutSurvivesLaterPresents, RetirementIsBoundedRatherThanUnlimited`
  - Reported as *"lightbox crashes after the splash screen is gone and I input anything. I am unable to do anything"*, followed by *"there is no crashreport logged during this"*. The missing report is not a second problem, it is the diagnosis.
  - Cause, mine, from B122. `PresentedFrame.PresentCore` ended with `_image?.Dispose()` before taking the next snapshot, justified in a comment as "renders are sequential, so by the time a present runs the previous image is no longer being drawn". **The compositor may still be holding it**, and freeing an `SKImage` under Skia is an access violation inside `sk_canvas_draw_image_rect`. `Reset` was worse: a resize freed the image *and* the surface backing it.
  - **Why no report.** An access violation is a native fault. B117 and B119 between them cover `AppDomain.UnhandledException`, `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` and `Dispatcher.UnhandledException` — all three managed. None sees a native crash, so the process vanishes and the log is empty. Worth stating plainly because "no crash report" reads as "the reporter is broken" when it actually means *the fault was not managed*, which narrows the search enormously.
  - **This exact failure was already written down, in the file I was editing.** `CanvasControl.UpdateSnapshot` carries a comment about "the compositor drew an image that had just been freed underneath it: an access violation inside `sk_canvas_draw_image_rect`, plus flickering frames on the way", and the whole `_retired`/`RetiredKeep`/`NoteRendered`/`HeldImagesAlive` machinery exists for it. B122 added a second image with the same lifetime and reused none of it. The lesson is not "be careful with Dispose" but that **a comment explaining a past crash is a specification for the next thing that hands an image to the compositor**.
  - Fix, in two parts. The defect: images are retired into a bounded queue and the oldest freed, three deep, on `ComposeRing`'s reasoning that the compositor holds the current frame and at most one in flight. Bounded rather than unlimited because a snapshot of a surface still being drawn into forces Skia to copy on write, which is the cost B122 exists to avoid — an unbounded queue would trade a crash for that regression. And the retreat: **the durable frame is off unless `LIGHTBOX_DURABLE_FRAME=1`**, because an optimisation that crashes the application has negative value, and the safe path (draw the publish's own image, whose lifetime `_retired` already manages) is the one that shipped for years.
  - Verified rather than reasoned: `AnImageHandedOutSurvivesLaterPresents` fails with `first handle FREED` when the eager dispose is reinstated, and the running application under Xvfb now survives the reported sequence — dismiss the splash, draw, zoom in and out, draw again — with no crash and no log. Cost: S
  - P1 without qualification: it made the application unusable, it reached `main`, and it was undiagnosable from the outside.

- [x] **B110** `P1` `canvas` Moving selected anchors or collision shapes wrote new undo history during an undo `evidence: RigMarkEditTests, MovingAGroupOfAnchorsIsOneUndoStep, UndoingAnAnchorGroupMovePutsThemAllBack, MovingAGroupOfCollisionBoxesIsOneUndoStep, UndoingACollisionBoxGroupMovePutsThemAllBack`

The guard arrived afterwards: `RigMarkEditTests` walks the undo stack *past* the drag, because one undo restored the marks in the broken version too, which is why it survived review. - [x] **B307** `P2` `canvas` A stroke steps at ordinary spacing, because the dab walk cannot resolve the dab's own soft band `evidence: StrokeFidelityTests, AStrokeAtAnOrdinarySpacingReadsAsALine, AWidenedSpacingStillLaysSeparateDabs, ThinningGivesBackExactlyWhatOneDabLaid, ABrushWhoseTextureIsItsDabsIsLeftAlone, SubdividingDoesNotMoveTheDabsThatWereAlreadyThere`

  - **The step was sized against the wrong feature.** The walk stepped `Spacing × diameter`, but what a step has to resolve is the dab's *soft band*, `(1-hardness) × radius`. At hardness 0.8 that band is 12 px on a 120 px brush while the step is 18 px, so the mark is sampled at less than one sample per feature and comes out corrugated at exactly the dab pitch.
  - **Measured**, straight strokes, peak-to-peak alpha wobble along the mark, hardness 0.2–0.9 at flow 1 / 0.5 / 0.3 — the wobble *is* the visible stepping, and it is measured across the mark rather than along it because alpha saturates along a stroke (the `brush-measurement` skill): spacing 0.25 → **81/255**; 0.20 → 51/255; 0.15 → 28/255; 0.10 → 13/255; 0.09 → ≤9/255; 0.05 → 4/255. After the fix, **≤5/255 across the whole grid**.
  - **Worse on a bend, and that is the same fault seen from the side.** Spacing is stepped along the path, so the outer rim of a dab travels `(R+r)/R` further per step — 1.67× on a 90 px bend with a 60 px brush. Sub-pixel measurement of the alpha-128 contour: a straight stroke's edge wobbles 0.43–0.93 px, the same brush round R=90 wobbles **1.39–2.29 px**, and the mark comes out up to **4.3 px narrower** on the outside of a tight bend. The subdivision brings the bend down with the straight run; explicit curvature compensation was measured as unnecessary once it did.
  - **Fix: the artist's `Spacing` keeps setting the texture, and the walk sets its own fidelity.** `BrushEngine.SubdividesForFidelity` splits one spacing interval into up to `MaxFidelity` dabs so the step never exceeds `min(0.09, band)` of the diameter, and `BrushEngine.Thinned` takes each dab's alpha to `1-(1-a)^(1/k)` so `k` of them composite back to exactly what one laid — without which subdividing would silently repaint every existing drawing heavier.
  - **Above spacing 0.25 the walk is untouched, deliberately.** Separated dabs are a thing an artist asks for by widening the spacing, and resolving them away would take a tool rather than fix a defect — which is the second half of the report. `AWidenedSpacingStillLaysSeparateDabs` guards it: at spacing 0.5 the mark still wobbles 175/255.

A **bitmap tip is excluded too, and that one is unfinished** — see B303.
  - **Cost, measured on a 600-point stroke.** Four of six shipped presets pay nothing, because they already sit at or under the 0.09 target: Pencil 1.03×, Ink 1.01×, Airbrush 0.95×, Wash 1.01×. That the target was set at 0.09 rather than 0.05 is what buys this — 0.05 doubled the dab count of brushes whose mark already wobbled 3/255.

Marks come out up to **8.9% denser** in the soft fringe, worst at soft + low flow + wide spacing — that is the coarse walk's under-deposit being corrected rather than a new error.

What it lacked was an origin: the document point its surface's (0,0) holds.

Re-framing invalidates all three buffers — their stale regions were recorded against the old window — but keeps their surfaces, because panning changes the origin on every pointer move and the size on none of them. A camera is excluded for the reason the tiled route excludes it.

    | zoom | before | after | |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | 1× | 5.88 ms | **1.81 ms** | 3.2× |
    | 2× | 5.90 ms | **0.57 ms** | 10.4× |
    | 4× | 5.73 ms | **0.32 ms** | 17.7× |
    | 8× | 5.94 ms | **0.24 ms** | 24.4× |

- [x] **B148** `P2` `canvas` Every cache miss during playback is rasterized inside the timer tick, on the UI thread `evidence: PlayingWarmsFramesTheTickHasNotReachedYet, AWarmedFrameIsBitIdenticalToOneRenderedOnThisThread, AWarmThatDoesNotFitIsDroppedRatherThanMakingRoom, AWarmThatWasSupersededIsNeverInstalled, AStrokeCommitDiscardsWhatWasWarmed`
  - **The cost B144 excludes by construction.** Every playback measurement in this file is taken on the *second* pass, so the first-pass rasterization — the one an artist meets before any other — has never been measured and was not filed. It is not a rounding error: a frame that misses the cache is a full replay of its stroke record, and it happens *between* the playhead moving and the frame being published, inside `PlaybackClock`'s tick, with nothing else on the UI thread able to run. B145 stopped that cost stretching the frame *period*; it cannot stop the frame being late.

  - **Fixed by rasterizing ahead of the playhead on a background thread.** `FramePrewarmer` runs one worker, renders the next `Lookahead` playhead positions from the stroke record, and queues the pixels; the next publish takes them into whichever cache the compositor is going to read. The prediction restates `StepPlayback`'s arithmetic and is driven against the real one (`ThePredictionAgreesWithStepPlayback`) so the restatement cannot drift.
  - **Safe off-thread because of invariant 2, and that is the whole argument.** A render is a pure function of the stroke record — no RNG anywhere, every dab dynamic seeded from geometry through `Hash01` — so which thread replays it cannot change what comes out. Measured rather than asserted: a stroke carrying scatter and all six jitters, rendered on four threads at once, is **0 differing bytes of 160 000** against the same frame rendered here. This is the first place the determinism invariant has been *spent* rather than merely kept, and it is worth noticing that the payoff was available the whole time.
  - **Speculative work never costs real work**, which is two rules rather than a slogan:
    - **A warm that does not fit is dropped, never made room for.** Eviction during playback is `EvictionOrder.MostRecent`, whose victim is the neighbour of the newest entry — which is, almost always, the frame on the screen. A warm that evicted would throw out the frame the artist is looking at to store one they are not, making playback measurably worse while appearing to work.
    - **A warm that arrives after the document changed is disposed, not installed.** A generation counter, bumped from the same funnel that invalidates the caches, plus one more place the funnel does not cover: `AppendToFrameRender`'s tile arm returns without caching anything, so a stale tile warm would have installed the drawing missing its newest line.
  - **Two things it does not do, and both are honest limits rather than backlog.** It warms only while playing — a prediction about where a hand is going is not worth a core — and it cannot win on a machine where rasterizing a frame costs more than the frame period, because then the tick gets there first and a second core repeats the UI thread's work. That case is *counted* (`Refused` against `Installed`) and named in `Help ▸ Write a render report` rather than inferred, because the totals alone cannot tell "working" from "losing the race".
  - **Not the same as offloading compositing**, which is B125 and stays open. Rasterizing a frame from strokes is cache-fillable and predictable; compositing the pass list is neither, it feeds a surface the canvas presents, and the GPU lease is UI-thread-bound. This moves the half that can move.

Neither branch contained a duplicate — and they landed in *different sections* of this file, so git saw no conflict either: both would have merged clean and left two B146 entries behind. That is the exact case this file's header says `bugs.py ids` exists for and CI cannot reach, since the collision only exists in the merged result. It was caught by reading the other open pull request's title, which is not a mechanism. **What would make it one: `ids` comparing against the ids on every open branch rather than only against HEAD's parents.** Left unbuilt rather than filed as a bug, because it is a change to the check and not a defect in the code — but the next collision will not have a title to give it away.

  - Cause: `TiledRasterizer` passes the tile as `targetPixels`, and that is what an effect brush *reads*. A tile only holds its own pixels, so a dab near the edge samples transparent black where the untiled render sees the neighbouring tile's paint.
  - **The damage is not confined to the seam, and that is worth writing down because the first hypothesis said it would be.** Only 62% of the differing pixels were within a brush width of the boundary. A smudge is a *stateful walk* — `carried = Mix(sample, carried, carryOver)` — so one wrong sample at the seam is inherited by every later dab, and the error travels the rest of the stroke. The test now asserts the true containment instead: **100% of the differences fall inside the smudge's own footprint**, which is what a read-neighbourhood defect can touch and nothing wider.
  - **Fixed, and not the way this entry predicted.** Effect brushes are refused by the tiled path (`TiledRasterizer.CanTile`) and their frames render whole and are sliced into the store, so the pixels come from the untiled path and cannot disagree with it. Measured: **0 differing pixels**, and the store still holds **1 tile of the 12 the document spans**, so what stays resident is proportional to ink even on the fallback. The cost is one document-sized allocation *while the frame renders* — today's peak memory, kept only for frames that actually contain an effect brush.
  - **The padded-read fix below was tried and is wrong, which is worth keeping rather than deleting.** Rendering the neighbourhood into an offset scratch made it *worse*: 3265 wrong pixels against 3876, with the worst alpha delta rising from 191 to a full **255**. The reason is the real root cause, and it is deeper than "a tile is too small to read": `SampleAverage` indexes its read bitmap with the dab's **document** position — `Math.Clamp((int)(pos.X + dx * spread), 0, pixels.Width - 1)` — and `LerpDab` does the same. The engine assumes **the read bitmap's origin is the document's origin**, which was true of every caller that existed before tiling. A shifted scratch violates that, and a sample read from the wrong place is further from the truth than one clamped short.
  - **Left open as B60**: thread a read origin through the effect path so the engine stops assuming, which is what lets an effect brush tile properly instead of opting out. Not done here on purpose — it edits the hottest and most invariant-critical file in the repository, and putting the discovery and the surgery in one diff is what the branch conventions exist to stop. `EffectBrushesAreRefusedByTheTiledPathUntilB59IsFixedProperly` pins the refusal so the fallback cannot be removed silently, and it is written to fail the day B60 lands.
  - Superseded plan, kept for the reasoning: render an effect brush against a **padded read source** — the tile plus a margin of its neighbours, at least the dab radius and the smudge sampling offset. That is a real cost (the margin is re-rasterised per tile) and it only applies to `BrushKind.Smudge`/`Blur`, so the paint path keeps the cheap read. The alternative — flatten the neighbourhood on demand — trades memory for the same thing.
  - **P2 rather than P1 because nothing renders through tiles yet.** `TiledRasterizer` is not wired into the canvas, the cache or export, so no artist can reach this today. It becomes a P1 the moment the render path moves, and it is the reason that move must not happen before this is fixed. Cost: M

        250   2 680 ms     10.7 ms      18.7 MB
        500   5 289 ms     10.6 ms      37.4 MB

Allocation at ~75 KB a stroke is a second cost: 150 MB of garbage to open a document lands on the interaction that follows it.

The two scenarios are sized to ~110 dabs a stroke each so the comparison isolates area: same dabs, **44× the coverage per dab, 5.3× the time** (2.0 ms a stroke for line art against 10.6).
