Unsynchronized they collide on the shared `.tmp` name — and the quieter, worse case is a stale snapshot finishing *after* a newer manual save and rolling the file backwards, which is silent data loss. The guard is `FinishPendingWrite`: every UI-thread save of a document file (`Save`, `SaveProject`) waits for the background write before touching the disk — a no-op when it is quiet, bounded by one write when it is not. `FinishPendingWriteLeavesTheDiskQuietAndTheFileComplete` pins the contract.

B80 shipped with this; the entry is here rather than reopened because the fix is the predicate, not the handler.
  - **Half landed, half did not, and saying so is the point.** The badge and the close prompt are built and guarded by `ANeverSavedDocumentBadgesButOnlyPromptsOnceDrawnIn`. **The docker-indexing half is not built**: a document created while a project is open still does not appear as a row. This entry stays open for that, because a bug half-fixed and ticked is worse than one left open — it is the thing that stops the ledger being trustworthy.
  - **The owner's decision, 2026-08-06: a new file badges, because it has not been saved at all.** Recorded with one nuance to settle when it is built — the badge and the close prompt want *different* predicates. Badge means "differs from disk", which a new empty document does. Prompting means "there is work to lose", which it does not, and File ▸ New followed by a close should not nag. B76's pending-versus-missing split is the same distinction: worth knowing is not worth acting on.
  - **The docker half landed 2026-08-06, to the owner's rule: a file created in a project gets a row marked unsaved, and closing it without saving removes it from the project view at once.** `File ▸ New` now files the document where the artist is — the same rule ＋ New ▸ Document follows — and `SaveProject` writes it, because the missing `Source` was what made a save skip it. `File ▸ New` still means *a new document* rather than *an animation under the selected character*: what changed is that the project knows about it.
  - **"Never written" is two conditions, and that is the part worth keeping.** Removal on close requires that no save has covered the id **and** that there is no file at its path. A document saved then edited is dirty and on disk, so closing it keeps its row; a document whose file was deleted from outside is not dirty, so it keeps its row and stays flagged missing — B61's rule that a vanished file is reported rather than removed on the artist's behalf. `ClosingASavedDocumentKeepsItsRow` and `ClosingADocumentWhoseFileVanishedKeepsItsRow` are the two guards, and they matter more than the fix: a close that quietly took a finished drawing out of the project would be worse than the bug.
  - **Adoption obliged a release, and the reporter caught its absence before it shipped.** Asked to verify "if I create a new document and place it outside of the project, it does not show in the project" — it did. Save As to a folder outside the project left the row in place, pointing at a path nothing had been written to and still saying *not saved yet*, and the next project save wrote a **second copy** inside the project. That is B106's one-drawing-two-files arriving from a different direction, and it is the general lesson: anything that takes a document into the project on creation owes it a way out when the artist chooses a home elsewhere.
  - Saved *into* the project is the opposite fix rather than the same one — the document stays and the **manifest follows the file**, path, name and folder, because a reference still pointing at the path it was created with also produced a duplicate, one directory over. `ProjectIo.RelativeInProject` is the counterpart to `ResolveInProject` that this needed, and it answers the only question that matters here: inside or outside.

B85/B86 added the folder tree beside it and the guard was never widened, so a drop that changes only `FolderId` reads as a real move even when the folder is unchanged.

  - Reported: the RMB context menu only offers "remove from project" which keeps files on disk. There is no option to permanently delete from both project and disk, and removed files should be marked so they are not unwantedly reloaded on subsequent checks.

  - **The containment check is why that method exists.** Every path it is given comes from the manifest, which is plain JSON a person or an agent can edit, so `../../../Documents` is one careless entry away from an operation that deletes a directory tree. The full path is resolved and compared against the resolved root, and the comparison includes the separator — `Production.lbproj-old` starts with `Production.lbproj`, so a plain `StartsWith` would delete a sibling. Both guards were verified by removing the check and watching the two tests fail with a real bystander file on disk.

The warning names the size of what is going — "Delete “Art” and the 1 folder and 1 document inside it?" — because *are you sure?* tells somebody nothing they can weigh. **Cancel is the default button**, which is the opposite of B75's save dialog and right for the same reason: Enter should land on the outcome that cannot destroy anything.
  - **Removing a folder returns its documents to the project root** rather than taking them with it. A drawing that vanished from every row because a folder was removed is a drawing that is gone as far as anyone can tell, and "remove" never touches disk.
  - **`MissingFilesAreTrackedAndNotReloadedOnNextOpen` needed no new machinery, and is worth having anyway.** The manifest *is* the index and nothing scans the folder, so a removed document already stays removed — the test pins a property that a later directory scan would silently break, and the folder tree makes such a scan tempting.
  - **One live crash found and fixed on the way.** `RemoveSelected` read `row.Character!` for anything that was not a document, so a scene row was a null reference — pre-existing, and made far easier to reach the moment folder rows existed. Folders are handled and the scene case reports rather than throws.

- [x] **B61** `P2` `project` The project docker shows what was on disk when it opened, not what is there now `evidence: ProjectWatcher, ProjectDockerTests, DeletingAFolderOnDiskRemovesItFromTheDocker, TheDockerRefreshesWithoutBeingReopened`
  - Reported: a project with several folders and documents; the folders and documents were deleted from disk and the docker went on listing them.
  - **The reporter diagnosed it themselves and the diagnosis changes the fix.** Their seventh note says that after closing and reopening Lightbox, the files on disk were correct — so nothing is wrong with what is *written*, only with what is *shown*. This is a refresh problem, not a persistence one, and the same note explains several of the entries below that looked like separate defects.
  - The docker reads the tree once and holds it. Nothing watches the directory, so any change made outside the app — another program, a file manager, a git checkout — leaves the docker asserting files that are gone and silent about files that appeared.
  - Fix: a `FileSystemWatcher` on the project root, debounced, re-reading the affected subtree rather than the whole project. The debounce is the part worth designing: a checkout or an unzip fires hundreds of events, and re-reading per event is how a docker becomes a stall. Cost: M
  - **Fixed, and it took two halves that landed in different sessions.** The first added `ProjectRow.Missing`, `MarkMissing` and three tests — and every one of those tests called `Refresh()` by hand. **Nothing in the running application ever did**: a grep for `.Refresh()` across `src/` found the symbol browser and the shortcut editor and no project docker at all. So the flag was real, the tests were green, and the reported behaviour was unchanged. `ProjectWatcher` is the half that closes it.
  - Armed from `Adopt`, which is the funnel `NewProject` and `OpenProject` share — **and from `MarkAllSaved`, which a test found was necessary.** `ProjectIo.Create` builds a `Project` without creating its folder and `NewProject` adopts before it saves, so at `Adopt` time a brand-new project's root does not exist and there is nothing to watch. Left at that, a freshly created project would have gone unwatched for its whole session: the same class of miss as this bug, a fix that works on the path somebody tested and not on the one they use.
  - Debounced at 250 ms, coalescing on the `Notify`/`Flush` shape `AutosaveService` already uses. That is also what makes it testable without a clock: 200 notifications must produce exactly **one** re-read, counted rather than flagged, because "it refreshed" is also true when it refreshed two hundred times.
  - **The re-read had to be made idempotent before the watch could be armed, and an unrelated test is what found that.** `Rebuild` recreated every row, which is invisible on screen and destroys the object identity the docker's interactions live on — a rename in progress, an open context menu, a status flyout mid-click. Arming the watch made a save trip it, and `WorkspaceTests.TheProjectRowMenuActuallyDoesSomethingWhenClicked` started failing because its click landed on a discarded row. `ProjectRow.Describes` keeps a row when it stands for the same underlying objects, and the identity is those objects rather than the key: `Move` deliberately keeps a document's id while changing the character above it, so keyed reuse alone would have kept a row that is genuinely a different row.
  - **The subtree half of the original plan was deliberately not built.** `Rebuild` is proportional to the manifest, not the disk — one `File.Exists` per row — and the debounce is what prevents the stall the entry warns about. Per-subtree granularity would mean partial row updates for a list of tens of rows and would buy nothing measurable.
  - `F5` and a `⟳` button re-read on purpose, registered in `ShortcutMap` as `project.refresh`. Not a nicety: `ProjectWatcher.Watch` swallows an `IOException` so a project on a network share still opens instead of refusing to, and a swallowed failure with no manual path is this bug again with better manners.
  - **One thing is not asserted**: that the debounce *timer* fires. Whether a `DispatcherTimer` ticks under a headless pump is a fact about Avalonia's test harness rather than about this bug, and a test resting on it would fail for reasons nobody could read. The logic it drives is covered; the one line between them is checked by hand.

- [x] **B56** `P2` `project` A document with no layers takes the application down when it is opened `evidence: ADocumentWithNoLayersOpensRatherThanThrowing`
  - Repro: open any `.lightbox.json` whose scene carries `"layers": []`. `ArgumentException: '0' cannot be greater than -1`, thrown out of a property setter under `ActiveTab`, naming neither the file nor layers.
  - Cause: `Math.Clamp(ActiveLayerIndex, 0, layers.Count - 1)` is `Clamp(0, 0, -1)` with no layers, in **two** places — `SyncLayerRows` and `OnActiveTabChanged`. The line directly below the second one already guards its *frame* clamp with `Math.Max(0, …)`, so the defensive version was written once and not applied one line up.
  - Reachable rather than theoretical. Nothing in `DocJson` backfills a layer and `new Doc()` starts with none, so a hand-edited file, one written by a script or an agent through the MCP surface, or one saved by a version that allowed the state all do it.
  - Found sideways, while building the two-tab test **ai-engineer** asked for on B31 — the second document in that test was a bare `new Doc()`.
  - Fixed: both clamps take `Math.Max(0, Count - 1)`. Cost: S
  - **Not fixed, and deliberately: painting on a layerless document.** `ActiveLayer` indexes `Scene.Layers[…]` and has nowhere to go, so opening one now works while drawing on it would still throw. The precedent for the rest is already in the tree — `DeleteLayer` backfills a `Paint 1` layer when a delete would leave nowhere to draw, which is this application's own answer to "a document must have somewhere to draw". Applying that at open time is a second and larger decision, because it edits the artist's file on load, so it is named here rather than smuggled into this fix.

The branch entries moved to **Q53**, **B132**, **B133** and **B134**.

A conflicted PR is not "green but conflicted", it is untested, and the checks page says `0` rather than saying so.
    - **`BUGS.md` auto-merged clean.** The two B138s landed in different sections — one `canvas`, one `ui`, hundreds of lines apart — so `git` had nothing to report and produced a file with a duplicate in it and no marker anywhere. Precisely the silent half this entry was reopened for.
    - So the textual conflict is **not** the guard, and treating it as one is the trap: it caught the loud collision and, by blocking CI, hid the quiet one. `bugs.py ids` is what found B138, and `.githooks/pre-push` would have found it at push time regardless. The habit worth having is running `ids` **while resolving** a ledger conflict rather than after — the resolution is where both the duplicate and the deletion get made, and it is the last point either is still private.

Not *"removing an answered entry frees its number"* — that is the convention this entry was originally filed against, and it is not what happened; nothing was removed. Not *"the duplicate check only prints"* either, which is what the previous version of this line said: `duplicate_ids` has returned a non-zero exit since two bugs shared `B39`, `cmd_check` includes it in the failure condition, and `.github/workflows/build.yml` runs it. That claim was checkable in thirty seconds and was asserted instead.
  - **The cause is timing, and the gate was downstream of the damage.** A collision does not exist in either branch — each is internally consistent and each is right about its own next free id. It exists only in the *merged* file. So the earliest a check in CI can see one is after the merge has been pushed, by which point the resolution is public and other branches rebase onto it. A correct, enforced, non-optional check ran green through all four collisions because none of them was ever pushed in a state it could see.
  - Fixed by moving the check to the last moment the mistake is still private, and by closing the hole it cannot see:
    - **`bugs.py ids`** — the cheap half of `check`: ids only, no evidence anchors, no code index, no rebuild. Milliseconds rather than seconds, which is what makes it affordable on every push.
    - **`.githooks/pre-push` runs it**, before the hook's own early exit, so it guards feature-branch pushes and not only pushes to `main`. That is deliberate: the collision arrives on a branch.
    - **`lost_ids` catches the worse failure**, which no duplicate check can. Resolving a ledger conflict by taking one side is the mechanical thing to do and it deletes the other branch's entry — leaving a file with **no duplicate in it**, so every check passes and the loss is permanent. A duplicate is loud and costs a renumber; this is silent and costs an entry. When HEAD is a merge, every id in every parent must still be present, and `LIGHTBOX_ALLOW_LEDGER_DELETION=1` is the way to mean it.
    - `bugs.py check` reports the same loss, so a push that bypassed the hook, and a merge performed by GitHub where no hook runs at all, are still caught.
  - **The renumbering half was already done** and is why nothing shows as duplicated today: the second pair became **Q26** (textured line re-shape) and **Q27** (reference size), and the seven cross-references were updated with them.
  - **The same reasoning was applied one artefact along, in the same commit.** `INDEX.md` and `FEATURES.md` are committed *and* derived, which is the pair of properties that lets them be wrong with nothing failing — and the merge driver that rebuilds them cannot cover a merge GitHub performed, a build that was red while it ran, or a commit that simply forgot. `codemap.py verify` derives both and compares the bytes; CI runs it. Not the hook: a full analysis is ~10 s against milliseconds for the ids, and a hook nobody can afford gets switched off. *(Since Q55, 2026-08-08, this paragraph is history: the two files are no longer committed at all, `verify` is retired, and CI builds the index instead.)*

- [x] **B262** `P1` `timeline` Keeping a pose as a drawing re-points every hold after it, freezing those frames off the rig `evidence: TheFramesAfterItGoOnHoldingWhatTheyHeld, KeepingAPoseAsADrawingBreaksTheHold, InsertDrawingFromPoseAt`
  - Owner's report, 2026-08-18: *"When I posed the skeleton over 4 frames, each frame a different pose, and I insert from pose on the second frame, frames 3 and 4 lose their binding it seems and are not posed against the skeleton anymore."*
  - **The exposure sheet, not the rig.** A hold shows the nearest drawing *before* it, so dropping a drawing in at frame two silently re-points frames three and four at the new one — and the new one is baked, which is precisely a drawing that answers to no rig. The frames after the insert froze at the second frame's pose. Nothing about the binding was lost; they were showing a different drawing.
  - It also explains *"the weight painting does not always show, but I am unsure how to reproduce"*: after an insert, the later frames were showing the baked copy, which carries no weights, so the heat overlay had nothing to draw.
  - The command already promised the opposite, in the manual and in this ledger — **only the frame you are on becomes a drawing** — and the test that guarded it asserted the wrong thing: that the neighbouring *cels* were still holds, which stayed true while what they *showed* changed underneath. Stating a promise about the picture as a claim about the data structure is the whole defect, and the test now asks `ExposedFrame`.
  - Fixed by re-exposing the held drawing on the next cel, so the row reads exactly as it did: same drawing, same frames, still the object every later hold resolves to — an edit to it reaches all of them the way it did when they were one long hold. The X-sheet shows that cel as a drawing rather than a hold, which is honest: it is a re-exposure, and it is what an X-sheet has always been able to say.

- [x] **B207** `P1` `timeline` Editing lines on a held cel rewrites the drawing the hold borrows, so the edit lands on the earlier frame `evidence: StrokeEditOnAHoldTests, PathEditOnAHoldKeysTheCel, MovingSelectedLinesOnAHoldKeysTheCel, TheSelectionSurvivesTheKeying, PickingALineOnAHoldStillAuthorsNothing`
  - **B206 through a tool B206 did not reach**, found by the adversarial pass on it: `CommitPathEdit` (`MainViewModel.PathEditing.cs`) and `PickableStrokes` (`MainViewModel.StrokeSelection.cs`) resolve their frame with `PaintTarget()` rather than `PaintTargetOrKey()`, so dragging a bezier node on a hold opens isolation on the borrowed drawing and commits the moved points straight into it. Reproduced: after `BeginPathEdit` + `DragPathPart` + `CommitPathEdit` on a held cel, the cel is still unkeyed and the earlier frame's stroke has moved.
  - Filed rather than fixed in B206's own branch for the one-objective rule — that branch was already three fixes and a feature, and this needs a change to a file it does not touch. It is next, not later.
  - **The fix is not a one-line swap, which is why it wanted its own branch.** Keying produces a *copy*, and `KeyedCopyOf` gives the copied strokes fresh ids — so a session holding a stroke id from the borrowed drawing would commit into a frame where that id does not exist.
  - **It was two gates, not one.** `CommitPathEdit` was the reported half; `StrokeEditTarget` (`MainViewModel.StrokeActions.cs`) is the same hole for *every* stroke-selection action — delete, move, nudge, recolour — and its own comment argued for `PaintTarget` on the grounds that "acting on a selection must not bring a cel into existence, for the same reason picking must not". That is half right in the way that cost this bug: **picking must not author, and an edit that lands must**. The keying therefore sits at the commit, which is also what keeps Ctrl+T-then-Escape from leaving a drawing behind (B206).
  - **This entry recommended the wrong fix and the code corrected it.** It proposed that `KeyedCopyOf` preserve stroke ids, "which `Frame.Clone` already does". Reading `Frame.Clone` says the opposite: it carries ids *because it is an undo snapshot* and has to restore the frame that was there, and it names `DocumentEditor.CloneFrame` as the contrast — a duplicate of a drawing an artist can see gets a **fresh** id. Keying a hold is that second thing, so fresh ids were already right and preserving them would have contradicted a documented distinction. The edit re-resolves instead: `KeyHeldCelForStrokeEdit` records each stroke's *index* before keying and re-points the ids afterwards, exact rather than heuristic because `KeyedCopyOf` copies in order. The selection is re-pointed with it, so an artist who picked three lines still has three picked.
  - No question reached the owner in the end, because the codebase settled it. The wrong recommendation is left above rather than quietly deleted: a ledger that edits out its bad guesses stops being evidence of how a decision was actually reached.
  - Same shape as B206 for severity: silent, lands on a frame the artist is not looking at, and is only found by scrubbing back. P1. Cost: S once the id question is answered.

- [x] **B206** `P1` `timeline` Moving or transforming on a held cel rewrites the drawing the hold borrows, so the edit shows up on the earlier frame too `evidence: AMoveOnAHoldKeysTheCel_AndLeavesTheHeldDrawingAlone, UnderEditTheHeldDrawing_AMoveStillEditsTheHeldDrawing`
  - Reported: draw on frame 1, stand on frame 2 (a hold), move the drawing — frame 1's drawing moves with it. **This covers the move, the transform and the placement drag; the pen's own reshaping is B207**, filed from this entry's adversarial pass and not closed by it. The auto-key that makes a *mark* on a hold safe (`PaintTargetOrKey`, the Drawing-on-a-hold setting) was only wired into the brush path; the transform tool's `ActiveCel` scope resolved the hold with `ExposureSheet.ExposedFrame` and handed the *held* frame to the session, so the commit rewrote the borrowed drawing's stroke points. Placement drags had the same shape through `PlacementsHere`, which reads `PaintTarget()`.

It also composes with holds' whole purpose — animating on 2s means half the timeline is holds, so "edit the current frame" hit the wrong frame half the time.
  - Fix: the gesture asks *when it opens* whether it is standing on a hold (`HeldCelNeedingKey`) and acts on the answer *at the commit* (`KeyHeldCelForCommit`), swapping the borrowed drawing for the keyed copy in the frames the commit writes to. The Configure switch keeps its meaning for every edit: under *Edit the held drawing* a move still moves the source and keys nothing.

The preview is not an edit (invariant 1 and `ThePreviewIsNotAnEdit`), so an abandoned transform has to leave the document exactly as it found it. `OpeningATransformOnAHoldAndCancellingKeysNothing` and `AMoveThatGoesNowhereKeysNothing` are the two shapes of that mistake, and both failed against the first draft.

Placement ids survive the copy, which is what lets the drag keep hold of what it grabbed.
  - Multi-cel scopes (whole layer, whole animation, a marked range) are deliberately untouched: there a hold *should* follow its key — moving a whole layer dedupes shared drawings and moves each once — and that is the existing, correct behaviour.
  - **Filed as B203, renumbered to B206 on merge.** `main` took B203 for the quick-bar entry while this branch was open, and a duplicate id exists in neither branch — only in the merged file, which is why `bugs.py ids` in the pre-push hook could not see it here and CI saw it at once. Renumbered above the highest id on either side; main's entry keeps B203 because it is cited from `WorkspaceStore.cs` and `QuickBarWorkspaceTests.cs`, and this one is cited from nothing outside the ledger.
  - Cost: S, once B204's copy existed to key with.

- [x] **B202** `P1` `timeline` Undo re-rasterizes every drawing in the timeline, so Ctrl+Z on a structural edit freezes for over a second `evidence: ThumbnailCache, ThumbnailCacheTests, UndoingAnAddedLayerRerastersNothing, ReorderingLayersRerastersNothing, UndoingAStrokeStillRefreshesThatOneThumbnail, ClearingALayersContentStillDropsEveryThumbnailItHad`
  - Repro: 60 keyed frames on one layer, add a layer, press Ctrl+Z. **Measured 1,295 ms and 61 full-resolution frame rasterizations** — in a document where not one drawing had changed. Redo the same, 1,308 ms. It scales with scene length, so a 200-frame scene is roughly four and a half seconds per press, on the most-used command in the application.
  - **The undo step itself is free, and that is what made this hard to see.** `UndoScoped` is a pointer swap for a snapshot (`SnapshotStep.Swap`) and two closure calls for a delta — microseconds either way. Every millisecond is in the invalidation afterwards, which is why reading the undo machinery finds nothing.
  - **Two independent faults, one symptom, and neither is fixable alone.** First, `SyncLayerRows` maps row *i* to `layers.Count - 1 - i`, so adding or removing a layer slides every row onto a *different* layer — and staleness was decided by comparing the cell's remembered frame id against the frame now under it, so every cell in the timeline mismatched and re-rendered. Second, `SnapshotStep.FrameId` returned null unconditionally, so `ApplyEditScope` could only read the edit as document-wide: `ClearFrameRenders()` then dropped every cached bitmap, which is what the re-render had to pay full price for.
  - **Attributed by experiment, not by reading.** Gating `_allThumbsDirty` alone left all 61 rasterizations in place, which is what proved the row-reshuffle half; gating `RefreshThumbnails` entirely gave 97 ms and 3 rasterizations, which is what proved the thumbnails were ~99% of the cost. The first gate is the one worth remembering — it refuted the obvious diagnosis, and taking it as read would have shipped a fix for the wrong half.
  - Fix, both halves: a **`ThumbnailCache` keyed by frame id** rather than stored on the cell that displays one — a thumbnail is a property of a drawing, so rows may be re-pointed at will and the pixels follow their drawing — on the same invalidation funnel as the bitmaps it is shrunk from, so it is dropped exactly when those pixels are. And **`Perform` gains `frameContentUnchanged`**, an opt-in declaration carried on the step and surfaced as `EditScope.FrameContentUnchanged`, so undo of a structure-only edit invalidates nothing at all. Thirteen layer operations declare it, each verified by reading its mutation; the default stays pessimistic because a wrong declaration shows the artist pixels the document no longer describes, where the cost of not declaring is only slowness.
  - **After: undo 75 ms with 0 rasterizations, redo 25 ms** — 17× and 53×. Better than the arm with the thumbnails removed entirely, because that one still threw the frame cache away.
  - **What is deliberately still open.** The residual ~75 ms is `OnDocumentChanged` running the whole document-wide storm on *every* undo — `InvalidateWholeCanvas`, `_composeRing.InvalidateAll()`, four registry re-registrations, both docker reloads, `RefreshDocumentStats` walking every cel — plus the publish. A stroke commit has a fast path (`_committingScopedEdit`); undoing that same stroke has none, so committing a mark is bounded work per invariant 6 and undoing it is not. That asymmetry is its own fix and its own branch. So is deferring the thumbnail strip to background priority, which is what a *genuine* document-wide invalidation (opening a file, undoing a re-time) still needs. Cost: S each.

- [x] **B162** `P1` `timeline` Dropping a frame to catch up renders it anyway, so being late costs four times as much as being on time `evidence: DroppedFramesAreNotRenderedTests, ATickThatOwesSeveralFramesCompositesExactlyOne, ThePlayheadStillAdvancesByEveryFrameItOwed, CatchingUpCostsNoMoreThanAnOrdinaryTick, CatchingUpStillHonoursTheEndOfAnUnloopedRange`
  - **The bug six rounds of instrumentation were circling.** `PlaybackClock.Pace` returns a frame count — 1 normally, up to `MaxCatchUpFrames` when a tick is late — and `OnPlaybackTick` implemented "skip 3 to catch up" as `for (i < frames) StepPlayback()`. Every one of those writes `CurrentFrameIndex`, and that setter runs a whole publish. **Dropping frames cost four times as much as keeping them**, which is the exact inverse of what dropping is for.
  - **A feedback loop rather than a constant overhead, which is why it ran away instead of settling.** A late tick asks for more frames → more frames cost proportionally more → the next tick is later still. The capture that found it: **178 ticks advanced the playhead and 568 composites came out of them** — 3.2 per tick — with mean lateness climbing across captures (59 → 197 → 232 ms) and **104 occasions where the clock gave up and re-based**, on a five-frame scene.
  - **The artist-visible symptom follows directly, and it is the one that was reported first.** On a five-frame loop, advancing 3–4 frames per tick is the playhead landing somewhere unrelated to where it was — *"random frames are jumped to"*. Not a rendering artefact and not a perception issue: the playhead really was jumping, because the clock really was dropping, because dropping was making it later.
  - **It is also why the report kept saying the budget was fine, and that is the part worth remembering.** The tick breakdown divides by profiled ticks, one per `StepPlayback` — so it reported 38 ms against an 83.3 ms period and B161's brand-new verdict called it **"comfortable"**, while a single timer fire was doing 3.2 of them: **138 ms of an 83.3 ms period, 165%**. The per-tick number was true. The per-*frame-period* number, which is the one that decides whether a clock can keep time, was never shown — so the instrument agreed with the code's own mistaken unit.
  - Fix: the frames before the last advance the playhead with `_skippingFrame` set, and `OnCurrentFrameIndexChanged` returns before publishing. A skipped frame still moves the playhead, still wraps the loop, still stops at the end of an unlooped range and still tracks audio — everything except the composite, which is the one part nobody was ever going to see. Cost: S
  - **Three of the eight tests fail against the old loop**, and the other five pass under both — those are what the change must not break: the playhead still advances by everything it owed, and catching up still honours the end of a range.
  - **CI caught a real defect in this PR's own tests, and it is worth recording because it will recur.** `LoopPlayback` is backed by `AppSettings`, and its setter calls `Save()` — a file on disk that every later `MainViewModel` loads in the same run. The new unlooped-range test turned looping off and never put it back, so every view model built afterwards played without looping; `ComposeCostScalesWithAreaTests` then paused after its warm-up and measured a 1920×1080 composite at **0.00 ms**. Green locally on one ordering, red on CI with another.
  - **The lesson is not "restore the setting" but "a test that writes a persisted global is writing to every other test".** Fixed both ways here: the unlooped test restores in a `finally`, and all three playback suites now set `LoopPlayback` explicitly rather than inheriting whatever is on disk. A measurement suite that silently measures nothing is the worst shape of failure available — it passes as easily as it fails.
  - **What it does not explain is the pointer.** The owner's *"moving the mouse on the canvas is the only place playback is smooth"* is still unexplained by anything measured. The plausible reading now is that pointer events break the tight fire-composite-fire loop and pace it externally — but B156's cohort split has twice shown canvas input making individual frames wait *longer*, so this stays a suspicion. Re-test after this lands: if the loop no longer runs away, the pointer should stop mattering.

- [x] **B145** `P1` `timeline` Playback ran slow and uneven whatever the document, because the clock counted ticks instead of keeping time `evidence: TwentyMsOfWorkEveryFrameDoesNotStretchTheFramePeriod, ALateTickShortensTheNextIntervalInsteadOfShiftingEveryFrameAfterIt, ALongStallIsCappedAndResynchronisedRatherThanRacedThrough, TheDelayIsNeverZeroOrNegativeHoweverFarBehindTheClockIs`
  - Reported as *"running the animation frames low and with visible stutter"* on a **mid/high-end laptop at FullHD**, on a document with **two layers, one brush stroke a frame and seven frames**. That description is what found it: a scene that trivial cannot be render-bound, and the reporter's own aside — *"maybe it's the front end side"* — was right. The two entries above it (B125's compositing, B144's cache) are both real and neither explains a near-empty document, because **both scale with pixels and this does not**.
  - `PlaybackClock` was a `DispatcherTimer` re-armed at the frame interval, and `StepPlayback` advances the playhead, which recomposites and publishes **synchronously inside the tick**. Two independent defects follow, and neither has anything to do with how expensive a frame is:
    - **The interval was a delay between ticks, not a frame period.** The real period was `interval + however long the handler took`. At 12 fps with a 20 ms frame that is 103.3 ms — **9.7 fps for a scene marked 12**, with nothing measuring the shortfall and nothing ever recovering it. That is the "frames low" half, and it is present on an empty document because 20 ms of compositing two layers is enough to cause it.
    - **Errors accumulated instead of cancelling.** A timer is a lower bound; the OS delivers it late by a scheduling quantum, a GC, or the compositor. Advancing exactly one frame per tick means every late tick permanently displaces every frame after it, by a varying amount — which is *uneven frame duration*, and uneven duration is what an eye reads as stutter. **A steady 9.7 fps looks smooth; 12 fps with a wandering period does not**, which is why the report said both "low" and "stuttering" and why they are two bugs in one line.
  - **Fixed by pacing against a wall clock.** Each frame has a due time; the next delay is what remains until it, so the tick's own cost comes *out* of the interval rather than being added to it, and a late tick shortens the next one instead of shifting the rest. Due time advances a whole period from where it **was**, never from now — that single choice is the difference between errors cancelling and accumulating. Measured through the pacing arithmetic: **83.3 ms mean period against 103.3 ms unpaced, and a steady-state spread under 1 ms**.
  - Catch-up is capped at four frames and then resynchronises, because the unbounded form turns a one-off stall — a breakpoint, a save dialog, a lid — into a burst that races through the scene. Falling behind and skipping ahead are both wrong; skipping is merely the one that also looks broken.
  - **A one-frame startup transient survives and is deliberate**: the first tick waits a whole period and its work lands on top before pacing has anything to correct against, so the first gap is 103 ms and every gap after it is 83.3. Asserted with the transient excluded and printed with it included, so the exclusion is visible rather than convenient.
  - **What is not measured, and why it cannot be here.** The magnitude on real hardware. The headless dispatcher does not deliver timer ticks in real time, so a test that appeared to measure jitter would be measuring the harness — it would pass on a build with pacing removed entirely. `Pace` is pure so the arithmetic is testable without a dispatcher; the defects themselves are structural, read off the code rather than inferred from a number. **Confirmation that the stutter is gone has to come from the machine that reported it.**
  - **The sequencing lesson is the reusable part.** This was found while scoping GPU compositing, which was asked for and would not have fixed it: compositing is `n^1.03`, so on a two-layer 1080p document it is a fraction of the budget, and a *fixed* per-frame overhead is invisible to any amount of GPU. The detail that settled it was the document's contents, not a profile — **"it stutters on a near-empty scene" rules out everything that scales with pixels in one sentence.** Ask what is in the document before optimising the thing that draws it.

- [x] **B113** `P1` `timeline` Inbetweening crosses matched strokes over, so a moved box collapses `evidence: BoxEdgeMatchTests, EachEdgePairsWithItsOwnEdge, TheMidwayFrameIsStillABox, TheMatchIsMinimumTotalCostRatherThanCheapestFirst, Assignment`
  - Reported from a real drawing: two boxes, two frames, four unlabelled lines each. Run the inbetweener and **the top edge animates downwards through the shape** instead of travelling with the box.
  - Reproduced exactly. A box at y=20..80 moved to y=60..120 pairs **old-bottom → new-top** and **old-top → new-bottom**, and at t=0.5 all four edges land on y=70 — the box has no height at all mid-motion. The reported symptom is the top edge; the worse half is the collapse.
  - Cause is `StrokeMatcher`'s second pass, which sorted every candidate pair by cost and took them cheapest-first. old-bottom→new-top costs 20 and is the single cheapest pair on the board, so greedy commits to it and leaves old-top nothing but new-bottom at 100. **Greedy total 120; optimal 80.** The right answer was reachable and not taken.
  - A box is the smallest drawing that exposes it: top and bottom are the same length and differ only in position, so the cost function is symmetric between them and only global optimality breaks the tie correctly. Anything that moves by more than half its own height hits it — which is most of a walk cycle.
  - **P1 because it is silent and it is the floor.** No error, no warning, just wrong art; and the deterministic engine is what the AI path falls back to, so a wrong pairing here is wrong output with or without a model.
  - Fixed by replacing the greedy pass with minimum-total-cost assignment (`Assignment.Solve`, Hungarian). The cost function is unchanged — this is which pairs get taken, not how they are scored. Cost: M

- [x] **B9** `P1` `timeline` The paper disappears on every frame but the first `evidence: AddingAFrame_HoldsThePaperRatherThanBlankingIt`
  - Repro: open the app, add a frame. The new frame has no paper — transparent canvas, checkerboard.
  - Cause: `DocumentEditor.AddFrameAfter` inserts `NewEmptyFrame(layer)` on **every** layer, including the Background. A blank key on the paper layer shadows the paper.
  - Fix: the paper holds. A background layer gets `Frame = null` on an added frame, so the exposure sheet resolves it back to the one paper drawing — which is what a paper layer means.
  - Found while writing B1's regression test: the ghost was visible in the test only because the paper had gone missing. Cost: S

- [x] **B3** `P1` `timeline` Thumbnail never returns after a cel is cleared and redrawn `evidence: RedrawingAClearedCel_BringsTheThumbnailBack`
  - Repro: clear a cel, draw on it again. The timeline cell stays blank.

  - Cost: S

- [x] **B2** `P1` `timeline` Cannot draw on a layer whose cels are all cleared `evidence: PaintingWithNoKeyAtThePlayhead_CreatesOne`
  - Repro: clear every cel on a layer, pick the brush, drag on the canvas. Nothing happens and nothing is said.
  - Cause: `PaintTarget()` returns null when no cel at or before the playhead is keyed, so `BeginStroke` returns silently. Fill and gradient no-op the same way.

- [x] **B1** `P1` `timeline` Onion skin invisible since the document gained a paper layer `evidence: OnionGhostsShowOverThePaper`
  - Repro: open the app (paper layer present), draw on frame 1, add frame 2, turn onion skin on. No ghost.
  - Cause: `MainViewModel.PublishSnapshot` queues **every** onion pass first and then composites every layer over them. The paper is opaque and at the bottom of the stack, so it paints over all the ghosts. Before the paper existed the ghosts showed through a transparent stack.
  - Fix: interleave — for each layer, its own ghosts, then the layer. That is also what makes multi-layer onion read correctly.
  - Regression I introduced with the paper layer. Cost: S

- [x] **B301** `P2` `timeline` Motion trail and spacing chart measure erased ink `evidence: InkAnEraserTookAwayIsNotTheSubjectEither, ACleanupBetweenDrawingsIsNotMovement`
  - Found 2026-08-24 by sweeping every consumer of the raw stroke record after B290/B297, on the reasoning that four bugs in a row (B232, B233, B243, B297) had the same shape: a caller reading the record as if it were the drawing. Two of the derived *views* did.
  - **`MotionTrail.Locate` had rule two and not rule three.** It skipped erasure strokes — "where they went says nothing about where the subject is" — and still took the bounds of the ink they had removed. Measured on the regression: a subject at x=30 with a rubbed-out scribble at x=200 marked the subject at **x=115**, between the drawing and something invisible. The half-applied rule is what made it hard to see: the code looked like it had already thought about erasing.
  - **`SpacingChart.Centroid` had neither.** It meant every point of every stroke, so an eraser's own path and the line it removed both entered the mean: a cleanup on one drawing read as **70 units** of movement where the artist had animated **10**. That is the chart's own claim (Q58 — it measures the artwork, not a transform) failing on the drawings most likely to have been reworked.
  - Both fixed by `StrokeRecordCleaner.EffectiveStrokes`, which is the right one of the two implementations here and not by luck: `StrokePicker`'s remarks explain that the cleaner is a whole-stroke judgement *with a tolerance* while the picker answers per point, and a measurement of where a drawing sits wants the tolerance — a nearly-erased line contributes nearly nothing to what the artist sees.
  - **What the sweep cleared**, so the next reader does not redo it: every AI and MCP path already goes through the cleaner (B233 holds, and the surface is insertion-only, so no agent can address an erased stroke by id); crop, resize, merge, symbols, cel copy/paste and frame duplication all copy whole records in record order or refuse (`LayerMerge.PairIsLossless`), so none can separate an erasure from what it erased. One cosmetic leak is left and is deliberately not fixed here: `TransformOps.Bounds` with no selection wraps the gizmo around erased ink too, so plain Ctrl+T on a reworked drawing shows a box larger than the art. It moves everything together, so no pixel is wrong — it is a box, on its own branch, and not worth widening this one.

- [x] **B266** `P2` `timeline` Camera and bone keys are visible on the timeline and cannot be selected, so nothing can be done to several of them at once `evidence: TrackKeySelectionTests, CtrlClickPicksKeysAcrossKinds, ARetimeMovesEveryKindInTheSelectionTogether, ARetimeIsOneUndoStep, ARunShiftedRightMovesFromTheRightmostBack`
  - Reported by the owner as a question, and the question was the finding: "certain elements like bones do not create xsheet cells but are visible on the timeline, same for camera and perhaps other keyframeable elements". They do not, and they were unreachable. The X-sheet's grid is built from `LayerRows` alone, so only drawings have cells; `TimelineTracks` also carries the camera and the armature. The cel selection is keyed `(layer, frame)` and could not describe either.
  - **Nor could the gesture reach them.** The Ctrl/Shift handler finds cels through `CellUnder` — a `Button` whose DataContext is a `FrameCell` — and those exist only in the X-sheet's grid. `TrackView` draws its keys and read no modifiers at all: a click armed a retime drag, right-click opened a menu, anything else scrubbed. So the multi-select an artist had just been given stopped at the tab boundary, which reads as the application being arbitrary rather than as a missing feature.
  - Fix: `TimelineKey` — cel, camera or pose — and one selection holding all three, shared with the X-sheet (Q: two views over one animation, so a selection that emptied itself on a tab switch would be the surprise). `TrackView` gains modifiers and a selected-dot ring, and stays ignorant of what a key means: it is handed (row, frame) pairs to light, exactly as its menu event hands the host a row and lets it decide.
  - **Only retiming spans the kinds, and that was the owner's call** rather than a shortcut. A drag already retimed all three, so it is the one verb a mixed selection can be asked for; delete is not one verb with three names, so the pose menu covers the pose keys in the selection and leaves a camera key beside them alone.
  - Two things the fix needed from Core, both extractions rather than new behaviour: `CameraOps.MoveKey` and `DocumentEditor.MoveCelIn`, pure so a batch of retimes fits inside one `Perform`. A drag that moves four keys is one edit to an artist and must be one to Ctrl+Z.
  - Cost: M. P2 — nothing was broken, but the inconsistency is in the middle of the two gestures this application is for.

- [x] **B265** `P2` `timeline` Half the cel actions ignore the multi-selection, and the re-timing three swallow the cels a Ctrl+click left out `evidence: CelSelectionActionsTests, ExtendExposureCoversEverySelectedCel, InsertFrameMarksEverySelectedCel, AHoledSelectionDoesNotSwallowTheCelsBetween, RetimingAHoledSelectionTreatsItAsRunsRatherThanOneSpan`
  - Repro: select several cels in the X-sheet or the timeline, right-click one and pick **Extend exposure**, **Reduce exposure** or any **Insert** — only the cel under the pointer changes. Reported by the owner as "multiselect seems to work but the actions are not applied across the selection".
  - **Half true, which is why the highlight looked right.** `DeleteCelAt`, `ClearCelAt`, `CopyCel` and `CutCel` were made selection-aware when the selection landed; `ExtendExposureAt`, `ReduceExposureAt` and `InsertFrameAt` were not, and those are the three at the top of the cel's right-click menu. The manual had promised the exposure half since before the selection was a set.
  - **The re-timing three were worse than not covering it.** `StretchExposureAt`, `ReduceToStepAt` and `ApplyTimingAt` took `OpRangeFor`, which answered "first selected to last selected" — a span. That was harmless while a selection could only be a contiguous Shift+click range, and became wrong the moment Ctrl+click could leave holes: they re-timed cels the artist had deliberately deselected. `OpRangeFor` is deleted rather than fixed, because a range is not what a selection is and leaving it available invites the next operation to make the same mistake.
  - Fix: two helpers, `ForEachSelectedCel` and `ForEachSelectedRun`, both descending. Descending is the load-bearing part — extending an exposure pushes the rest of the row down, so applied up the row the second cel picked no longer means the cel that was picked.
  - Cost: S. P2 rather than P1 — nothing is destroyed and no art is at risk, but every one of these is a gesture an artist repeats all day.

- [x] **B197** `P2` `timeline` A breakdown restarts the easing, so one slow-in/slow-out across a run comes out as two `evidence: BreakdownRunTests, ABreakdownOnTheArcDoesNotChangeTheMotion, FillingARunFillsEveryGapAndLeavesTheBreakdownAlone, TheWholeRunIsASingleUndoStep, WithNoBreakdownsARunIsJustTheInterval, RunAt, InbetweenRun`
  - Found while building Phase 1b of `docs/DESIGN-ai-correctness.md`, which asked for "`FrameRole.Breakdown` as a hard constraint — the arc must pass through it". Measuring first showed the premise was already met, for a reason the doc does not mention: `ExposureSheet.NextKeyIndex` finds the next *drawing* whatever its role, so a breakdown was already the interval's endpoint. There was no constraint to add — and a real defect underneath it.
  - **The timeline held two notions of a span.** The inbetween command closed one at the next *drawing*; `SpacingChart.Intended` closes one at the next *extreme*, or the end of the sheet. On key(0) · breakdown(1) · key(2) the chart overlay saw one run of 0→2 while the command saw an interval of 0→1.
  - Two consequences. The easing restarted at the breakdown, so a single slow-out/slow-in drawn across a run came out as **two, with a stutter in the middle** — measured on a straight y=0→100 move with a breakdown at the midpoint, the inbetweens landed at 25 and 75 where the same movement without a breakdown gives 12.5 and 87.5. And a Q58 timing chart authored on the opening key meant "to the next drawing" here and "across the run" in the overlay, so the artist's ladder said two different things.
  - Fix, per **Q83**: `ExposureSheet.RunAt` gives one span both readers can share, using `SpacingChart`'s own closing rule including its end-of-sheet fallback. `Inbetweener.InbetweenRun` eases once across the run and interpolates each gap **linearly** at the local fraction the global curve landed on — easing inside the gap as well would be the bug restated. `DocumentEditor.InsertRunInbetweens` fills every gap back-to-front in one `Perform`, because a single action has to be a single undo. Cost: M
  - **Nothing is moved.** Each waypoint keeps its frame and its pose, and a renormalized local fraction cannot leave its own bracket, so no inbetween between the key and the breakdown can show a pose from beyond it. A breakdown that disagrees with the easing is not corrected — `SpacingChart` exists to *show* that disagreement, and re-spacing a drawing the artist placed would be the app arguing with them.
  - P2 — wrong output × occasional. It needs a marked breakdown, which nothing in the default workflow produces (`Key` is the default role), and the result is bad timing rather than damaged art. That is also why a document without breakdowns is provably unaffected: every drawing is an extreme, so a run *is* an interval, and `WithNoBreakdownsARunIsJustTheInterval` is the guard that keeps it that way.
  - **The AI path deliberately does not follow, and that is a recorded cost rather than an oversight** (Q83.3): `✦ AI Inbetween` still asks per gap, because a third drawing is roughly +50% strokes — the dominant token cost — and `InbetweenVerifier` would need piecewise betweenness, which is Phase 3/4. So the two producers now disagree about the span, which is the disagreement this entry existed to remove, moved rather than resolved. It is bounded and written into the manual instead of left to be discovered.

- [x] **B196** `P2` `timeline` Which stroke pairs with which depends on the order the artist drew them in `evidence: StrokeShapeMatchTests, DrawOrderDoesNotDecideWhichStrokePairsWithWhich, CrossingDiagonalsKeepTheirOwnEnds, MirroredArmsDoNotSwapWhenTheFigureTravels, SignedBow`
  - B113's other half, and it was left behind on purpose: that fix changed **which assignment is chosen** and deliberately did not touch **what the cost knows**. Centroid distance and length ratio cannot see orientation at all, so any two strokes sharing a centroid and a length are indistinguishable to it.
  - Two strokes crossing in an X are exactly that, and they are an ordinary drawing — a cross, scissors, crossed legs, a pair of folded arms. Measured on an X rotated 20° about its own centre, **all four entries of the cost matrix were 0.0000**. Not a close call: no information whatsoever, so the pairing fell out of the solver's internal ordering. Listing B's two strokes the other way round swapped the match on the same drawing.
  - A figure's two arms are the same fault with the volume turned down. Bowing opposite ways and travelling right 20 and down 5, identity scores **41.23** against a crossed **41.37** — a 0.3% margin that hand jitter decides either way.
  - **The tie is structural rather than unlucky, which is why optimal assignment could not help.** When two strokes of A share a centroid, every row of the matrix is identical and *every* assignment has the same total; there is nothing for a better solver to find. Both cases sit exactly there.
  - Fix: two more terms in the cost — **where the ends went** (mean endpoint displacement) and **which way it bows** (`GeometryOps.SignedBow`, the averaged sagitta). Both are already pixels, so they add rather than scale and neither carries a tuned weight. **Additive is the load-bearing part**: the case they exist for has a centroid distance of zero, and a multiplicative term would be multiplying zero. The endpoint term scores the better of the two orientations, because `StrokeInterpolator` already reverses B when its ends are crossed and an artist redrawing a line from the other end has not made a different mark. Cost: S
  - P2 rather than P1 — wrong output × occasional, where B113 was blocks-work × common. It needs a drawing whose strokes share a centroid, and half the time the coin lands the right way up. It is the same silent-art failure mode either way.
  - **The evidence needs reading with one caveat, recorded rather than smoothed over.** Only `DrawOrderDoesNotDecideWhichStrokePairsWithWhich` fails on the pre-fix build, and it does so by matching the same drawing twice with its strokes listed in each order — either order alone passes. A tie cannot be caught by asserting an outcome, only by asserting that two orderings agree. The X and arms tests passed before the fix and are guards on the new terms rather than proof of the old fault: they catch a shape cost that overshoots and starts crossing pairs that used to be right.

- [x] **B159** `P2` `timeline` Space starts playback and will not stop it — the wiring is sound, so this is the stutter wearing a different hat `evidence: SpaceTogglesPlaybackTests, SpaceStartsPlaybackAndSpaceStopsIt, SpaceStillTogglesWhenTheTransportButtonHasFocus, ThePlayPauseBindingIsGlobalRatherThanScopedToTheTimeline`
  - Reported as *"Space starts the playback, but if playback runs I want to be able to press space again to stop it directly"*.
  - **Investigated end to end through the real window and the wiring is correct**, which is the useful half of the answer: the gesture resolves to `timeline.playPause` from any scope because it is a **Global** binding, the handler runs `TogglePlaybackCommand`, the command is a real toggle (`if (IsPlaying) Pause(); else Play();`), and a blanket `e.Handled = true` after the switch means the missing per-case one is harmless. Space toggles both ways with focus nowhere in particular **and** with focus on the transport button — the state a click leaves behind, and the one most likely to swallow a key. **So a fix to the binding would have been a fix to nothing.**

  - **The strongest candidate found, and it is real work that should not be there: `OnCurrentFrameIndexChanged` calls `RefreshLayerThumbs()`, unconditionally, and that runs inside the timer callback.** The staleness test is `row.ThumbFrameId != frame.Id` — and during playback the exposed frame changes on *every tick by definition*, so it misses every time. Each miss calls `ThumbSource` → `_cache.Get(frame, Scene.Width, Scene.Height, celIndex)`, **a full 1920x1080 render**, then scales it to 44x26. Per layer. Per frame. Behind a moving playhead nobody can read.

  - **What the artist reports is the *mitigation*, not the fault.** `PlaybackClock.Pace` drops frames to stay in time, which is right — the comment above `MaxCatchUpFrames` says so: *"Falling behind by a second and skipping a second of animation are both wrong; skipping is merely the one that also looks broken."* 469 drops across 336 ticks is the playhead advancing two or three frames at a time, constantly, which is exactly the reported *"jumps all over the place"*. The 52 resyncs plus a looping range are the *"sometimes even seems to go backwards"*: a burst of four wraps past the end.

The reason is that `_cache.Get` *hits* in both — the documents are small enough to sit inside the 512 MB budget, so a "render" is a dictionary lookup. **So the mechanism is confirmed and the magnitude is not.** The 159 ms is unexplained by anything measured here.

Under those conditions every tick's thumbnail is a genuine full replay from the stroke record, per layer, and B30 prices that in tens of milliseconds per hundred strokes. That is a coherent story and it is a story: **the way to settle it is another render report from the same machine and the same scene after this lands.** `mean lateness` is the instrument, and it should fall from 159 ms toward single figures if this was it. If it does not, this fix was worth making anyway and the cause is still out there.

The pattern is worth naming: **a staleness check keyed on "has the thing changed" is useless in a loop whose whole job is to change that thing**, and the surrounding code reads as careful precisely because the check is there.   - P1 rather than P2: playback is the feature, it was unusable on a machine well above the target spec, and the symptom pointed at everything except the cause.

- [x] **B142** `P2` `timeline` Adding a layer to a painting stalls for a second, because every structural edit clones the whole document `evidence: TheFastCloneMatchesTheSerializerItReplaced, NoMutableObjectAppearsInBothGraphs, CloningChangesNothingAboutTheOriginal, UndoSnapshotFidelityTests, AStructuralEditIsUndoneByteIdentically, NothingOptionalIsLostOnTheWayThroughASnapshot, UndoingAndRedoingRepeatedlyLandsOnTheSameTwoDocuments, AMutationCannotReachIntoTheSnapshotItWasTakenAgainst, TakingASnapshotCostsFarLessThanRebuildingOne`

Right about the scale it names; a painting is past it.

This is *record cloning* — copying the document object graph.    
    ```
    strokes    DocJson.Clone      Doc.Clone      alloc
        500        180.8 ms         0.6 ms    7 271 → 506 KB
      2 000        328.7 ms         8.1 ms   28 984 → 2 018 KB
      5 000        614.9 ms         5.8 ms   72 542 → 5 041 KB
    ```

The absolute figures are now small enough that the sweep's three iterations put p95 in the noise — 2 000 reads slower than 5 000 — so the order of magnitude is the result, not the individual numbers.

Enumerating every field by hand fails in the direction that corrupts a document rather than slowing it.

It kept the first fix's improvement — compact UTF-8 through `ToSnapshot`/`FromSnapshot` rather than an indented string — so the callers that need the round trip got faster too.

  - **What remains is turning structural edits into deltas where they can be** (most touch one layer or one list, not the whole document). At ~6 ms it is no longer urgent; it competes on merit with everything else rather than jumping the queue.

- [x] **B28** `P2` `timeline` Past the frame cache's size, playing or scrubbing misses every single time `evidence: EvictionOrder, AnLruScanThrowsAwayEverythingItIsAboutToNeed, EvictingTheMostRecentKeepsHalfTheSheetResident, ScanEvictionIsBetterThanLruOnAScan, TheFrameBeingShownIsNeverTheOneEvicted, PlayingSwitchesTheCacheToScanEviction`
  - Repro: a 3-layer scene at 1280×720. A cel is 3.5 MB, so 48 frames is 506 MB against `FrameBitmapCache.ByteBudget` of 512 MB, and 96 frames is 1 GB. Walk the sheet in order — which is what playback does, and scrubbing, and export.
  - Cause: an LRU against a sequential scan, which is the one access pattern LRU is worst at. Walking 96 frames evicts the frames at the start to make room for the ones at the end, so by the time the playhead comes round again *everything it is about to ask for has just been thrown away*. The hit rate is not degraded, it is **zero** — the cache stops being a cache and every frame is re-rasterised from strokes. Found by the sweep in `tools/Lightbox.Bench` refusing to terminate at 192 frames, which is the same fact stated less politely.
  - It is a cliff and not a slope, which is what makes it worth its own entry: at 48 frames everything is instant and at 96 nothing is, with no warning in between. It also gets *worse* with the canvas — the same scene at 1080p crosses at 21 frames, and at 4K at 5.
  - Fix: `FrameBitmapCache.EvictionOrder`, set to `MostRecent` for the duration of a scan. Evicting the newest stops the scan destroying itself — the frames that arrived first stay resident and the tail of the sheet fights over what is left, so a sheet twice the capacity goes from **every** frame missing to about half hitting. Half a cache beats none. The frame being shown is explicitly never the victim, or the cache would be a no-op on exactly the frame the artist is looking at. LRU stays the default because while drawing, recency does predict reuse.
  - Not a bigger budget, which only moves the cliff. The other candidate — caching playback frames at display resolution rather than document resolution — is still worth doing and multiplies capacity rather than shifting it; it is a bigger change and wants its own measurement, so it is not folded in here.
  - **The test for the defect nearly did not work**, and the reason is worth keeping: counting cached frames and bytes to detect a hit reports every *miss* as a hit, because a miss that inserts one entry and evicts one leaves both totals exactly where they were. It read 24 of 24 hitting on a cache that was thrashing completely. Bitmap identity is the honest signal. Cost: M
  - Charter §3's memory objective (O4) already says caches are sized in bytes rather than item count, and this one is. Being correctly sized is not the same as being correctly *evicted*, which is the gap this fell through.

  - Cause: never built. `DeleteFrame` is a different operation — it deletes across every layer.
  - Fix: a ripple delete on one layer's row, one undo step.

- [x] **B267** `P3` `timeline` The timeline ruler numbers every twelfth frame at any zoom, so at a wide frame width the playhead's own chip is the only number on it `evidence: TimelineRulerTests, NumbersStayAtLeastAsCloseAsTheOldFixedTwelve, TheWidestZoomNumbersEveryFrame, EveryStepKeepsTheSecondBoundariesNumbered, ARulerNumberIsBuiltOnceAndKept, AChangeOfStyleThrowsTheKeptNumbersAway`
  - Reported by the owner: "the timeline's scrubbing bar only shows the frame number when the scrubbar is on it". Accurate, and the cause is arithmetic rather than the playhead: `TrackView` drew a ruler label every 12 frames whatever `FrameWidth` was. At the slider's top setting of 72 px that is one number every 864 px — a ruler with one or two numbers on the whole strip — while the playhead paints its own chip over everything. So the only readable frame was the one under the playhead.

So a long scene at the widest zoom would have spent the whole frame budget on ruler text. The numbers are now built once and kept, keyed by frame, dropped when the typeface, size or brush changes (a `FormattedText` holds its brush, so a stale cache would paint the old colour through a theme change) and cleared past a ceiling so a pathological document cannot retain a heap.

### transform

- [x] **B208** `P1` `transform` Ctrl+T breaks its own session: the handles do nothing and the press paints across the drawing instead `evidence: TransformGizmoInputTests, AfterCtrlTTheHandlesTransformRatherThanPaint, ABorrowedToolIsNotAChoiceAndDoesNotCancel, ChoosingAToolMidSessionCancelsTheTransform, EndingTheSessionGivesTheCanvasBackToTheTool, AGizmolessSessionDoesNotFreezeTheCanvasMode`
  - Reported: "After pressing CTRL + T to enter it I am unable to consistently drag the handles to actually transform."
  - **The release of Ctrl is the bug, which is why nobody suspected the shortcut.** Holding Ctrl borrows the eyedropper (`ApplyHeldModifiers` → `BorrowedFor`), the `T` starts the session and sets `Canvas.ToolMode = Transform` — and then *letting go of Ctrl* hands the brush back, fires `ActiveTool`, and reaches `SyncCanvasToolMode`, which asserts the canvas mode from the tool alone and puts it back to `Paint`. `_txActive` is still true so the gizmo is still drawn; the press branch that routes to it is `_txActive && ToolMode == Transform`, and that half is now false.
  - **"Inconsistent" was the exact word for it.** `BorrowedFor` only borrows *from* the brush, eraser, fill, shape and gradient. Press Ctrl+T holding the Move tool, either arrow, the pen or the width tool and no tool change happens, nothing overwrites the mode, and the gizmo works perfectly — so the same gesture worked or did nothing depending on which tool was in hand when it was typed.
  - **P1 rather than P2, on the second half of the symptom.** The press does not merely miss the handle: it reaches the brush, so dragging a handle lays a stroke across the drawing the artist was trying to transform. *Corrupts art* × *common* — it fires on the ordinary way of entering a transform from the ordinary tool.
  - **Why the suite was green.** `TransformPreviewTests` drives the view model and the pixels move; the gizmo's own arithmetic is exact and tested. Neither half touches the *routing* between them, and no test had ever sent a real key event followed by a real press. A test that calls `BeginTransform()` directly passes with the bug in place, and so does one that presses Ctrl+T without releasing Ctrl.
  - Fix: `SyncCanvasToolMode` returns early while `Canvas.TransformSessionActive`. A session owns the canvas until Enter or Escape, and `TransformEnded` clears the flag before calling it, so the hand-back still runs. Guarded on the *gizmo's* flag rather than `TransformActive` because the Move tool opens a gizmoless session that must keep following the tool.
  - **What choosing a tool mid-session means was asked rather than assumed, and the owner chose cancel (Q94).** The guard alone would have left a highlighted brush that does not draw until the session ends, which is coherent and reads as broken. So a deliberate tool choice now ends the transform, and `LeaveToolStateBehind` is where it goes — beside the polygon, the pen path and the isolation session, all of which already work that way.
  - **It discards rather than applies, and that asymmetry is the point.** The preview was never an edit (invariant 1), so cancelling costs a drag and leaves no undo step to want back; applying would write to the document from a gesture that never said apply, and *that* is the one you cannot take back cheaply. Enter is still the only thing that commits.
  - **The borrow must not count as a choice, and it is the same distinction twice.** Ctrl+T *is* a tool change followed by a tool change — Ctrl borrows the eyedropper on the way in and gives the brush back on the way out. Routing the cancel through `LeaveToolStateBehind` gets this free: `SetToolWithoutSideEffects` suppresses it, so a borrow cannot cancel the session it just started. `ABorrowedToolIsNotAChoiceAndDoesNotCancel` is the guard on the fix's own tail.
  - **The comment above the line has claimed this behaviour since B147** — *"Every other modal thing here behaves the same way ... the transform session"* — and the line was never there. A comment describing a rule nothing enforced, next to four rules that are enforced, is the exact thing the ledger's evidence anchors exist to prevent one level up.
  - Cost: S for the fix, M for finding it, and the diagnosis is the part worth keeping: both halves were tested and the join between them was not.

- [x] **B340** `P2` `transform` A transform leaves a clipped stroke's clip region behind `evidence: ClipTravel, TransformCarriesTheClipTests, AWholeLayerRotationEndsWhereTheDragSaidItWould, TheStencilMovesByWhatTheInkMovedBy, TheCarriedStencilIsPartOfTheRecord, TheMoveToolCarriesItToo`
  - **Reported 2026-08-28 as "rotating the layer moves one line somewhere else".** The drag showed the whole drawing turning correctly; the commit turned everything except one mark near the eye, which landed in a different place and a different shape. It looked like a single-stroke fault and it was a whole-class one: the only strokes that behave this way are the ones painted while a marquee was up, which is usually a handful in a drawing and often exactly one.
  - **The stroke moved and its stencil did not.** `TransformOps.TransformStroke` mapped points, holes and the authored path, and left `Stroke.ClipId` alone — so the moved geometry was carved by a clip standing at the old position. The ink that survives is the intersection of the mark's new place with the clip's old one, which is neither where the drag showed it nor a piece of what was there before. B319's `MapClip` already knew a clip has to travel, but only for the strokes a *marquee cuts through* during a region transform; a stroke moving whole, and every transform with no selection at all, went through the path that did not.
  - **Measured, not eyeballed**: a 90° whole-layer rotation of a drawing with one clipped line published 27,738 inked pixels in the preview and 23,738 after the commit, with 6,697 pixels disagreeing. 90° because a quarter turn of a bitmap is a permutation rather than an interpolation, so preview-against-commit is an exact comparison and any difference is geometry. The same drawing with an erasure, and with a fill, was bit-identical — which is what said the fault was the clip and not the transform.
  - Fixed by carrying the region through the same map as the ink (`ClipTravel`), memoised per region because carrying one costs a serialize and a SHA-256 over its contours, and writing what it made into `Doc.ClipRegions` — a clip the strokes name and the document does not reloads as an unclipped stroke, which is the whole line back at both positions (invariant 3).
  - The Move tool commits through `CommitTransformAffine` too, so it had the same fault and the same fix; `TheMoveToolCarriesItToo` is what keeps that true.
  - **The cost, named rather than hidden:** each commit that moves clipped ink adds one region per distinct clip to `Doc.ClipRegions`, and nothing prunes the ones no stroke names any more. That is not new — B319's split has done it since it landed — but this widens the set of gestures that do it. Small (a marquee's outline is a handful of points), bounded per commit, and the alternative is ink in the wrong place. A sweep that drops unreferenced regions on save belongs with whoever next touches serialization.

It is a property of the layer — the ramp colours everything wherever its two axis points sit — so "the part of it inside the selection" is not something the record can say apart from the ramp itself, and B7 had already made it the special case in this file.
  - **The argument that won**: a marquee has to mean one thing everywhere. Once a stroke moves only what you boxed, a gradient that alone ignored the box was the odd one out, and Photoshop moves the pixels you selected whatever laid them down.

- [x] **B320** `P2` `transform` Moving ink out of a selection reveals the paint an erasure had rubbed off it `evidence: TransformCarriesTheCarvingTests, ABandAcrossTheMiddleTakesTheCarvingWithIt, TheCarvingTravelsWithTheInkItCarved, TheInkLeftBehindKeepsItsOwnEdge, TheBiteIsThereToBeginWith`
  - **Measured on `main`, on the drawing the test builds: `gap 255`.** A line with a bite rubbed out of it, a marquee dragged down, and the rubbed-off paint arrives at the destination at full opacity — not a ghost, the whole mark back. With the fix the same probe reads `0`.

Every point of a horizontal line is inside it; neither end of a vertical eraser is, because its two recorded points are above and below. Reading vertices alone, the ink was selected and the eraser was not.
  - **An erasure is duplicated, never divided — and getting that wrong cost two of B290's own tests.** The first attempt clipped the half left behind to "outside the selection", by symmetry with ink. That takes its carve off everything *inside* the selection that did not travel — and wholly rubbed-out ink is exactly that, because rule three says a stroke with no surviving ink is never caught. The lasso then lifted the eraser off a line it was holding down and the line came back: the bug this class exists to prevent, reintroduced through its own fix. The old stay-copy special case survives for an erasure that is *wholly* inside the region and so has nothing left behind to do the holding.

  - **Reported as two bugs that read as opposites** — freehand, circle and square "do not seem to trigger transform at all", polygon and magic wand "transform whatever's on canvas" — and they are one rule seen from two sides. The shapes you reach for to grab part of a drawing fail the majority test and do nothing; a generously drawn polygon and a wand click on a connected region enclose whole strokes and move everything.
  - **Measured on `main`**, one line from (100,200) to (500,200): a box over 100–200 returns false with *"Nothing to transform in this scope."*; a box over 50–320 dragged down 100 leaves the record reading `first=(100,300) last=(500,300)` — both ends down, the whole line carried off by a box covering a bit over half of it.
  - **The precedent that decided the fix, and the reason it is not new design.** Copy already solves this in the same model through the same filter: `SelectedStrokesForAnOperation` gives each caught stroke the selection as a `ClipId` and intersects through `ClipMeeting`. The manual has documented it for copy since it landed — *draw a box across half a line and the paste shows that half; the line is not cut in two to do it*. The transform borrowed the filter and never got the clip. Q166 records the alternatives and what they cost.
  - **A stroke is never cut, and that is invariant 2 rather than tidiness.** `Hash01` seeds every dab dynamic from position, so cutting a polyline restarts the dab walk and re-rolls scatter, size, flow, roundness, rotation and all three colour jitters along both halves — a split line would be a different *mark*, not the same mark in two places. Two clipped copies re-render dab for dab as the original did.

It is prepared once per frame rather than asked per stroke, because both questions it answers need every erasure's position and the stroke's own index, and computing either per call makes the walk quadratic in the stroke count.
  - **What deliberately did not change.** A stroke wholly inside the region still moves whole with no clip and no copy — the common case gets no slower and no more complicated, and clipping everything caught would cut a soft brush's spill at the boundary, which is ink the artist sees as inside. Picked lines are still taken whole however little of them the last marquee covered, which is the manual's own asymmetry.
  - **A gradient is not split, and moves whole as it always has.** It has no location — the ramp colours the layer wherever its two axis points sit — so "the part of it inside the selection" is not something the record can say apart from the ramp itself. Dividing one by a clip is expressible and was tried; it turns every region-limited move on a layer with a background gradient into a shifted rectangle of background, which is a decision about what a marquee means over a *fill* rather than the stroke bug this work was about. Interleaving in place is what keeps the record's order, which is what an artist reads as depth — appending all moved strokes at the end would fix the sliver and bring a moved background element in front of everything it was behind, which is the worse trade.

  - Reported by the owner: *"the transform auto scales to all sides. Like Photoshop and all other tools. That should only happen when pressing alt."* The gizmo scaled around the pivot whatever handle was dragged — Photoshop's *Alt* behaviour as the only behaviour — so pulling one side moved the side the artist was holding still against.
  - Fixed in the one scale arm rather than a second code path: the fixed point of a scale drag is now an **anchor** — the opposite corner for a corner handle, the opposite edge's midpoint for an edge handle, and the pivot when Alt is held. One formula, because with the anchor at the pivot every term reduces to the old behaviour verbatim; Alt is read per pointer event, so it can be pressed and released mid-drag and the box follows, which is Photoshop's feel exactly.
  - Two things the maths had to get right, both found by reasoning rather than by a failure. The cursor is measured in the **press-time frame** (`TxLocalAtStartFrame`): the old code measured from the live pivot, which was safe only because a scale drag never moved the offset — anchored scaling adjusts the offset per event, and measuring from a pivot the previous event just shifted makes the box chase its own correction. And the anchor is held still through the **offset**, not by moving the pivot: the pivot is an authored thing the artist can place, and a scale drag has no business relocating it.
  - Uniform (Shift) composes: distances are measured from the anchor rather than the pivot, so Shift+drag keeps proportions about the held corner, and Shift+Alt about the pivot. Dragging across the anchor mirrors, exactly as dragging across the pivot always did.

- [x] **B223** `P2` `transform` The transform session cannot express a line selection, so lines never scale or rotate `evidence: BeginLineMove, TransformSubject, ScopeIsPinnedToThisCel, TransformingWithLinesPickedScalesOnlyThose, ThePickedLinesCanBeRotated, APickedLinePinsTheScopeToItsOwnDrawing, AMarqueeOutranksThePickedLines, TheSessionSaysWhatItIsMoving, DraggingAPickedLineIsOneSessionAndOneUndoStep, APressOnALineThatDidNotMoveCommitsNothing, ThereIsNoLineMoveWithoutPickedLines`
  - **The roadmap's diagnosis was wrong, and that is the useful part of this entry.** `ROADMAP.md` said scaling or rotating a line selection "wants a `TransformScope` meaning 'these strokes inside this cel'; every scope today is a set of cels, so the transform session cannot express it yet", and `MainViewModel.StrokeActions` repeated it as the reason its move could not reuse `BeginTransform`. **Scope was never the obstacle.** `TransformSession` has carried a `Func<Stroke, bool>` filter since the marquee shipped, `TransformOps.TransformFrame` takes it, and `PartsFor` already renders the moving/static split it implies. What was missing was a filter built from the line selection — one method — and a scope that stops offering cels the picked lines are not on.
  - **Two things were being conflated: which *frames* are in scope, and which *strokes* within them move.** They are orthogonal and the code already knew it; the prose did not, and the prose is what stopped anybody trying for two releases.
  - **Scope pins to the active cel while lines are the subject** (Q97's sibling decision). A stroke id resolves in exactly one drawing, so "all layers at this frame" would collect a hundred cels and find the picked lines on one — not a wider transform, the same transform with ninety-nine frames that resolve to nothing. `ScopePinnedReason` says why rather than silently disabling the control.
  - **The marquee outranks the lines when both are up** — the owner's call against the recommendation, recorded in Q97 with what it costs. The cost is that a marquee left off screen silently decides what a transform moves, which is precisely the state `Ctrl+D` is documented as the cure for. `TransformSubject` is what the choice obliges: the session names what it took, so a precedence whose failure is silent stops being silent.
  - **The Arrow's drag now runs through the session too**, which is what `StrokeActions` wanted and could not have.
