  - **A drag does not obey the precedence, deliberately.** A menu command asks what is selected; a drag asks what you are holding. `BeginLineMove` passes its filter explicitly, because a marquee outranking the line under the pointer would mean grabbing one line and watching another move.
  - Two ratchets moved, both for gesture and wiring code that cannot leave the handler that receives it; the four new canvas events went to `CanvasControl.Overlays.cs`.

- [x] **B205** `P2` `transform` The transform and move preview repaints the whole canvas per pointer event, so on a heavy document the drag reads as no live update at all `evidence: TransformPreviewBoundsTests, AMovePreviewRepaintsARegion_NotTheCanvas, TheRegionCoversWhereTheDrawingWas_AcrossSuccessiveEvents, ABaselineRidesTheLayer_SoThePreviewFallsBackToTheWholeCanvas, WithASelection_TheBaselineStaysPut_AndTheRegionIsStillBounded`

A brush stroke stays live on the same document because its repaint is bounded (invariant 6); the preview was the one drag that wasn't.

- [x] **B190** `P2` `transform` Escape-cancelling a transform leaves the abandoned preview on screen `evidence: CancellingATransformPublishesTheRevert`
  - Found by the adversarial pass on B189's publish pacing, hunting for interactions whose last act could leave a deferred publish stranded — and this one turned out not to publish at all, pacing or no pacing. `CancelTransform` → `EndTransformSession` → `ClearTransformPreview` reverts the model and repaints nothing, while the commit path repaints for free through the editor's document-changed publish. So Escape left the screen showing the preview until something else happened to publish, which reads as the cancel not having worked.
  - Fixed the way `CancelShape` and `CancelGradient` already do it: the cancel invalidates the whole canvas (the preview can land anywhere) and publishes directly. The test was shown to fail without the fix.

- [x] **B5** `P2` `transform` Transform shows no live pixels, only the gizmo `evidence: TransformPreviewMovesThePixels`
  - Repro: Ctrl+T, drag a handle. The quad moves; the drawing does not until commit.
  - Cause: the gizmo is view-only chrome and nothing maps the strokes until `CommitTransformAffine`/`Perspective`.
  - Fix: a per-pass matrix on `RenderPass`. The gizmo hands its shape to the view model on every change and the composite draws the moving pixels through it — no geometry is re-mapped until apply, so undo and invariant 1 are untouched. - [x] **B302** `P3` `transform` Transform gizmo box wraps erased ink on a plain Ctrl+T — and an imported drawing cannot be transformed at all `evidence: VisibleDrawingBounds, TransformBoundsTheVisibleDrawingTests, ARubbedOutLineDoesNotStretchTheGizmo, AHalfRubbedLineIsBoxedRoundWhatSurvives, AnImportedDrawingCanBeTransformed, AnImportedDrawingWithOnlyErasedStrokesCanStillBeTransformed, AnEmptyLayerIsStillRefused, UnderAMarqueeTheBaselineIsNotBoxed`

Cosmetic only — everything moves together, so no pixel lands wrong and no ink is resurrected. The region-limited case is already correct, because B297's `MovingWithin` decides what moves and it never returns an erased stroke.
  - **Filed rather than fixed because the obvious fix breaks something else, and that is worth writing down before someone tries it.** Wrapping the strokes in `StrokeRecordCleaner.EffectiveStrokes` makes `Bounds` return null for a frame whose strokes are all erased — and `BeginTransform` reads exactly that null as *"Nothing to transform in this scope."* So a drawing that is a **raster baseline plus erased strokes** would stop being transformable, which is a real loss of function traded for a tidier box.
  - That collision exposes an older gap the fix would have to settle first: `Bounds` measures strokes only, so a frame carrying **nothing but baseline pixels** already cannot be transformed at all today — Ctrl+T on an imported drawing says there is nothing to transform. Both want the same answer, which is that the gizmo should bound *the visible drawing* (baseline included) rather than the stroke record. That is a change to what `Bounds` is for, with the import and crop paths reading it, and it belongs on its own branch with its own tests — not bolted onto a one-line tidy.
  - **Fixed 2026-08-26 on its own branch, and the title was widened first**, because the entry's own second paragraph turned out to name the more serious half. What was filed as a cosmetic box was also *a whole class of document that could not be transformed*, and the two are one fault: `Bounds` measured the record instead of the drawing.
  - **Measured, `main` against the fix**, on the drawings the tests build:

    | | `main` | now |
    | --- | --- | --- |
    | Frame that is nothing but imported pixels | **refused** — *"Nothing to transform in this scope."* | `(0, 0, 960, 540)` |
    | Line drawn to x=700 and rubbed out, one visible line ending near x=200 | right edge **750** | **208** |
    | Line to x=500 with its right end rubbed off | right edge **600** | **308** |
  - **Why the failure went unreported for so long**: refusing an imported drawing produces the same sentence as an honestly empty layer, so it reads as the artist's mistake rather than the application's. `AnEmptyLayerIsStillRefused` keeps that sentence meaning what it says.
  - **`TransformOps.Bounds` is untouched and still measures centrelines**, which is the right place to leave it: the two facts the new answer needs — how far past its points a brush throws paint, and whether a later erasure took a given point away — both live in Raster, and Core cannot see either. That constraint is *why* it measured the record. `VisibleDrawingBounds` sits in Raster beside `StrokePicker`, and `BeginTransform` is its only caller.
  - Ink is judged **per point**, not per stroke, which is what makes a half-rubbed line keep a box round the half you can still see. `StrokeRecordCleaner`'s 85% coverage rule answers that case "the whole line" and a fully-rubbed one "nothing" — the two wrong answers the paragraph above predicted.
  - Under a marquee the baseline is left out on purpose: a region-limited commit leaves baseline pixels where they are, so boxing the page would promise a drag the commit will not make.
  - **Two overreaches in the first version, both caught by tests that already existed, and both worth recording because each looked like an improvement.**
    - **The margin.** Padding by `BrushEngine.ReachBounds` instead of half the brush size is the truer answer to "where can this mark land" — and it moved the box 4 px on an ordinary brush, which moved **guide snapping** with it (B225 ties `SnapBounds` to the box an artist lines up against a guide). `MovingADrawingSnapsItsEdgeToAGuide` came back *expected 300, got 296*. Tightening the box to the paint may be right; it is a change to where a drawing lands rather than to which strokes are counted, and it is not this bug.
    - **Dropping erasures.** Excluding them outright is what shrinks the box in B302's reported case — the eraser sits where the ink it rubbed out sat, so filtering only the ink leaves the box the same size. But a marquee that catches *only* an eraser stroke then measured as empty and offered no handles, for a gesture that plainly changes the drawing: it un-erases at the origin and erases at the destination. B290's `MovingASelectionDoesNotResurrectErasedStrokes` moves exactly that and caught it. The rule is therefore two-tier — the box wraps what you can see, and wraps the rub instead when a rub is all that is moving.

- [x] **B7** `P3` `transform` Transform does not affect gradients `evidence: TransformingAGradient_MovesItsAxis`
  - Repro: lay a gradient, Ctrl+T, move it. The ramp does not follow.
  - Cause: reproduced — it is the region filter, and only with a selection. Without one the ramp does follow. `MajorityInside` counts a stroke's points, and a gradient's two points are the ends of its axis, not a centreline; the ramp colours the whole layer regardless of where they sit. A marquee drawn straight over a visible gradient reported "nothing to transform in this scope".
  - Fix: judge a gradient by what it covers. It joins any region-limited transform and moves whole, which is the rule the filter already followed for everything else.
  - Cost: M

### ui

- [x] **B294** `P1` `ui` A browser drag whose formats are not the three we ask for reads as an empty drop `evidence: DragPayloadFormatTests, AWindowsBrowserDragIsReadThroughItsOwnFormatNames, APictureCarriedInTheDragIsFoundWhateverFormatHoldsIt`
  - Reported 2026-08-24, Pinterest as the site: *"sometimes I am able to drag and drop an image but oftentimes Lightbox states: that drop had no picture in it that Lightbox could read."* That message is the no-candidates branch — not a fetch that failed, but a drag that read as carrying **nothing at all**.
  - **The three format names were an X11 spelling.** `text/uri-list`, `text/html` and the text member are what a Linux browser offers; Windows offers `UniformResourceLocatorW` (UTF-16, trailing NUL) and `HTML Format` (CF_HTML, a header in front of the fragment), macOS `public.url` and `public.html`, Firefox `text/x-moz-url`. Asked for by name, a drag spelled any other way yielded no candidates. It worked when the browser *also* offered a real local file — B282's half — and not otherwise, which is exactly the reported "sometimes".
  - **P1 rather than P2**, unlike its two predecessors: those cost a second drag or a page-URL resolution, this one made the feature unusable on the reporter's main platform for its main use.
  - Fixed by reading the drag's own format list rather than three names, sorting identifiers into the three roles by what their names contain, and treating anything unrecognised as plain text. Two things fell out of the sweep and are worth the lines: **a picture the drag carries itself** — Windows `FileContents`, or a bitmap member — is now used when every URL fails, behind the fetch because it may be a thumbnail and reference is drawn against; and **the format names of a failed drop go to the diagnostics log**, names and sizes only, never the values, because they are the whole diagnosis and no report can supply them from memory.
  - **Driven, not asserted about.** The earlier drop fixes were pinned by regexes over the window's source, because a real drag payload cannot be synthesised here. `IDataTransfer` has two members, so this one has a stand-in instead and the reading is exercised for each platform's real format names. Mutation-proved: restoring the three-name read turns four of them red.

It does — `DataFormat.ToSystemName` returns a platform identifier verbatim, and Win32's `ClipboardFormatRegistry` round-trips whatever `GetClipboardFormatName` gave it, with no mapping back to the media-type spelling. Had it normalised, the whole entry above would have been wrong.

- [x] **B199** `P1` `ui` Every docker-scoped shortcut falls through to the canvas in the running application `evidence: HoverScopeRobustnessTests, LiftingThePenOverTheTimelineKeepsTheTimeline, IStillInsertsAKeyAfterThePenLifts, TheScopeSurvivesTheRowsRebuildingUnderThePointer, MovingToTheCanvasReleasesTheRememberedPanel`
  - Reported from a build, hours after the feature landed green: *"hovering the timeline docker and pressing I still selects the color picker"*. Delete over the Layers docker emptied the layer instead of deleting it - which is the **canvas** binding (`select.clear`), not the docker's. Two different panels, one answer: the scope was the canvas everywhere, so every panel binding silently fell through to the general one.
  - **Why nothing was red.** `ShortcutMap` was correct, the binding was intact (confirmed in Configure), and `HoverShortcutScopeTests` drove the real window and passed. Those tests move the mouse and press a key against a *still* visual tree, which is the one situation the old implementation could not get wrong. The application is never still.
  - Cause, and it is one sentence of code with two weaknesses in it: the scope came from a **cached** element - the source of the last `PointerMoved` - resolved through **derived** bookkeeping, `Docker.ActiveTab`. The cache goes stale when a docker rebuilds the row under a stationary pointer, which the timeline does on every frame change: the remembered visual is detached, its parent chain no longer reaches a docker, and `PanelUnder` returns null. The bookkeeping goes stale if anything writes it without a layout pass.
  - **Both failures land on the canvas, which is why it reads as a feature that was never wired rather than as a fault.** A wrong scope that threw would have been found in minutes; a wrong scope that returns a *plausible* answer just makes the key quietly mean the wrong thing.
  - Fix: ask the dockers what the pointer is over (`IsPointerOver`, which Avalonia maintains on every element under the pointer, ancestors included) instead of remembering it, and read the docker's own `PanelId` instead of its `ActiveTab`. The two ids agree whenever the bookkeeping is right - a tab group's visible control *is* `_panels[active]` - so this changes which of them is trusted, not what a healthy layout resolves to. The cache stays as a fallback.
  - **The lesson for the next feature, not just this one.** The end-to-end tests were written against a static tree and read as thorough because they drove the real window. What they could not see is the application's ordinary condition: things moving. A UI test that never rebuilds anything under the pointer is testing a screenshot. `ForgetHoveredElementForTests` exists because that state cannot be reached by moving a headless mouse.
  - P1 on blocks work x always: the feature is advertised in the manual and does not work at all outside a still window. Cost: S
  - **The first fix was refuted from the build, same day** - *"Still does not work"* - and the refutation carries the real mechanism. `IsPointerOver` is a live flag, and the owner draws with a **pen**: a pen leaves proximity a centimetre off the tablet, between pointing at a panel and pressing the key with the other hand, and the proximity leave kills every live pointer signal at once. The first fix changed *which* live signal was read; both die together. A mouse never leaves proximity, which is why no mouse-driven test - headless or the real app under Xvfb, where the whole flow was verified working - could reproduce what the tablet reproduces every time.
  - **The X11 run added the other half**: after the pointer left the window, a docker's `IsPointerOver` was observed stale-*true* (`window.IsPointerOver=False`, `Timeline over=True`). So the live flags are unreliable in both directions once the pointer is gone, and the second fix gates them on the pointer being known present.
  - **The mechanism that survives is a decision remembered from the last move**: the panel id is resolved at `PointerMoved` time - while the element under the pointer is guaranteed attached - and kept on `PointerExited`. The next move overwrites it, so moving to the canvas releases the panel, and lifting the pen does not, which is the distinction between *the pointer going away* and *the artist pointing somewhere else*. The artist-visible rule the manual now states: **keys go where you last pointed.**
  - **The proximity state cannot be staged headlessly against the old code** - a headless move to "outside" is still a move and overwrites the very memory under test, and headless cannot clear a child's `IsPointerOver` without one. `SimulateProximityLossForTests` stages it for the new mechanism; the evidence against the old one is the artist's tablet and the X11 trace, and this entry says so rather than pretending a red test exists.

- [x] **B135** `P1` `ui` Switching between tabbed dockers kills the application `evidence: TabSwitchCrashTests, SwitchingBackAndForthBetweenTabsDoesNotCrash, TheOtherPairInTheReportBehavesTheSameWay, TheDockerShowingAfterASwitchIsTheOneInTheStrip`

An infinite loop rather than a crash — it presents as a freeze with no stack trace. `Docker.ShowTabs` now sets both under a flag that says "the host is writing the answer in, not the artist choosing one". Assigning in the other order also works, for exactly as long as nobody swaps two lines.

Nothing drove the *ListBox*, which is what a click actually touches, so the whole re-entrant path had no coverage. The new tests set `SelectedItem`, and the first run of them crashed the test host with exit code 134 rather than failing an assertion. That is the third time in this redesign that the model was right and the thing in front of the artist was not.
  - Cost: S

- [x] **B48** `P1` `ui` Docking a floating panel crashed the application `evidence: FloatingPanelTests, APanelCanBeTornOutAndDockedAgainWithoutCrashing, ADockedPanelIsInTheStripRatherThanParkedInThePool, FloatingAndDockingRepeatedlyStaysStable`
  - Repro: drag a panel out so it floats in its own window, then drag its header back onto a dock zone. `NullReferenceException`, and the manual promised this worked.
  - **Two bugs on one line, and the crash was the less serious of them.** `CloseFloating` did `Park(window.Release())`. Docking a floating panel reaches it through `ApplyDockLayout`, which detaches every panel it is about to restrip — so the window's `Content` was already gone and `Release` had nothing to give back.

The exception surfaced two frames later in `MainWindow.Detach`, a long way from the line that was wrong — which is the general lesson worth keeping. A `!` does not assert; it suppresses, and it moves the failure somewhere less informative.
  - The second bug is what a crash fix alone would have left: even without the throw, parking whatever the window handed back would have pulled the freshly docked panel **straight out of the strip it was just dropped into** and stored it in the pool — present in the layout and invisible. Five of the six fail against the old code, and the failure cascades: the crash left the layout half-applied and took nine tests down with it.
  - Cost: S

- [x] **B330** `P2` `ui` The stroke-to-screen report is mean-and-worst only, so its numbers can name the wrong phase `evidence: EveryPhaseOfTheChainCarriesAMedian, ADistortedMeanIsNamedRatherThanLeftToBeNoticed`
  - **`Tally` was written for exactly this and had been applied everywhere except the chain the lag is read from.** Its own remarks record why: a capture read *"building each frame 8.27 ms, describing it 5.34"* and the report concluded the cost was in the pass list — when a single 2,062 ms stall was the entire figure and the true cost was **0.16 ms**. The frame build got a median and a distortion warning out of that. `StrokeToScreen.Segment` did not, so `stamping the dabs`, `event -> publish`, `publish -> drawn`, `PEN -> SCREEN` and `TIP -> SCREEN` stayed mean-and-worst — the five numbers an artist's lag is actually diagnosed from.
  - **It was not theoretical.** Captures of 2026-08-27 carry `stamping the dabs mean 4.8 ms worst 50.87`, `event -> publish mean 55.2 worst 2807`, `PEN -> SCREEN mean 93.72 worst 3374`. Those means are minutes of drawing plus one stall each, and every conclusion drawn from them this session had to be re-checked by hand against something else that happened to disagree.
  - **Fixed by giving each phase a `Tally` rather than a total and a worst**, so the median comes for free along with the percentiles, and by printing the median first. The section also names which phases are distorted rather than leaving a reader to divide: *"a stall is doing the talking in: …"*, the same warning the frame build already carried.
  - **First capture with medians, 2026-08-27 14:04, and it caught three numbers this session had been quoting wrong.**

    | | median | mean | mean/median |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | stamping the dabs | **2.45 ms** | 4.22 | 1.7x |
    | event -> publish | **18.57 ms** | 42.72 | 2.3x |
    | `PEN -> SCREEN` | **47.20 ms** | 73.93 | 1.6x |
    | `publish -> drawn` | 29.51 ms | 29.64 | 1.0x |

    The claim *"the stamp is 4.8 ms against a pen delivering every 5.46, so the UI thread is near saturation during a fast stroke"* was argued from that mean and used to reason about where work should go. On the median it is **2.45 ms against 5.36 — 46%, not 79%.** Not saturated. `PEN -> SCREEN` is 47 ms typical rather than the 94 that had been quoted. Only `publish -> drawn` was honest throughout, because it is the vsync floor and has no stalls in it — which is itself a useful check on B321.
  - **Found while auditing B322's stamp instrumentation**, after that entry had measured wrong four times and the owner asked for the numbers to be double-checked. The audit's own rule applies here: **an instrument that reaches the report needs a test like any other output**, so this closes on tests that assert the median is carried and that a distorted mean is announced — not on the report merely compiling.

Underneath it, **seven sibling bars that gate their inner panel rather than the control** sat visible at zero width, each still costing a 14px gap: 98px of a 273px row spent on nothing. Fixed in `OverflowBar` (a child wanting no width now costs no gap), plus the group split so the face never parks.

The Tool options docker had no text section at all. Fonts loaded only when the font button was clicked, so its label read *"Loading…"* until an artist pressed the control that was telling them it was not ready.

The mechanism was live-pose painting (Q101) taken one step too far: heat dots and dab hit-tests recomputed the posed points from the *current* weights per dab, so painting influence toward a bone moved the points toward that bone's transform — the artist was aiming at a target their own gesture pushed away — and `EndWeightStroke` invalidated the rigged frames, so the ink jumped on commit.
  - The decision, from the owner in two lines: weight paint must not influence lines directly (bones influence lines; painting only edits how much), and the overlay only recolors — no pushing. So the session's geometry is frozen: captured per frame + playhead when the brush is armed, dropped by every rig edit and by disarming, and weight edits explicitly do not drop it. The rigged-frame invalidation *and* the rig-index rebuild both defer to disarm — deferring only one would re-key a newly-bound stroke's frame and re-render it mid-session, the same jump through a different door.
  - The pixel test is the spec: pose moves ink (sanity), the weight commit moves zero bytes, disarming moves the ink to its new deformation.

- [x] **B241** `P2` `ui` The cursor never says what a press on the gizmo, a box or a guide handle would do `evidence: CanvasCursorChoice, ResizeAt, ACornerHandleScalesAlongItsOwnDiagonal, AnEdgeHandleScalesAcrossItselfRatherThanAlongItself, InsideTheBoxMovesAndOutsideItTurns, ARotatedViewSwingsTheHandleCursorsWithIt, APerspectiveCornerIsNotAScale, TheCursorHoldsForTheWholeDragRatherThanFollowingThePointer, AHeightScalesTopResizesItAndItsPostMovesIt, GuidesSayNothingWhenTheyCannotBePickedUp, TheCameraFramesThreeGripsReadAsThreeDifferentGestures, ARolledCameraZoomsAlongItsOwnDiagonal, OnlyASelectedReferenceBoxOffersItsCorners, DraggingTheCanvasItselfShowsTheHand, AKeyOrAToolChangeReDecidesTheCursorWithNoPointerEventToHangItOn, WithThePointerOffTheCanvasThereIsNothingToReAskAbout`
  - Reported as a request rather than a fault — *"update all on canvas icons based on their actions: scaling shows a double-sided arrow, moving shows the four-way, and I bet there are more that I am missing"* — and there were. **Twelve grabbable things, one of which had a cursor.**
  - **The gizmo is the worst of them, because it is six gestures inside one box.** Krita's layout: pivot, four corner handles, four edge handles, inside-is-move, outside-is-rotate. It drew the same square handle for a scale and for a perspective corner, and the pointer stayed whatever the toolbar had put there — so which of the six a press would take was discoverable only by trying it. The camera frame is the same shape of problem one gizmo along: pan, zoom and rotate grips, all silent.
  - **One of them was not silent but wrong.** A height scale's top rung *resizes* it — the gesture that says "this character is this tall" — and it wore the four-way move cursor like every other guide grab, so it was indistinguishable from sliding the chart sideways.
  - **Two writers of one property, which is why this could not be fixed in place.** `UpdateGuideHoverCursor` set `Cursor` on hover and the `PointerIntent` handler set it on tool change, and the later one won whatever it happened to be. `CanvasCursorNow` is the single writer now; the guide method keeps only the emphasis, which is the half that was always guide-specific.
  - **The order inside it is the feature.** Live gestures are asked first and the hit test second, which is what makes the owner's two rules fall out rather than needing machinery: the cursor **holds for the whole drag** (a hover test cannot overwrite a drag, because it never runs while one is live), and a **held modifier shows what it would do** (`RefreshCanvasCursor()` re-asks at the last pointer position when something other than the pointer changed — a tool swap, a gizmo appearing, Ctrl going down under a still hand).
  - **Angles are measured through `DocToView`, not in the record.** Invariant 5: the view can be zoomed, rotated and mirrored, so a handle's direction on screen is not its direction in the document. Every angle here takes two points through the view matrix and reads the result, which is right under all three without knowing any of them exist — `ARotatedViewSwingsTheHandleCursorsWithIt` is what stops that regressing to the version that looks correct on an unrotated canvas.
  - **A corner's angle comes from the opposite corner, not from the pivot**, and that is not arbitrary: the pivot is draggable, so measuring from it would swing every corner cursor while the box itself had not moved. An edge's angle is its *normal*, because an edge grows the box perpendicular to itself — pointing the arrow along the edge is the version that looks right in a screenshot and is wrong under the hand.
  - **The choice is separated from the bitmap** (`CanvasCursorChoice`), because rendering one wants a render surface a headless run has not got: a test that asked for the `Cursor` object would be asserting against `PointerCursors`' catch-and-fall-back rather than against the answer. The rendering half is one switch with nothing in it to get wrong.
  - **Drawn cursors at the exact angle, which was the owner's call against the recommendation — Q107 records what it costs.** The platform's eight cover 45° steps and inherit the user's cursor theme; ours are right at every angle and inherit nothing, including the accessibility cursor-size setting. Cached mod 180, because a double-headed arrow has no front and rendering a bitmap per pointer move is the per-event cost invariant 6 rules out.
  - **Two grabs are still undifferentiated and this entry is not hiding it.** A path node, handle or segment under the white arrow all show `PickRecords`, and the Width tool's grab shows `Precise`. Both need a *non-mutating* hit test the canvas can ask on hover, and the two that exist — `GrabPathPart` and `GrabWidthAt` — enter isolation and change the selection as a side effect of being asked. That is a second objective (a query split out of each grab), not an "and" on this branch.
  - Each test was proved by mutation: dropping the gizmo's hover branch, the edge normal, the `Selected` gate on reference boxes, the panning check, the height-scale test and the held-key re-ask each fail exactly the tests that name them; measuring the angles in document space fails only the rotated-view one; moving the in-flight gizmo check below the hit test fails only the hold-during-drag one; and making a perspective corner a scale fails only `APerspectiveCornerIsNotAScale`.

- [x] **B230** `P2` `ui` Save current workspace forks an “(edited)” copy instead of overwriting `evidence: WorkspaceStoreTests, SaveCurrentOverwritesABuiltInInPlace, ResetOnABuiltInRestoresHowItShipped, SaveAsWithTheUnchangedNameMakesAnEditedCopy, WorkspaceMenuTests, TheSaveCurrentMenuItem_OverwritesInPlace_AndAddsNoTab`
  - Reported by the owner: pressing **Save current workspace** created a new workspace with “(edited)” trailing behind it, rather than saving the one on screen.
  - Cause: `SaveCurrent` was `SaveAs(SelectedName)`, and the store refuses to overwrite a built-in — reset needed the stored copy to reset *to* — so saving while in any built-in forked "Default (edited)" and silently switched to it. None was found; the remaining reproduction paths are a binary built before the merge, or the forks the old behaviour left behind (a pre-fix “Default (edited)” tab stays until deleted by hand — right-click it ▸ *Delete this workspace*). The one genuine confusion the recurrence surfaced is fixed: the *Save as new workspace…* dialog opened titled plain “Save workspace”, which reads as save-current on a dialog whose unchanged prefilled name now deliberately forks “(edited)”.
  - Cost: S

  - Reported as "no clear indication of what bone is selected", and the indication was never the problem — the *selection* was. `BoneRows` is rebuilt on every rig change; the panel's two-way-bound picker answered each rebuild by clearing itself and writing `SelectedBoneId = null` back into the view model. - [x] **B227** `P2` `ui` The ledger gate cannot tell a renumber from a deletion, so its own --fix trips it `evidence: ARenumberedEntryIsNotReportedAsLost, ARenumberDoesNotHideARealLossBesideIt`
  - **The tool tripped over its own advice.** `lost_ids` compared ids alone, so an entry that was *renumbered* — still present, under a different number — looked exactly like one that had been deleted. That is precisely what `ids --fix` does, what the message printed beside the loss recommends in as many words ("keep both and renumber"), and what `.githooks/pre-push` runs on your behalf. Three parts of the same mechanism producing a state the fourth refuses.
  - **On a merge it was permanent, not momentary.** The pre-renumber commit stays a merge parent for ever, so the vanished id is missing from every future comparison against that parent. Once a branch renumbered a question and merged, its gate could never go green again — no amount of further work clears it, and `LIGHTBOX_ALLOW_LEDGER_DELETION=1` is the wrong tool because nothing was deleted.
  - **Found by hitting it.** Resolving a real ledger conflict on `fix/canvas/move-snapping`: main's parallel session had taken Q98, `ids --fix` renumbered this branch's to Q99 exactly as designed, and the gate then refused the result.
  - **The title settles it, and both sides already carry one.** An id that vanished while its title reappeared under a different id has moved; only a title that is gone as well is a loss. Compared normalised, because a renumber rewrites the heading around the id.
  - **Comparing titles rather than recording renames is the point.** A rename ledger would work only for renumbers the tool performed, and the whole reason the message says "keep both and renumber" is that somebody resolving a conflict at 2am will do it by hand. This defends that case identically.
  - `ARenumberDoesNotHideARealLossBesideIt` is what stops the fix degenerating into "stop reporting losses": one entry moves and another genuinely goes in the same comparison, and only the one that went is named.

Each captured it, performed the gesture, and asserted it had not changed. It is a constant: they were green whether the gesture recorded a step or not.
  - **The title said four and there were six.** The first sweep matched `var steps = vm.UndoDepth`; three more used `var undos`. Recorded because the count in a bug title is a claim like any other.
  - **All six were asserting true things** — a guide drag that went nowhere, a cancelled transform, a hold that was not keyed, a placement click that did not move — and every one still passes against `RecordedStepCount`, which counts the undo line for real. That is the good outcome and it is also why this survived: nothing was ever red, so nothing drew attention to it.
  - **A test that cannot fail is worse than no test**, because it is counted as coverage. The name is the fix as much as the property is: `UndoDepth` reads like a depth and is a capacity, which is what made six authors reach for it.
  - **Fixed in B223's branch rather than its own**, which the one-objective rule usually forbids. The exception is the one that rule already makes for a P2 found in the blast radius: it is a two-line seam plus six one-line call sites, all in tests the branch was already editing, and splitting it would have meant a branch whose diff is six identifiers.

Only the white arrow said what it was about to take: `HoverPathAt` was invoked under `CanvasToolMode.PathEdit` and nowhere else. So the one tool that reaches *into* a line previewed its geometry, and the two that act on *all* of it showed nothing at all.

That is B172 exactly, one tool along, and B172 was filed as a defect and fixed for the white arrow. What hid it is that every existing width test in `PathEditingTests` calls `BeginPathEdit` by hand before reaching for the tool, so the suite only ever exercised it from inside a session somebody else had opened.

A width guessed for a layout decided at runtime is a width that will be wrong; the general form is that **a magic number and an adaptive layout cannot both own the same dimension.**

A new `RailSplitter` resizes it against the grid's **starred** column instead of its neighbour, which is where the width was always going to come from. A drag writes pixels, and the pixels are how the reflow tells a width the artist chose from one it is free to pick; three columns and the labelled list still need that drag, exactly as the manual has always said. Cost: S
  - **The self-sizing rail all but removes the shrink direction, and that is the right trade rather than a loss.** It now opens a few pixels above its own `MinWidth`, so there is almost nothing left to drag inwards — because there is nothing left to reclaim. Growing was always the direction that meant something (two columns, three, labels) and it was the one that did not work.

  - Cause: Fluent's theme padding for text controls is `10,6,6,5` — eleven vertical pixels, which in a 22px field leaves less room than one line box. The probe that found it printed the template's padding where ours was expected.

Fields take a white **tint**, so they lift whatever they land on — an opaque `SurfaceElevated` field is right on a panel and *invisible* on a dialog, and the dialog is the case somebody would only find by opening one. Borders take `BorderStrong`. Anything that floats takes the elevated surface, like dialogs.
  - **Why B128's fix could not have covered this, which is the part worth keeping.** A `ColorPaletteResources` entry is a *seed*: the theme derives a family from it, so `Accent` corrected fifty controls at once and it felt like the whole problem was solved. These are *leaves* — nothing is computed from them, so nothing else moves when they do, and there is no way to find them except by asking the theme what it currently resolves and reading the list. The probe that produced this entry took two minutes and should have run during B128.

The test was deleted rather than adjusted because the rule was reversed rather than refined, and `FieldShapeTests.AFieldIsAWellRatherThanARaisedSurface` owns it now - including the half that survived the reversal, that **hover must lift**, which is where Fluent's `#66000000` against `#99000000` was actually wrong. The anchor now names that test, so the checkbox derives from a guard that exists.
  - **What was verified before ticking it, rather than inferred from the anchors resolving.** Each half of the report, against the theme as it stands: the bright wire is gone (`TextControlBorderBrush` resolves to `BorderStrongBrush`); the hover no longer dims (asserted by the test above); context menus, combo drop-downs and flyouts take `SurfaceElevated` rather than Fluent's `#ff2b2b2b` (`NothingThatFloatsKeepsFluentsGrey`). The one part of the report that is *not* fixed is the headline - fields really are darker than what surrounds them - and that is the owner's reversal rather than the original defect surviving.

- [x] **B128** `P2` `ui` The palette never reached the theme, so every stock control still paints Windows blue `evidence: PaletteTests, TheThemeAgreesWithThePalette, TheThemePaletteIsWrittenInHexOnPurpose`
  - Repro: open any docker. The eye and lock toggles, every slider thumb, checkboxes, radios, focus rings and list selection are `#0078D7`. Open any dialog: pure black. Sampled, not squinted at — the opacity slider read `#FF6A3D` on the track and `#0078D7` on the thumb, twelve pixels apart.

The application wore two colour systems, and one control wore both at once.
  - Fix: `<FluentTheme.Palettes><ColorPaletteResources x:Key="Dark" Accent="#7B61FF" RegionColor="#222634" />`. Two properties, and they replace roughly fifty setters that would each have had to be written and then remembered. The `ToggleSwitch` and `CheckBox` accent setters were deleted in the same commit — with the theme accent right, they were a second opinion about what "on" looks like.
  - **Why stage 1 shipped green with half the system missing.** Both halves were internally consistent: every token resolved, no view named a hex, and the theme was perfectly coherent in its own colours. Nothing was in conflict, so nothing failed. A colour system is only as wide as the surfaces that resolve *through* it, and no assertion about the tokens can enumerate which surfaces those are.

- [x] **B127** `P2` `ui` Every tab in a group looks the same, so the strip never says which panel is showing `evidence: WorkspaceTests, TheTabShowingIsTheOneThatLooksLikeItIsShowing`

Handing an enum to `SelectedItem` is not an error — **nothing simply ever matches**, so the strip has no selection at all and `:selected` never applies to anything.

Plus the `:selected` foreground moved onto the ContentPresenter, because the theme sets one there and it beats anything inherited from the item; without that the active tab looked right by the theme's accident and would have changed with it.

What was wrong was the one thing no assertion looked at. It took a screenshot to see, and then a pixel measurement to believe: all three labels read `#9AA1B2` exactly, which is the sort of coincidence that is never a coincidence.

- [x] **B123** `P2` `ui` Switching or saving a workspace silently resets rulers and guide visibility `evidence: DockLayoutTests, CloningALayoutKeepsTheRulersAndGuideFlags, ACloneSharesNothingWithTheOriginal`

  - **Why nobody filed it.** Nothing fails. Three booleans quietly return to their defaults, which reads as the application forgetting a preference rather than as a bug with a place to look — and forgetting is the kind of thing software is expected to do a bit of.
  - Found while planning tabbed dockers, because tab state would have been a new field on the same type and would have dropped through the same hole. A new feature inheriting an old bug and getting blamed for it is the usual way this is discovered, and it is a worse way.

- [x] **B119** `P2` `ui` The crash reporter does not listen where crashes actually come from `evidence: CrashScenarioTests, TheReporterListensOnAllThreeChannelsAFailureCanArriveBy, TheDispatcherHandlerRecordsWithoutChangingWhatTheAppDoes, TheTriggersAreAbsentUntilDiagnosticsAreTurnedOn, EveryMenuEntryNamesAScenarioThatExists, TheDestructiveOnesAskFirstAndTheHarmlessOnesDoNot, TheSurvivableFailureIsSurvivableAndLandsInTheLog`
  - B117 registered `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException` and `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`. Neither is where a desktop application usually dies. **An exception thrown in a click handler, a pointer handler or a binding callback runs under the dispatcher**, and Avalonia 12 has its own machinery for those — `Dispatcher.UnhandledException`, documented as firing for anything uncaught "during execution of a delegate by way of `Invoke` or `InvokeAsync`", with an internal handler that runs unless a subscriber marks the exception handled.
  - Found by planning how to *test* the reporter rather than by a report, which is the useful part: B117 shipped, looked complete, had a test suite, and nothing in it could have noticed. The gap is only visible from the question "how would I see this work".
  - **What is not known, and is not guessed at.** Whether an unhandled dispatcher exception eventually reaches the AppDomain handler could not be determined from the shipped artefacts — the ref assemblies carry no IL and there is no decompiler here. It may be that B117 was accidentally fine. Registering the dispatcher handler makes that question stop mattering, which is the right outcome either way for the one component whose whole job is to miss nothing.
  - Fix: `CrashReporter.Install` registers `Dispatcher.UIThread.UnhandledException` and writes the report there too, **without marking it handled**. Marking it handled would make the app survive crashes it currently dies from — a change to what the application does, smuggled in under a change to what it records. `TheDispatcherHandlerRecordsWithoutChangingWhatTheAppDoes` asserts the absence directly.
  - **And the scenarios that found it, kept.** Seven deliberate failures under `Help ▸ Trigger a test failure`, absent unless the diagnostics toggle is on, each travelling the real path rather than faking a report. They cover the three handlers, the survivable log, the inner-exception chain, the console plumbing on its own, and a hard kill that proves the honest negative — `Environment.FailFast` writes nothing, which is what this ledger already claimed and nobody could show.
  - Warning behaviour is per scenario, at the owner's instruction: nothing that leaves the app running interrupts, anything that ends it asks when the drawing is dirty, and the hard kill always asks. A tester who is prompted every time learns to click through the prompt.
  - **And the reports gained line numbers, which is half of what makes one actionable.** The bundle published with `DebugType=none` — no debug information at all, so `ex.ToString()` named methods and stopped there. Changed to `embedded`, which puts the information inside the assembly rather than in a `.pdb` beside it, so it survives single-file publishing without adding a file to a root that is deliberately four. **Measured rather than assumed: +0.4 MB on the executable and no change at all once zipped**, against the 44 MB the app publish already costs. `portable` would also have worked and would have dropped loose `.pdb` files into the root, undoing B116 — `CrashReportsCanNameTheLineTheyCameFrom` refuses both alternatives by name, so the cheaper-looking one is declined on purpose rather than by luck.
  - Worth noting when this was caught: the caveat had already been written into the checklist as a thing to expect, and it took the owner asking *"should we add this first?"* to turn an accepted limitation back into a question. It was accepted because it was measured against nothing.
  - What the evidence covers: the registration, the non-handling, the gating, and that the menu and the scenario list cannot drift. Whether a report appears on screen is Windows — `MANUAL_TESTING.md` owns it, and now has a line per scenario in place of the old "rename `libSkiaSharp.dll`", which was cruder and tested one path out of seven. Cost: S

- [x] **B117** `P2` `ui` A crash leaves nothing behind at all — no file, no message, no stack `evidence: DiagnosticLogTests, ACrashIsWrittenDownWithTheBuildItCameFrom, TheCauseUnderneathIsNotLost, TheNextRunIsToldOnceAndThenNotAgain, ASurvivableFailureIsRecordedOncePerContext, AnUnwritableFolderIsSurvivedRatherThanThrown, TheLogSitsBesideTheOtherAppData`
  - Repro: make the app throw where nothing catches. The window vanishes. No dialog, no file, nothing in the app data folder to look at — the artist's whole account of it is "it closed".
  - Cause: nothing was ever registered. No `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException`, no `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`, no try/catch around startup — searched, not assumed. The process died and the runtime printed a trace to a console.
  - **B115 removed the last place that trace could land.** While the app was a console program the stack went to the terminal, which is thin but not nothing. As a GUI program there is no console at all, so fixing the terminal window quietly took away the only crash diagnostic that existed. The two belong together.
  - The gap is wider than crashes. `App` launches the start screen as `_ = window.OfferStartScreenAsync()`, a fire-and-forget whose fault nobody observes and which is dropped in silence at collection. `TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` catches that class, and is now registered.
  - **B52 is what this costs when it is missing**: a 16-second freeze during brush import where *"the main window becomes transparent as if about to crash"* — and it was not crashing. Telling "hung" from "died" took a person and a debugger; it is one file now.
  - Fix: `DiagnosticLog` writes to `%AppData%/Lightbox/logs/`, beside the autosave copy the manual already points at. A crash report names the time, the OS, the runtime and — the part that makes it actionable — the exact build, because the SDK already stamps `AssemblyInformationalVersion` as `1.0.0+<sha>` and *"1.0.0"* identifies nothing when every build says it. `CrashReporter` writes the file first and only then tries to speak, so a failing dialog cannot lose a report that already succeeded.
  - **The dialog is Win32 rather than Avalonia deliberately.** This runs when something has already gone wrong, and the likeliest thing to be wrong is the UI. Asking a broken toolkit to render a window explaining that it broke is how a crash reporter becomes the second crash. `MessageBox` needs nothing of ours to be working; `FileReveal` — which exists already and already promises not to throw — opens the folder.
  - **The canvas breadcrumb moved here rather than being left beside it.** `CanvasControl.LogDiag` was a real logger already, but it wrote to `%TEMP%/lightbox-canvas.log` — a second location nobody would think of and one the OS may empty. Finishing with two places to look would have been worse than starting with one. Its once-per-context de-duplication is kept, and the reason is kept with it.
  - **What is still not covered**, so nobody reads more into this than it says: a hard kill, a power cut, or a native crash inside Skia never reaches managed code and leaves nothing. The autosave copy is the only thing that survives those, and *nothing reads it back* — recovery is still "open the file yourself". The marker this writes is the missing ingredient for a start screen that offers it, and that is a separate objective. Cost: S

- [x] **B115** `P2` `ui` A terminal window opens beside the app and closing it kills the app `evidence: WindowsSubsystemTests, TheAppShipsAsAGuiProgramSoNoConsoleWindowOpensBesideIt, TheStdioProgramsStayConsolePrograms, TheOptInTracesStillHaveSomewhereToPrint`
  - Repro: run `Lightbox.App.exe` from the Windows bundle. A console window opens alongside it and stays for the life of the app; closing that window takes the app down with it, mid-drawing, with no save prompt.
  - Cause: one word. `Lightbox.App.csproj` declared `<OutputType>Exe</OutputType>`, which builds a **console-subsystem** apphost. Windows gives a console-subsystem process a console when it has none, and the process is tied to it — a close on the console is a close on the app. `WinExe` builds a GUI-subsystem apphost and is never given one.

Both readings agree the attach is harmless and agree the traces work with it; they disagree only about whether it was needed. Worth writing down, because the tempting future edit is to delete it as dead code, and the evidence for that is not in hand either.
  - `Lightbox.Mcp` and `Lightbox.Bench` stay `Exe` deliberately: a stdio server and a CLI harness want the console the app does not. The tests assert both halves, so "fix" the wrong one and it fails.
  - **What the evidence covers, and what it cannot.** The tests close the *declaration* — that the project still says `WinExe`, that the two tools still say `Exe`, and that the traces still have somewhere to print. Whether a console window appears is a Win32 fact no Linux runner can observe, so `MANUAL_TESTING.md` owns that half. Worth asserting the declaration anyway: the regression is a one-word edit and is invisible in review until somebody runs the bundle on Windows. Cost: S

- [x] **B98** `P2` `ui` Dirtiness is asserted by each edit path rather than derived, so paths keep getting it wrong `evidence: DirtyRevisionTests, ADocumentAtItsSavedRevisionIsNotDirty, TrimmingTheUndoStackDoesNotFakeACleanDocument, UndoingBackToTheSavedStateClearsTheBadge, RedoingToTheSavedStateIsStillSaved`
  - The shape behind B79, B94, B95, B96 and B97 — four spurious sets and one impossible clear, all in one week, all because **`IsDirty` records "a code path ran" rather than "this differs from disk"**. Any path that forgets to ask whether anything changed sets it, and there will always be more of them.
  - **`DocumentEditor` already has the counter.** Edits go through a `Stack<IEditStep>` — a command log, not snapshots — so dirtiness can be derived: record the revision at the top of the undo stack when the document is saved, and it is dirty exactly while the current top differs.
  - **Use a per-step sequence number, not `_undo.Count`.** `MaxUndo = 64` trims the bottom of the stack, so a depth comparison reads clean on the 65th edit after a save — the trap is silent and the failure is lost work. A monotonic revision on each step is unaffected by trimming, and an empty stack is revision zero.
  - Fixes each reported symptom without a special case: a no-op drag and a focus change push no step, choosing a brush pushes no step (Q24 becomes structural rather than remembered), and undoing back to the saved revision goes clean.
  - **Honest limit**: revision equality is not content equality. Edit, undo, then make a different edit that happens to produce the same document, and it still reads dirty. That is the standard trade and it is wrong far less often than a flag.

  - **Not a missed clear — the flag cannot represent this.** `IsDirty` is a boolean set by edits and cleared only by a save, so *returning to the saved state* has no way to be expressed. Every undo-to-clean has the same shape.

  - `evidence: manual`, for the reason B78 records: the dialog and the picker are not reachable headlessly.
  - **Fixed.** The dialog returns a three-way choice, Save reuses `SaveOrSaveAsAsync`, the closing tab is activated first, and a cancelled picker abandons the close. Cost: S
  - **Ticked 2026-08-06 after re-reading the code rather than the entry.** It sat open with the fix described twice because `evidence: manual` cannot close itself and nobody had confirmed it. `OnCloseTabClicked` and `ConfirmDiscardAsync` are in `MainWindow.axaml.cs` with all four properties the entry claims — three-way choice, Save default, closing tab activated first, cancelled picker abandoning the close. The manual confirmation that remains is only that the dialog *looks* right; the behaviour behind it is present and readable.

  - Reported with three examples and they are not the same feature: a reference added to one document is still shown after switching to a document that has none; brush and fill settings carry across; a zoom set in one document applies to the next.
  - **What is right already is the useful half of the report.** Layers, Timeline and the character sheet do follow the document. So the shape of the fix exists — the defect is that the rest of the dockers and the tool state read from one process-wide store instead of from the active document, and `BrushStateIsolated` in the test suite exists because that store is process-wide.
  - The reporter's own framing is the acceptance criterion: a new document that is not part of a project should not be showing the project docker, project symbols or another document's brush. Cost: L
  - **Measured before designing, and two of the three examples were already right.** A probe through the real view model: `ReferenceSheetsView` returns 1 for a document with a sheet and 0 for one without; `ActiveReference` reads `Scene.References` off the active document; the project docker is gated in `MainWindow.IsPanelUsable` on `HasProject`, so a standalone document never shows it. `Workspace.ProjectPanelVisible` is `true` with no project and that is *not* the defect it looks like — the workspace keeps the slot and the view leaves the panel out, which is what lets closing and reopening a project restore the arrangement.
  - **The brush example is answered against, by Q9, and building it would have been the mistake.** Q9 considered per-document brush *first* and rejected it the same day: it "fixes the page you already drew and leaves the next one starting from whatever you last used elsewhere". The store is `ProjectManifest.Brush`, chosen by project type, and with no project the effective scope is Global — so the brush carrying between two loose documents is the shipped decision, not a bug. `TheBrushDoesNotFollowTheDocument_BecauseQ9SaysSo` guards the decision, and fails if a `Brush` field ever appears on `DocumentScopedState` — reinstating a rejected design under a second name being the `BlendOrNormal` failure mode.
  - **So what was actually broken was two things, and one of them was invisible rather than merely untidy.** The canvas framing (zoom, rotation, mirror, pan) lived in four private fields on a `CanvasControl` that outlives every document it shows, so a face framed at 156% opened the next drawing at 156%. And `ActiveReferenceIndex` was one shared int, bounds-checked against the *active* document's strips — so a document holding one reference, visited after a document where strip 2 was selected, resolved `ActiveReference` to null and **showed no reference at all**. The reference was there and could not be seen. That one is not in the report; the probe found it.
  - **Fixed.** `DocumentScopedState` on `DocumentTab` holds frame, layer, reference index and a nullable framing — nullable so "never looked at" opens fitted while "left at 100%" is restored verbatim. It absorbs `SavedFrameIndex`/`SavedLayerIndex`, which were the same idea as two loose ints. `CanvasControl.Framing` reads and writes the transform as one value, `MainViewModel.TabSwitched(leaving, arriving)` carries it, and the window subscribes because the view model must not know what a canvas is. Invariant 5 holds: nothing touches the `Doc` and nothing is serialized, so reopening a file next session opens it fitted.
  - **The tool is deliberately still global**, and this is the weakest of the three calls: a tool is a mode of the hand rather than a property of the drawing, and every comparable application keeps it that way. One field and one line if that turns out to be wrong.
  - Cost: L estimated, **S–M actual** — because two thirds of the report was already built or already decided. The estimate was made from the report rather than from a probe, which is the lesson worth keeping.

Pointer wiring in `CanvasControl` to `PressRig`/`DragRig` comes with the painter. Cost: M
  - P2 rather than P1: it blocks a whole advertised workflow, but it damages nothing and corrupts no art — every anchor and shape already authored through the API or the file still round-trips and still exports.

Allocation grows linearly at ~0.26 KB per mark per press (11.6 KB at 50, 156 KB at 600) and is worth a look only once the overlay is wired to hover.

That comment is now true.

Removing it exposed the second — the overlay-bar rule in `Density.axaml` sat *above* the plain `Button` and `ToggleButton` rules, and **Avalonia resolves competing styles by order, not by specificity**, so the generic `Padding="8,0"` won and the content box shrank to **10 px**.
